children.title: Element Channels
children.top_down_role: Channels linking selected collection entries to value variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Element Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Channeling an index variable to the selected entry of a finite array.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) be an array whose entries are constants or finite-domain variables, let \(i\) have domain contained in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(v\) be a finite-domain variable. The element channel is the constraint
\[
\operatorname{element}(i,a,v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=a_i.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), it enforces \(i=k\Rightarrow v=a_k\); conversely, any assigned pair \((i,v)=(k,w)\) is feasible exactly when \(w=a_k\) under the same assignment to variable entries of \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An element channel equates a value variable with the array entry selected by an index variable.
assumptions_latex: \(D(i)\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Every variable entry of \(a\) has a finite domain.

notation.meaning: Indexed array of constants or variables.

review_flags: authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The element-channel definition matches the leaf and is mathematically standard, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Indexing Channels
children.top_down_role: Channels linking index variables to positional model structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Indexing Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-hot Boolean representation of a finite-domain index variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(i\) be a variable with domain contained in \(K=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and introduce Boolean variables \(b_k\in\{0,1\}\) for \(k\in K\). The exact indexing channel is
\[
b_k=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i=k\qquad(k\in K),
\]
together with
\[
\sum_{k\in K}b_k=1.
\]
Consequently, each value of \(i\) determines a unique one-hot Boolean vector, and each Boolean vector satisfying the channel and displayed sum determines the unique index \(i=\sum_{k\in K}k b_k\). If some index values are excluded, their corresponding Boolean variables are fixed to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An index variable is represented exactly by one-hot Boolean indicators, one for each possible index value.
assumptions_latex: \(D(i)\subseteq K=\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
\(b_k\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(k\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_k=1\Longleftrightarrow i=k\) and \(\sum_{k\in K}b_k=1\).

notation.meaning: Indicator that the index equals k.

review_flags: authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

children.title: Index-Value Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Consistency relationships between selected positions and represented values.

knowledge_statements.title: Index-Value Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-array channeling for two permutation representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I=J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with variables \(x_i\in J\) for \(i\in I\) and \(y_j\in I\) for \(j\in J\). The index-value correspondence constraint is
\[
x_i=j\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y_j=i
\qquad(i\in I,\ j\in J).
\]
Every satisfying assignment makes \(i\mapsto x_i\) a bijection from \(I\) to \(J\), makes \(j\mapsto y_j\) its inverse, and therefore entails that both arrays are all-different. Conversely, every permutation represented by \(x\) has the unique inverse array \(y\) satisfying these equivalences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two arrays are inverse representations when an entry maps index i to value j exactly when the other maps j back to i.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in J\) and \(y_j\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i=j\Longleftrightarrow y_j=i\) for all \((i,j)\in I\times J\).

notation.meaning: Value assigned to index i in the forward representation.
Index assigned to value j in the inverse representation.
Equal finite index and value sets.

review_flags: authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-array correspondence is mathematically coherent and appropriately classified as a definition, but no authoritative locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Constraint Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable adjacency graph induced by common constraint scopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite constraint network with variable set \(X\), constraint set \(C\), and scope map \(\operatorname{scope}:C\to 2^X\), the primal constraint graph is the simple undirected graph \(G_P=(X,E_P)\) satisfying
\[
\{x,x'\}\in E_P
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\ne x'\ \text{ and }\ \exists c\in C:\{x,x'\}\subseteq\operatorname{scope}(c).
\]
Thus every constraint scope induces a clique on its distinct variables. Unary constraints create no edges, and parallel adjacency induced by several constraints remains a single edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal graph has variables as vertices and joins two distinct variables whenever some constraint contains both in its scope.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(C\) are finite.
Each \(\operatorname{scope}(c)\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_P=(X,E_P)\) with adjacency determined by shared membership in a constraint scope.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard primal-graph definition for constraint networks
supplied sparsity-graph locator is only indirect support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal-graph definition is correct and fits the leaf, but the inventory's sparsity-graph section is only indirect support and the record cites no source.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Constraint Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint adjacency graph induced by shared variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite constraint network with variable set \(X\), constraint set \(C\), and scope map \(\operatorname{scope}:C\to 2^X\), the dual constraint graph is the simple undirected graph \(G_D=(C,E_D)\) satisfying
\[
\{c,d\}\in E_D
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
c\ne d\ \text{ and }\ \operatorname{scope}(c)\cap\operatorname{scope}(d)\ne\varnothing.
\]
Its vertices are constraints rather than variables. Distinct constraints therefore are adjacent precisely when their satisfaction conditions depend on at least one common variable; multiple shared variables still induce only one edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual graph has constraints as vertices and joins two distinct constraints exactly when their scopes share a variable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(C\) are finite.
Each \(\operatorname{scope}(c)\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_D=(C,E_D)\) with adjacency determined by nonempty scope intersection.

notation.meaning: Constraint set and vertex set of the dual graph.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard dual-graph definition for constraint networks
authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual constraint graph is correctly defined, but no inspectable constraint-programming citation supports it.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable–Constraint Incidence Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite graph retaining variables, constraints, and scope incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite constraint network with variable set \(X\), constraint set \(C\), and scope map \(\operatorname{scope}:C\to 2^X\), its variable–constraint incidence graph is the bipartite graph
\[
G_I=(X\mathbin{\dot\cup}C,E_I),
\qquad
E_I=\bigl\{\{x,c\}:x\in X,\ c\in C,\ x\in\operatorname{scope}(c)\bigr\}.
\]
There are no variable–variable or constraint–constraint edges. Hence the neighborhood of a constraint vertex is exactly its scope, while the neighborhood of a variable vertex is the set of constraints in which that variable occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence graph is bipartite: variable and constraint vertices are joined precisely when the variable belongs to the constraint's scope.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(C\) are finite and disjoint vertex classes.
Each \(\operatorname{scope}(c)\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x,c\}\in E_I\Longleftrightarrow x\in\operatorname{scope}(c)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard incidence-graph definition for constraint networks
authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bipartite incidence-graph definition is precise and fits the terminal container, but it lacks a cited source and locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Hypergraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypergraph preserving each constraint scope as a hyperedge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite constraint network with variable set \(X\), constraint set \(C\), and scope map \(\operatorname{scope}:C\to 2^X\), its constraint hypergraph is
\[
H=(X,\mathcal E),
\qquad
\mathcal E=\bigl(\operatorname{scope}(c)\bigr)_{c\in C}.
\]
The vertices are variables, and each constraint contributes one labeled hyperedge equal to its scope. Treating \(\mathcal E\) as an indexed family, rather than an ordinary set, retains distinct constraints having identical scopes. Unary and empty scopes are permitted when the underlying constraint formalism permits them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint hypergraph uses variables as vertices and represents every constraint scope as a possibly labeled hyperedge.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(C\) are finite.
Each \(\operatorname{scope}(c)\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=(X,(\operatorname{scope}(c))_{c\in C})\).
review_flags: authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indexed-family formulation appropriately preserves duplicate scopes, but the constraint-hypergraph definition has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Hidden-Variable Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encodings introducing variables that represent admissible constraint tuples.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Variable Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding of nonbinary constraints using tuple-valued auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a finite-domain constraint network have variables \(X\), and for each constraint \(c\) let \(R_c\subseteq\prod_{x\in S_c}D_x\) be its allowed relation on scope \(S_c\). The hidden-variable encoding introduces one auxiliary variable \(h_c\) with domain \(R_c\). For every \(x\in S_c\), it adds the binary compatibility constraint
\[
h_c[x]=x,
\]
where \(h_c[x]\) denotes the component of the tuple selected by \(h_c\) at coordinate \(x\). The original nonbinary constraint \(c\) is replaced by these binary constraints; original variables and their domains are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each nonbinary constraint becomes a tuple-valued auxiliary variable linked componentwise to the original variables in its scope.
assumptions_latex: Every \(D_x\) is finite.
Each \(R_c\) explicitly denotes the allowed tuples of constraint \(c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_c\in R_c\) and \(h_c[x]=x\) for every \(x\in S_c\).

notation.meaning: Allowed tuple relation of constraint c.
Tuple-valued hidden variable for constraint c.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard hidden-variable encoding of nonbinary CSPs
authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hidden-variable representation is mathematically plausible and correctly classified, but its precise encoding semantics require an authoritative source.

children.title: Dual Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encodings replacing constraints with variables linked through compatibility structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-as-variable encoding with overlap-consistency constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each constraint \(c\) of a finite-domain network have scope \(S_c\) and allowed tuple relation \(R_c\). The dual encoding introduces a variable \(d_c\) with domain \(R_c\) and removes the original variables. For every distinct pair \(c,e\) with \(S_c\cap S_e\ne\varnothing\), it adds the binary constraint
\[
\forall x\in S_c\cap S_e,\qquad d_c[x]=d_e[x].
\]
Thus a dual assignment selects one satisfying tuple for each original constraint, subject to agreement on every variable shared by their scopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual encoding replaces each constraint by a tuple-valued variable and enforces pairwise agreement on coordinates shared by constraint scopes.
assumptions_latex: Every original domain is finite.
Each \(R_c\) is the allowed tuple relation on \(S_c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_c\in R_c\) and overlapping selected tuples agree on every shared coordinate.

notation.meaning: Allowed tuple relation of constraint c.
Dual variable selecting a tuple for constraint c.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard dual encoding of nonbinary CSPs
authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual encoding and overlap-consistency constraints fit the leaf, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Encoding Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural mappings between original, hidden-variable, and dual representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution correspondence among original, hidden-variable, and dual encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X'=\bigcup_{c\in C}S_c\) be the original variables occurring in at least one constraint. Every solution \(a\) of the original network uniquely extends to a hidden-variable solution by setting \(h_c=a|_{S_c}\), and induces a dual solution by setting \(d_c=a|_{S_c}\). Conversely, every hidden-variable solution projects to an original solution. Every dual solution determines a unique assignment \(a:X'\to\bigcup_{x\in X'}D_x\) by
\[
a(x)=d_c[x]\quad\text{for any }c\text{ with }x\in S_c,
\]
which is well-defined by overlap consistency and satisfies every original constraint. Variables outside \(X'\) remain independently assignable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Original solutions correspond exactly to compatible tuple selections in hidden-variable and dual encodings; unconstrained variables must be handled separately.
assumptions_latex: All dual overlap-consistency constraints are imposed.
Each encoded variable domain is the corresponding allowed tuple relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Solutions on \(X'\) are in bijection with solutions of either encoding.

notation.meaning: Original variables appearing in constraint scopes.
Restriction of assignment a to scope c.
Hidden and dual tuple variables for constraint c.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard solution-preservation correspondence for hidden and dual encodings
authoritative constraint-programming source locator not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The solution-correspondence property correctly distinguishes variables occurring in scopes from unconstrained variables, but the bijection claim lacks inspectable authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Constraint Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain decomposition using auxiliary variables and primitive constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be a global constraint over finite domains. A family of primitive constraints \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\), possibly involving auxiliary variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_k\), is a decomposition of \(C\) when
\[
C(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\iff \exists y_1\cdots\exists y_k\;\bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}c_j(x,y).
\]
Equivalently, the projection onto the original variables of the solution set of \(\bigwedge_j c_j\) equals the solution set of \(C\). This semantic equivalence does not imply that propagation on the decomposition matches propagation by a dedicated global-constraint propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition represents a global constraint by primitive constraints whose projected solutions are exactly the original solutions, although propagation strength may differ.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and any auxiliary variables have finite domains.
Each \(c_j\) is interpreted over the same domain store.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x}(\operatorname{Sol}(\bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}c_j))=\operatorname{Sol}(C)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically precise and matches the decomposition leaf, but no inspectable constraint-programming source supports the equivalence and propagation caveat.

children.title: Redundant Constraints
children.top_down_role: Additional constraints preserving the represented solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic redundancy relative to a finite-domain constraint model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(X,D,C)\) be a finite-domain constraint model and let \(r\) be an additional constraint on variables in \(X\). The constraint \(r\) is redundant relative to \(M\) if adding it leaves the feasible assignments unchanged:
\[
\operatorname{Sol}(C\cup\{r\})=\operatorname{Sol}(C).
\]
Equivalently, every assignment satisfying all constraints in \(C\) also satisfies \(r\), written \(C\models r\). Although semantically redundant, \(r\) may permit additional domain pruning when its propagator exposes consequences not obtained from the original propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is redundant when every original solution satisfies it, so adding it preserves feasibility but may strengthen propagation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and every variable in \(X\) has a finite domain.
\(r\) uses variables from \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\models r\), equivalently \(\operatorname{Sol}(C\cup\{r\})=\operatorname{Sol}(C)\).

notation.meaning: constraint model with variables, domains, and constraints
assignments satisfying every constraint in C

children.title: Implied Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraints entailed by other parts of the model.

knowledge_statements.title: Implied Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical implication by the complete original constraint family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite-domain model with constraint family \(C\), a constraint \(q\) is implied by \(C\) if
\[
C\models q,
\]
meaning that for every complete assignment \(a\) to the model variables, \(a\in\operatorname{Sol}(C)\) entails \(a\models q\). Thus adjoining \(q\) preserves the complete solution set. Implication is a semantic property of the whole model; it does not require that any single constraint in \(C\), or the current collection of propagators, derive \(q\) locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implied constraint is true in every complete solution of the original model, whether or not existing propagators derive it locally.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a family of constraints over common finite-domain variables.
\(q\) is defined on variables of the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\models q\) and \(\operatorname{Sol}(C\cup\{q\})=\operatorname{Sol}(C)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic definition is precise and distinct from local propagator derivability, but it has no inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Propagation Roles of Added Constraints
children.top_down_role: Search-space and filtering effects associated with redundant or implied additions.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Roles of Added Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of a sound monotone propagator for a logically implied added constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a finite domain store. For each constraint in \(C\), let its propagator be sound, contracting, and monotone under componentwise set inclusion, and let \(p_q\) have the same properties for an implied constraint \(q\). Define \(P_C(D)\) and \(P_{C\cup\{q\}}(D)\) as the greatest common fixpoints below \(D\) of the respective propagator families. If \(C\models q\), then
\[
P_{C\cup\{q\}}(D)\subseteq P_C(D).
\]
Every solution of \(C\) represented by \(D\) remains represented after either propagation, and the inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a sound, contracting, monotone propagator for an implied constraint preserves every solution and can produce a smaller domain-store fixpoint than the original propagators.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite domain store.
\(C\models q\).
All propagators are sound, contracting, and monotone under componentwise set inclusion.
Each propagation operator denotes the greatest common fixpoint below \(D\), as obtained by fair iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{C\cup\{q\}}(D)\subseteq P_C(D)\), with every solution of \(C\) represented by \(D\) preserved.

notation.meaning: propagator for the added implied constraint

children.title: Variable Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Symmetries induced by interchangeable variables or variable positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry induced solely by permuting variable coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(X,D,C)\) be a finite-domain constraint model. A variable symmetry is a permutation \(\pi:X\to X\) that is compatible with the variable domains and preserves feasibility: for every complete assignment \(a\),
\[
a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\iff \pi\cdot a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M),
\qquad (\pi\cdot a)(x)=a(\pi^{-1}(x)).
\]
Hence \(\pi\) maps every solution to another solution by rearranging variable coordinates without relabeling values. All such permutations form a group under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable symmetry permutes variable coordinates while preserving domains and mapping every solution to a solution.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and all domains are finite.
\(D(\pi(x))=D(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\iff \pi\cdot a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly describes a domain-compatible variable permutation and its action on assignments, but no inspectable symmetry source is supplied.

children.title: Value Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Symmetries induced by interchangeable domain values.

knowledge_statements.title: Value Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry induced by consistently relabeling domain values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(X,D,C)\) be a finite-domain constraint model and let \(V=\bigcup_{x\in X}D(x)\). A value symmetry is a permutation \(\sigma:V\to V\) compatible with the domains and preserving feasibility: for every complete assignment \(a\),
\[
a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\iff \sigma\cdot a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M),
\qquad (\sigma\cdot a)(x)=\sigma(a(x)).
\]
The same relabeling is applied consistently wherever a value occurs. Such permutations form a group under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value symmetry consistently relabels domain values and maps every feasible assignment to another feasible assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(X\), \(V\), and all domains are finite.
\(\sigma(D(x))=D(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\iff \sigma\cdot a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\).

notation.meaning: assignment obtained by relabeling assigned values

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly describes consistent value relabeling and domain compatibility, but no inspectable symmetry source is supplied.

children.title: Combined Symmetry Actions
children.top_down_role: Interactions between variable permutations and value permutations.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Symmetry Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous compatible actions on variables and values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(X,D,C)\) be a finite-domain constraint model, let \(\pi:X\to X\) permute its variables, and let \(\sigma:V\to V\) permute the values in \(V=\bigcup_{x\in X}D(x)\). Their combined action on a complete assignment \(a\) is
\[
((\pi,\sigma)\cdot a)(x)=\sigma(a(\pi^{-1}(x))).
\]
The pair \((\pi,\sigma)\) is a combined symmetry when the transformed assignment respects every variable domain and
\[
a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\iff (\pi,\sigma)\cdot a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M).
\]
A combined symmetry may exist even when neither component acting alone is a symmetry of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combined symmetry simultaneously permutes variables and relabels values so that the joint transformation preserves the solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(V\) are finite.
\(\pi:X\to X\) and \(\sigma:V\to V\) are bijections.
\(\sigma(D(\pi^{-1}(x)))=D(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\iff (\pi,\sigma)\cdot a\in\operatorname{Sol}(M)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Static Symmetry Breaking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit-preserving constraints installed before search begins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a symmetry group \(G\) act on the solution set \(S\) of a constraint model. A static symmetry-breaking constraint family \(B\), added before search, is orbit-complete if
\[
\forall s\in S\;\exists g\in G:\ g\cdot s\models B.
\]
It is complete symmetry breaking if additionally
\[
\forall s\in S:\ \left|G\cdot s\cap\operatorname{Sol}(B)\right|=1.
\]
Orbit-completeness preserves satisfiability and at least one representative of each solution orbit; completeness selects exactly one representative per orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static symmetry-breaking constraints preserve at least one solution per symmetry orbit; complete breaking preserves exactly one.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on the model's solution set \(S\).
\(B\) is fixed before search.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is sound for orbit reduction when every orbit in \(S/G\) retains at least one representative.

notation.meaning: orbit of solution s under G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbit-completeness and unique-representative conditions accurately characterize static symmetry-breaking constraints, but no inspectable source supports the terminology or criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Symmetry Breaking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search-time pruning using canonical representatives of symmetric nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite-domain model, a search tree, and a symmetry group \(G\) acting on search states. Maintain a set \(R\) of previously accepted canonical states, initially empty. At each generated state \(u\), compute a canonical representative \(\kappa(u)\) satisfying \(\kappa(g\cdot u)=\kappa(u)\) for every \(g\in G\). If \(\kappa(u)\in R\), prune \(u\); otherwise insert \(\kappa(u)\) into \(R\), propagate, and branch. Stop when the remaining search is exhausted, and output all discovered solutions or one representative per orbit, according to the search objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: During search, canonicalize each state and prune it when an equivalent state under the symmetry group was already explored.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) maps valid search states and their completions to symmetric states and completions.
\(\kappa(u)=\kappa(v)\) exactly when \(u\) and \(v\) are in the same relevant orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No two explored states have the same canonical representative, while every unpruned solution orbit remains reachable.

notation.meaning: symmetry group acting on search states

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a particular canonical-state memoization algorithm rather than a source-neutral definition of dynamic symmetry breaking. Its correctness depends on the stated orbit equivalence and search-state completion assumptions, so a source for this exact variant is required.

children.title: Global Constraint Families
children.top_down_role: Canonical global constraints grouped by modeled combinatorial structure; detailed filtering methods follow under propagation.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Régin, A Filtering Algorithm for Constraints of Difference in CSPs
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Régin, A Filtering Algorithm for Constraints of Difference in CSPs

knowledge_statements.title: Hall-Set Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tight Hall subsets for an AllDifferent constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) with current domains \(D_i\). A nonempty index set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a Hall set when
\[
\left|\bigcup_{i\in S}D_i\right|=|S|.
\]
If the constraint is satisfiable, Hall's condition requires \(\left|\bigcup_{i\in T}D_i\right|\ge |T|\) for every index set \(T\). For a Hall set \(S\), every satisfying assignment uses all values in \(H=\bigcup_{i\in S}D_i\) on variables indexed by \(S\); consequently, values in \(H\) can be removed from every \(D_j\) with \(j\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hall set has exactly as many available values as variables; those values are reserved for its variables and removable elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: All variables and domains are finite.
The variables are constrained by \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(j\notin S\Longrightarrow D_j\leftarrow D_j\setminus\bigcup_{i\in S}D_i\) is solution preserving.

notation.meaning: union of domains of variables indexed by S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hall-set equality, Hall condition, and resulting solution-preserving pruning are mathematically consistent, but no Hall-theorem or AllDifferent source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Based Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-consistency filtering through the variable-value bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input finite domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\) for \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). Form the bipartite graph whose variable vertices are \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), whose value vertices are the elements of \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}D_i\), and whose edges satisfy \((x_i,v)\in E\) exactly when \(v\in D_i\). Compute a maximum matching. If no matching covers all \(n\) variable vertices, report failure. Otherwise, delete every edge that belongs to no matching covering all variables, equivalently removing its value from the corresponding domain. Output the reduced domains, which are domain consistent for the AllDifferent constraint.

children.title: Bounds Filtering

knowledge_statements.title: Bounds Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hall-interval filtering for integer-domain AllDifferent constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input integer variables \(x_i\) with current bounds \(l_i=\min D_i\) and \(u_i=\max D_i\). Repeatedly inspect integer intervals \(I=[a,b]\) and define
\[
S_I=\{i:[l_i,u_i]\subseteq I\},\qquad |I|=b-a+1.
\]
If \(|S_I|>|I|\), report failure. If \(|S_I|=|I|\), then for every \(j\notin S_I\), apply the solution-preserving updates
\[
a\le l_j\le b<u_j\Longrightarrow l_j\leftarrow b+1,
\]
and
\[
l_j<a\le u_j\le b\Longrightarrow u_j\leftarrow a-1.
\]
Iterate these tests and updates to a fixpoint and output the resulting bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Detect overloaded Hall intervals, and for each tight interval exclude that interval from the overlapping lower or upper endpoint of every variable not contained in it.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D_i\) is a nonempty finite set of integers represented for bounds filtering by its interval hull \([l_i,u_i]\).
All variables occur in one \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}\) constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S_I|>|I|\) certifies failure, while \(|S_I|=|I|\) justifies the stated solution-preserving bound updates.

notation.meaning: interval hull of the current domain of x_i
indices of variables whose interval hull lies inside I
number of integers in I, equal to b-a+1

children.title: Table Representation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Memory, tuple density, and domain-change regimes affecting representation choice.

assumptions_latex: A positive table contains \(m\) tuples over \(n\) variables.
Bitsets use words of \(w\) bits, while a sparse tuple list stores tuple indices explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No representation uniformly dominates: density, deletion pattern, arity, and search restoration costs determine whether bitsets, sparse lists, or hybrid tables are preferable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard asymptotic comparison of extensional-table representations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic and operational comparison for positive extensional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dense tuple bitset requires \(\Theta(m)\) bits for the current table and can intersect or scan it in \(O(\lceil m/w\rceil)\) word operations. An explicit sparse list requires \(\Theta(k\log m)\) bits for surviving indices and scans in \(O(k)\) tuple operations, but deleting arbitrary tuples and restoring search states may require additional indexing or trailing. Thus bitsets favor dense or moderately dense tables and word-parallel filtering; sparse lists favor very small \(k\). Hybrid sparse-bitset schemes retain \(\Theta(m)\) mask storage while avoiding scans of zero words.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense bitsets offer word parallelism; sparse lists benefit highly reduced tables; hybrid compact tables trade mask memory for skipping empty words and cheap restoration.

Equivalently, the Cartesian products
\[
\prod_{k=1}^r[x_{i,k},x_{i,k}+d_{i,k})\quad\text{and}\quad\prod_{k=1}^r[x_{j,k},x_{j,k}+d_{j,k})
\]
are disjoint. Setting all presence indicators to one gives the mandatory-object form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every pair of present axis-aligned boxes with positive side lengths must be separated in at least one coordinate dimension; boxes may touch at their boundaries.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric No-Overlap Constraints

assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive and use one cumulative resource of capacity \(C\).
Each activity \(i\) has start domain \([\operatorname{est}_i,\operatorname{lst}_i]\), duration \(p_i\), and demand \(r_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires \(P(t)\le C\) for every time \(t\); any time with \(P(t)>C\) certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: Compulsory-part resource profile at time t.
Earliest completion time of activity i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compulsory-part timetable test for a single cumulative resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each activity \(i\), its compulsory part is \([\operatorname{lst}_i,\operatorname{ect}_i)\) when \(\operatorname{lst}_i<\operatorname{ect}_i\), and is empty otherwise. Define the timetable profile by \[P(t)=\sum_i r_i\mathbf{1}\{\operatorname{lst}_i\le t<\operatorname{ect}_i\}.\] Every feasible schedule satisfies \(P(t)\le C\) for all \(t\). Hence a point \(t\) with \(P(t)>C\) is an independently checkable infeasibility certificate. Timetable propagation may also reject a candidate placement of activity \(j\) whenever adding its demand over that placement makes the profile exceed \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sum demands of activities forced to execute at each time. If this compulsory profile exceeds capacity, the cumulative constraint is infeasible; candidate placements causing overload can be removed.
knowledge_statements.title: Timetable Reasoning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compulsory-part overload certificate is standard, but no inspectable source is supplied. The placement-pruning sentence must specify that the tested activity's existing compulsory contribution is excluded or subtracted to avoid double counting.

assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive and share a cumulative resource of capacity \(C\).
A sound lower-bound procedure is available for the resource-time consumption required by a set under an imposed relative order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If one relative placement of \(i\) against \(\Omega\) necessarily overloads the resource while the opposite placement remains possible, that placement is removed and the corresponding start or completion bound is tightened.

notation.meaning: Set of activities considered as a block.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-form cumulative edge finding; exact polynomial implementations vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a set \(\Omega\) and an activity \(i\notin\Omega\), evaluate the two conditional cases in which \(i\) lies entirely before the activities of \(\Omega\), or entirely after them. For each case, compute a sound lower bound on required resource-time consumption in every relevant interval and compare it with available energy \(C(b-a)\) on \([a,b)\). If the before-case necessarily violates some capacity inequality, impose that \(i\) cannot precede all of \(\Omega\) and tighten its earliest start accordingly. Apply the symmetric test to tighten its latest completion. Iterate until no bound changes or an overload proves infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test whether an activity can lie before or after a task set. A conditional overload eliminates that ordering and tightens the activity’s time bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Finding Reasoning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Cumulative edge-finding has several non-equivalent formulations. The asserted before/after tests and resulting bound updates are not precise enough to validate without an authoritative algorithm statement and locator.

assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive with start bounds \(\operatorname{est}_i\le s_i\le\operatorname{lst}_i\).
Activity \(i\) has duration \(p_i\), demand \(r_i\), and all activities share capacity \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible schedule satisfies \(\sum_i r_i p_i(a,b)\le C(b-a)\) for every \(a<b\).

notation.meaning: Minimum processing time of activity i forced into interval [a,b).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval-energy feasibility test for nonpreemptive cumulative scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{ect}_i=\operatorname{est}_i+p_i\) and \(\operatorname{lct}_i=\operatorname{lst}_i+p_i\). For every interval \([a,b)\), define the processing forced into that interval by \[p_i(a,b)=\max\{0,\min\{p_i,b-a,\operatorname{ect}_i-a,b-\operatorname{lst}_i\}\}.\] The mandatory energy in the interval is \(E(a,b)=\sum_i r_i p_i(a,b)\). Since the resource supplies at most \(C(b-a)\), feasibility requires \[E(a,b)\le C(b-a)\qquad\text{for every }a<b.\] A violated inequality proves infeasibility; conditional violations support domain pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every interval, mandatory activity energy must not exceed capacity times interval length. A violated interval inequality proves infeasibility and conditional violations permit pruning.
knowledge_statements.title: Energetic Reasoning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interval-energy condition and forced-processing formula appear standard and internally consistent, and content_kind condition fits, but no source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Bin-Packing Constraints
children.top_down_role: Assignment structures involving multiple capacity-limited containers.

assumptions_latex: There are items \(i\in I\) with nonnegative sizes \(w_i\) and bins \(b\in B\) with capacities \(C_b\).
Each finite-domain variable \(x_i\) denotes the bin receiving item \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An assignment satisfies the bin-packing constraint exactly when \(\sum_{i:x_i=b}w_i\le C_b\) for every \(b\in B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment-variable form with heterogeneous bin capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bin-packing constraint on variables \((x_i)_{i\in I}\) holds when \(x_i\in B\) for every item \(i\), each item is assigned to exactly one bin through its single value \(x_i\), and \[\sum_{i\in I}w_i\mathbf{1}\{x_i=b\}\le C_b\qquad\text{for every }b\in B.\] If load variables \(L_b\) are included, their defining equalities are \(L_b=\sum_i w_i\mathbf{1}\{x_i=b\}\), together with \(0\le L_b\le C_b\). Thus the constraint couples all assignment variables sharing a bin capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each item chooses one bin, and the sum of sizes assigned to every bin must not exceed that bin’s capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Bin-Packing Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent, but the cited productive-capacity section does not specifically establish bin-packing global-constraint semantics, assignment variables, or the optional load-variable formulation.

children.title: Knapsack Constraints
children.top_down_role: Selection structures governed by capacity usage and item contributions.

assumptions_latex: Variables \(y_i\) have finite domains \(D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z\).
Coefficients \(w_i\) and bounds \(L,U\) are fixed integers with \(L\le U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The knapsack constraint holds exactly when \(L\le\sum_i w_i y_i\le U\).

notation.meaning: Finite-domain decision variable for item i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain bounded-sum form, including binary selection as a special case.

source_refs.source_title: Bilevel Programming Problems: Theory, Algorithms and Applications to Energy Networks

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bounded knapsack constraint over finite-domain variables \((y_i)_{i\in I}\) is satisfied precisely when \[L\le\sum_{i\in I}w_i y_i\le U.\] The common binary-selection form has \(D_i=\{0,1\}\), lower bound \(L=0\), and upper capacity \(U=C\); then \(y_i=1\) means that item \(i\) is selected. Equality knapsack is obtained by setting \(L=U\). Negative coefficients are permitted by the algebraic definition, although packing interpretations conventionally require \(w_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A knapsack constraint restricts a weighted sum of finite-domain variables to an interval; binary variables give the usual capacity-limited item-selection model.
knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Constraints

source_witnesses.source_title: Bilevel Programming Problems: Theory, Algorithms and Applications to Energy Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A bounded weighted sum is coherent, but calling arbitrary finite-domain variables with possibly negative coefficients a knapsack constraint is convention-dependent. The cited full text must confirm this exact variant rather than only binary, continuous, or nonlinear knapsack models.

children.title: Capacity Coupling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Shared-capacity, multiple-container, and profit-coupled modeling regimes.

assumptions_latex: All item sizes and capacities are nonnegative.
Assignment and selection variables have finite domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Per-container coupling has constraints \(\sum_i w_i\mathbf{1}\{x_i=b\}\le C_b\) for each \(b\), whereas aggregate coupling has one bound \(L\le\sum_i w_i y_i\le U\).

notation.meaning: Selected quantity or indicator for item i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between assignment-indexed and aggregate discrete-capacity coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two discrete capacity-coupling regimes are distinguished by the index of the capacity restriction. In assignment-indexed coupling, each item chooses a container and every container has its own inequality, \[\sum_i w_i\mathbf{1}\{x_i=b\}\le C_b\qquad(b\in B).\] In aggregate coupling, decisions share one bounded weighted sum, \[L\le\sum_i w_i y_i\le U.\] Bin packing belongs to the first regime, while a knapsack constraint belongs to the second. Introducing assignment indicators converts the first regime into a family of knapsack inequalities, but does not remove their shared exactly-one-assignment coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bin packing couples choices through one capacity per bin; knapsack couples them through one aggregate weighted bound. Indicator expansion links the forms but preserves assignment coupling.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Coupling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison is plausible, but the named two-regime classification and the claim relating indicator-expanded bin packing to knapsack inequalities are not supported by the generic productive-capacity locator.

children.title: Reservoir Constraints
children.top_down_role: Resource-level structures driven by discrete inflow or outflow events.

assumptions_latex: Events \(i\in I\) occur at finite-domain times \(t_i\) and change a stored level by signed amounts \(q_i\).
The initial level is \(R_0\), and admissible levels lie in \([R_{\min},R_{\max}]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reservoir constraint holds exactly when every event-prefix level remains in \([R_{\min},R_{\max}]\).

notation.meaning: Time and signed level change of event i.
Reservoir level immediately after all events through time tau.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-based reservoir balance with simultaneous changes aggregated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Aggregate all changes occurring at the same time. The event-based reservoir level after time \(\tau\) is \[R(\tau)=R_0+\sum_{i:t_i\le\tau}q_i.\] Positive \(q_i\) denotes inflow and negative \(q_i\) denotes outflow. The reservoir constraint is satisfied if and only if \[R_{\min}\le R(\tau)\le R_{\max}\] after every distinct event time \(\tau\). If an implementation instead orders simultaneous events individually, that ordering convention must be fixed explicitly because intermediate prefix levels can differ despite the same aggregate change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an initial level, apply signed changes in event-time order. The level after every simultaneous event group must remain between its lower and upper limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Reservoir Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited material-balance section does not establish the catalog-specific reservoir semantics. Moreover, checking only post-event levels omits an explicit requirement that the initial level be admissible, including the no-event case.

children.title: Inventory Constraints
children.top_down_role: Stock-level structures distributed across indexed planning periods.

assumptions_latex: Periods are \(t=1,\ldots,T\), with initial inventory \(I_0\).
Finite-domain quantities \(u_t,d_t\) denote inflow and demand, and \(I_t\) denotes ending inventory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inventory feasibility is characterized by \(I_t=I_{t-1}+u_t-d_t\) and \(L_t\le I_t\le U_t\) for every period \(t\).

notation.meaning: Inventory at the end of period t.
Inflow and demand during period t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Period-indexed deterministic inventory conservation without lead times or losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-horizon inventory constraint is the system \[I_t=I_{t-1}+u_t-d_t,\qquad L_t\le I_t\le U_t,\qquad t=1,\ldots,T.\] Thus each period's ending inventory equals the preceding inventory plus inflow minus demand, and must lie within its prescribed bounds. Eliminating the state variables yields the equivalent prefix form \[L_t\le I_0+\sum_{k=1}^{t}(u_k-d_k)\le U_t\qquad(t=1,\ldots,T).\] Additional losses, lead times, or backlogging require modified balance equations and are outside this local definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each period’s ending inventory equals prior inventory plus inflow minus demand and must satisfy its bounds; equivalently, every cumulative net-flow prefix is bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Inventory Constraints

children.title: Level-Balance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Capacity, deficit, replenishment, and temporal balance regimes.

assumptions_latex: Level changes are additive and the initial level is fixed.
All decision variables have finite domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Event-driven and period-indexed models share bounded prefix sums but differ in whether the ordering of changes is variable or fixed.

notation.meaning: Signed change associated with event i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between variable-order event balances and fixed-order period balances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an event-driven regime, event times are decision variables and the bounded level is \[L_0+\sum_{i:t_i\le\tau}q_i,\] so feasibility depends on the induced ordering of signed changes. In a period-indexed regime, the order is fixed and the bounded level after period \(t\) is \[L_0+\sum_{k=1}^{t}\Delta_k.\] Both regimes enforce lower and upper bounds on prefix sums. They coincide when every event is assigned to a fixed period and simultaneous changes are aggregated; they differ when scheduling decisions can reorder changes or when within-period intermediate levels are constrained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reservoir models use variable event order; inventory models usually use fixed period order. Both bound cumulative net-change prefixes and coincide when event periods are fixed and aggregated.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Balance Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison is plausible, but coincidence additionally requires aligned observation points and level bounds and the absence of relevant within-period intermediate constraints. The cited generic material-balance section does not support the synthesized regime classification.

children.title: Circuit Constraints
children.top_down_role: Hamiltonian-cycle structures over the selected graph.

assumptions_latex: The index set is \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(n\ge2\).
Each successor variable satisfies \(x_i\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The circuit constraint holds exactly when \(i\mapsto x_i\) is a permutation consisting of one directed cycle containing every vertex.

notation.meaning: Successor mapping induced by the variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successor-array Hamiltonian circuit on the full index set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The circuit constraint on \((x_i)_{i\in V}\) is satisfied if and only if the mapping \(f:V\to V\) defined by \(f(i)=x_i\) is bijective and has exactly one orbit. Equivalently, there exists an ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of all vertices such that \[x_{v_k}=v_{k+1}\quad(k=1,\ldots,n-1),\qquad x_{v_n}=v_1.\] Bijection gives every vertex one predecessor and one successor; the single-orbit condition excludes a disjoint union of two or more directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successor variables form a permutation containing exactly one directed cycle through every vertex, excluding disconnected collections of smaller cycles.
knowledge_statements.title: Circuit Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The full successor-array single-cycle definition is mathematically coherent and content_kind definition fits, but no authoritative catalog or textbook locator confirms the indexing and self-loop conventions.

children.title: Subcircuit Constraints
children.top_down_role: Optional-vertex circuit structures with excluded vertices.

assumptions_latex: The index set is \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Each successor variable satisfies \(x_i\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subcircuit constraint holds when nonfixed vertices form one directed cycle and every excluded vertex is a fixed point.

notation.meaning: Set of vertices included in the nontrivial circuit.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successor-array subcircuit with fixed points representing excluded vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{i\in V:x_i\ne i\}\). The subcircuit constraint is satisfied when every vertex outside \(S\) is a fixed point, the restriction of \(f(i)=x_i\) to \(S\) maps \(S\) bijectively onto itself, and, when \(S\ne\varnothing\), that restriction consists of exactly one directed cycle. Equivalently, the successor mapping is a permutation whose only cycles are singleton fixed points and at most one cycle of length greater than one. Whether \(S=\varnothing\) is admitted is a catalog-specific convention that must be declared explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Included vertices form one directed cycle; excluded vertices point to themselves. Whether the entirely empty subcircuit is allowed depends on the chosen constraint convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Subcircuit Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-point encoding is coherent, but admissibility of the all-fixed assignment is left unresolved and no source identifies the intended catalog convention.

children.title: Circuit–Subcircuit Modeling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Selection, exclusion, and coverage distinctions between the two families.

assumptions_latex: Circuit and subcircuit use the same successor-array indexing convention.
In a subcircuit, fixed points encode excluded vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Circuit is the subcircuit regime with \(S=V\); permitting \(S\subsetneq V\) changes the model by allowing excluded vertices.

notation.meaning: Vertices included in the nontrivial cycle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Modeling boundary determined by whether every vertex must belong to the cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A circuit requires \(S=V\), so every vertex belongs to the unique directed cycle and no fixed point is available to represent exclusion. A subcircuit permits \(S\subseteq V\), requires the vertices of \(S\) to form one directed cycle, and fixes every \(i\in V\setminus S\) by \(x_i=i\). Therefore replacing subcircuit by circuit is valid only when all vertices are mandatory. Replacing circuit by subcircuit without separately enforcing \(x_i\ne i\) for every \(i\) weakens the model and may admit solutions that omit vertices; the all-fixed assignment may also appear when the empty-subcircuit convention is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Circuit requires every vertex; subcircuit permits fixed-point exclusions. Substituting subcircuit for circuit weakens the model unless all self-loops are explicitly forbidden.
knowledge_statements.title: Circuit–Subcircuit Modeling Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The modeling-boundary statement is sound under the stated successor-array convention, and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but its validity depends on catalog-specific circuit and empty-subcircuit semantics for which no citation is supplied.

children.title: Path Constraints
children.top_down_role: Endpoint, simplicity, and vertex-selection regimes for constrained paths.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected simple graph.
\(x_v,y_e\in\{0,1\}\) indicate selected vertices and edges, respectively.
The selected vertex set \(S=\{v\in V:x_v=1\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=(S,F)\) is a simple path, where \(F=\{e\in E:y_e=1\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-graph characterization of a selected simple path
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected, vertex-and-edge selected simple paths; singleton paths are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The path constraint holds precisely when the selected subgraph \(H=(S,F)\) is connected and acyclic, and every selected vertex has selected degree at most two: \[\deg_H(v)\le 2\quad\text{for every }v\in S.\] Equivalently, \(H\) is connected, \(|F|=|S|-1\), and \(\deg_H(v)\le 2\) for all \(v\in S\). If \(|S|\ge 2\), exactly two vertices have degree one and all remaining selected vertices have degree two; if \(|S|=1\), then \(F=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The selected vertices and edges must form one simple undirected path, with a singleton allowed as a degenerate path.
knowledge_statements.title: Path Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and simple-path characterization are mathematically correct for the stated finite undirected setting, and the content kind fits the leaf. No inspectable citation is supplied, so the candidate requires an authoritative graph-theory or global-constraint source with a specific locator.

children.title: Connected-Subgraph Constraints
children.top_down_role: Connectivity requirements imposed on selected vertices or edges.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(S\subseteq V\) and \(F\subseteq E\cap\binom{S}{2}\) are the selected vertices and edges.
\(S\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=(S,F)\) is connected.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard cut characterization of connectivity in a finite selected subgraph
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity of a nonempty selected subgraph in a finite undirected host graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The connected-subgraph constraint holds when every pair of vertices in \(S\) is joined by a path using only edges of \(F\). Equivalently, every nonempty proper subset \(W\subset S\) has a selected edge crossing its cut: \[F\cap\delta_G(W)\ne\varnothing,\qquad \delta_G(W)=\{\{u,v\}\in E:u\in W,\ v\in S\setminus W\}.\] No restriction is imposed on cycles, branching degrees, or the number of selected edges beyond incidence in \(S\) and connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every two selected vertices must be linked by selected edges; cycles and branching are allowed.
knowledge_statements.title: Connected-Subgraph Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-based and cut-based connectivity characterizations agree and correctly allow cycles and branching. The definition fits the terminal container, but no source reference with an inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Path–Subgraph Structural Boundary
children.top_down_role: Branching, endpoint, and degree distinctions separating paths from general connected subgraphs.

assumptions_latex: \(H=(S,F)\) is a finite, nonempty, undirected selected subgraph.
A path means a simple path, including a one-vertex path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is a path}\iff H\text{ is connected and acyclic and }\max_{v\in S}\deg_H(v)\le2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary structural boundary between paths and connected subgraphs
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp undirected boundary separating simple paths from arbitrary connected selected subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A connected-subgraph constraint becomes a path constraint exactly after imposing both acyclicity and maximum selected degree two: \[H\text{ is a path}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H\text{ is connected},\ |F|=|S|-1,\ \max_{v\in S}\deg_H(v)\le2.\] Neither added restriction is redundant. A selected cycle is connected and has maximum degree two but is not a path, while the four-vertex star is connected and acyclic but is not a path because its center has degree three.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paths are exactly connected, acyclic subgraphs of maximum degree two; cycles and branching witness the two distinct failure modes.
knowledge_statements.title: Path–Subgraph Structural Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly identifies acyclicity and maximum degree two as the restrictions separating paths from general connected subgraphs, and failure_boundary is appropriate for this boundary leaf. An authoritative source with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: Tree Constraints
children.top_down_role: Undirected connected acyclic structures over selected graph elements.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(S\subseteq V\) is nonempty and \(F\subseteq E\cap\binom{S}{2}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=(S,F)\) is a tree.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite undirected tree characterization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrooted tree constraint on a selected subgraph of a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The tree constraint holds precisely when the selected subgraph \(T=(S,F)\) is connected and acyclic. For finite \(S\), this is equivalent to either of the following complete characterizations: \[T\text{ is connected and }|F|=|S|-1,\] or \[T\text{ is acyclic and }|F|=|S|-1.\] Thus a feasible selection contains a unique simple path between each pair of selected vertices. The case \(|S|=1\) is feasible exactly when \(F=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The selected undirected subgraph must be connected and cycle-free, equivalently connected with one fewer edge than vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite undirected tree characterizations, unique-path consequence, and singleton case are correct, and definition is the appropriate content kind. No inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Rooted Arborescence Constraints
children.top_down_role: Rooted directed tree structures with orientation requirements.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(r\in S\subseteq V\) is the designated root.
\(B\subseteq A\cap(S\times S)\) is the selected arc set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=(S,B)\) is an out-arborescence rooted at \(r\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard indegree-and-reachability definition of an out-arborescence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Out-arborescence convention: all selected vertices are reachable from the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rooted arborescence constraint holds precisely when \(r\) has selected indegree zero, every other selected vertex has selected indegree one, and every selected vertex is reachable from \(r\) in \(R=(S,B)\): \[\deg_R^-(r)=0,\qquad \deg_R^-(v)=1\quad(v\in S\setminus\{r\}),\qquad r\leadsto_R v\quad(v\in S).\] These conditions imply \(|B|=|S|-1\), exclude directed cycles, and give a unique directed path from \(r\) to each \(v\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The root has no incoming arc, every other selected vertex has one, and all selected vertices are reachable from the root.
knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Arborescence Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indegree and root-reachability conditions correctly characterize a finite out-arborescence and imply the stated edge count, acyclicity, and unique root paths. The definition fits the leaf, but it lacks a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Rooting–Orientation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of introducing a root and directed arcs.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(S,F)\) is a finite undirected tree.
\(r\in S\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) has a unique orientation that is an out-arborescence rooted at \(r\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard bijection between rooted undirected trees and out-arborescences
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence for a fixed root under the out-arborescence orientation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each edge \(\{u,v\}\in F\), orient it from the endpoint nearer to \(r\) toward the endpoint farther from \(r\). The resulting arc set is \[B_r=\{(u,v):\{u,v\}\in F,\ \operatorname{dist}_T(r,v)=\operatorname{dist}_T(r,u)+1\}.\] Then \((S,B_r)\) is the unique out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) whose underlying undirected graph is \(T\). Conversely, forgetting arc orientations in any out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) produces an undirected tree. Without specifying \(r\), the orientation is not uniquely determined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing a root uniquely orients every tree edge away from it; forgetting those orientations recovers the underlying tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Rooting–Orientation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-root orientation correspondence is correct, explicitly distinguishes the unrooted case, and representation fits the structural-boundary container. No inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Set Inclusion Relations
children.top_down_role: Subset and containment relations among finite-domain set variables.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite universe.
\(A,B\subseteq U\) are set-variable values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\subseteq B\).

notation.meaning: incidence indicators of membership in the two sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary incidence characterization of finite-set inclusion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-incidence formulation of inclusion between two finite-domain set variables.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B,C\) are subsets of a common universe \(U\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation consequences obtained by composing inclusion with set disjointness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Inclusion propagates disjointness downward: \[A\subseteq B\ \land\ B\cap C=\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\cap C=\varnothing.\] Dually, disjointness propagates upward through inclusion on the opposite side only in the contrapositive sense: if \(A\subseteq B\) and \(A\cap C\ne\varnothing\), then \(B\cap C\ne\varnothing\). A sharper same-pair interaction is \[A\subseteq B\ \land\ A\cap B=\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A=\varnothing.\] These implications are exact logical consequences of the two relations and require no cardinality assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of a set disjoint from another set is also disjoint from it; inclusion plus same-pair disjointness forces emptiness.
knowledge_statements.title: Inclusion–Disjointness Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: All stated implications between inclusion, disjointness, and nonempty intersection are correct, and property is appropriate for the interaction leaf. No inspectable citation is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set-partition constraint holds precisely when the sets cover \(U\) and are pairwise disjoint: \[\bigcup_{i=1}^m A_i=U,\qquad A_i\cap A_j=\varnothing\quad(i\ne j).\] Equivalently, every element of \(U\) belongs to exactly one part. With membership indicators \(z_{iu}=\mathbf 1[u\in A_i]\), this is represented exactly by \[\sum_{i=1}^m z_{iu}=1\qquad\text{for every }u\in U.\] Under the convention used here, labeled parts may be empty; if nonempty parts are required, one additionally imposes \(\sum_{u\in U}z_{iu}\ge1\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard contracting, monotone, solution-preserving propagator model on finite domain stores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain-reduction operator for \(c\) is a map \(F\) on domain stores such that, for all stores \(D\) and \(E\): contractingness means \(F(D)_x\subseteq D_x\) for every \(x\in V\); monotonicity means \(D_x\subseteq E_x\) for all \(x\in V\) implies \(F(D)_x\subseteq F(E)_x\) for all \(x\in V\); and solution preservation means \(\operatorname{Sol}(c,F(D))=\operatorname{Sol}(c,D)\). Domains of variables outside \(S\) are unchanged: \(F(D)_x=D_x\) for \(x\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain-reduction operator contracts domains monotonically without deleting any solution of its constraint and leaves variables outside the constraint scope unchanged.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Fixpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States finite termination and the greatest-common-fixpoint result for fair chaotic iteration of contracting monotone propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A store \(D^*\) is a common propagation fixpoint of \(\mathcal F\) when \[F_i(D^*)=D^*\qquad\text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}.\] Starting from \(D^0\), define \(D^{k+1}=F_{i_k}(D^k)\). If the schedule is fair in the sense that every operator that is not at a fixpoint is eventually selected, then the iteration terminates after finitely many strict reductions at a common fixpoint \(D^*\). Moreover, \(D^*\) is the greatest common fixpoint contained in \(D^0\) under componentwise inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair iteration of a finite family of contracting monotone propagators on finite stores terminates at the greatest common fixpoint contained in the initial store.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{F_1,\ldots,F_m\}\) is a finite family of contracting, monotone operators on finite domain stores.
\(D^0\) is the initial domain store.
The schedule is fair: every operator that is not at a fixpoint is eventually selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration terminates at the greatest store \(D^*\subseteq D^0\) satisfying \(F_i(D^*)=D^*\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).

notation.meaning: Greatest common propagation fixpoint below the initial store

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idempotence is stated relative to complete execution on one current store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The propagator \(F\) is idempotent when \[F(F(D))=F(D)\qquad\text{for every domain store }D.\] Thus, after \(F\) has completed on \(D\), immediately executing it again without any intervening domain change performs no further reduction. Idempotence concerns repeated application of the same propagator; it does not imply that \(F\) remains at a fixpoint after another propagator reduces a variable in its scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An idempotent propagator reaches its own fixpoint in one complete execution, although later reductions by other propagators can make it useful again.
knowledge_statements.title: Idempotent Propagators

children.title: Incremental Propagators

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Propagators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies semantic equivalence between incremental and from-scratch propagation after further deletions from the preceding output store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incremental implementation first computes and installs \(\bar D=F(D)\), leaving persistent state \(\sigma\) valid for \(\bar D\). If subsequent propagation produces a store \(D'\subseteq\bar D\), the implementation receives the new deletion events \(\Delta=\bar D\setminus D'\), updates \(\sigma\), and returns a store \(E\) and updated state \(\sigma'\). Correctness requires \[E=F(D').\] Initialization constructs the persistent state from the first input store, and each execution processes all events relevant to \(F\) before returning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incremental propagator reuses state from its preceding output and processes later deletions, while returning exactly the store that a complete execution on the new current store would return.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a propagator whose input stores change only through deletion of domain values.
The preceding execution installed \(\bar D=F(D)\), and \(\sigma\) is valid for \(\bar D\).
The new current store satisfies \(D'\subseteq\bar D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Processing \(\Delta=\bar D\setminus D'\) with the persistent state returns \(E=F(D')\).

notation.meaning: Installed output of the preceding execution
Deletion events since the preceding execution

children.title: Reexecution Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Scheduling and state-maintenance consequences of the two properties.

knowledge_statements.title: Reexecution Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes fair deferral from safe suppression and states a simple expected-cost criterion for event filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After a propagator reaches a fixpoint, its reexecution may be suppressed until a later event only when the scheduler can establish that no event observed since its last execution can make it productive. An execution that may be productive can still be deferred, but fairness requires it eventually to occur. In a simple per-opportunity cost model, where a relevance test costs \(C_{\mathrm{test}}\), execution costs \(C_{\mathrm{run}}\), and the test admits execution with probability \(p\), testing has lower expected cost than unconditional execution when \[C_{\mathrm{test}}+pC_{\mathrm{run}}<C_{\mathrm{run}}.\] This cost inequality is not a correctness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scheduler may defer a potentially productive execution but must eventually perform it; it may suppress reexecution until another event only when no observed event can have invalidated the propagator's fixpoint. Event testing is worthwhile only when its expected cost is below unconditional execution.
assumptions_latex: Propagation uses a finite family of sound, contracting operators.
The scheduler is fair to every operator that may be productive.
For the displayed cost comparison, \(C_{\mathrm{test}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{run}}\) are per-opportunity costs and \(p\) is the probability that the test admits execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Correctness permits fair deferral, while suppression until another event is safe only when the current event information establishes that the propagator remains at a fixpoint.

notation.meaning: Cost of testing whether reexecution is relevant
