knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clique-coloring family separating adjacent consistency levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the variables be the \(k+1\) vertices of \(K_{k+1}\), give every variable domain \(D=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), and impose \(x_i\neq x_j\) on every pair. Any consistent assignment to at most \(k-1\) variables uses distinct colors and extends to any additional variable using an unused color; hence the instance is strongly \(k\)-consistent. An assignment of distinct colors to \(k\) variables cannot extend to the remaining variable, so the instance is not \((k+1)\)-consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A (k+1)-clique with only k colors is strongly k-consistent but not (k+1)-consistent, separating the two levels.
knowledge_statements.title: Consistency-Level Separation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample content kind is appropriate for the Consistency-Level Separation leaf. The clique-coloring family does separate strong k-consistency from (k+1)-consistency for k at least 2, and the plain and formal statements agree. A specific authoritative citation is still required for this nontrivial separation claim.

assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite.
Arc consistency is the chosen underlying propagation property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every variable-value choice survives arc-consistency propagation when tested as a singleton assignment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interprets singleton consistency as singleton arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite CSP \(P\) is singleton arc consistent if, for every variable \(x\) and every value \(a\in D_x\), enforcing arc consistency on \(P|_{x=a}\) leaves every variable domain nonempty. Thus each currently retained value can be fixed temporarily without arc-consistency propagation detecting inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CSP is singleton arc consistent when fixing any retained value and enforcing arc consistency never empties a domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Singleton Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record precisely defines singleton arc consistency, but the immutable leaf is titled Singleton Consistency and does not itself establish that singleton consistency must mean the arc-consistency variant. A source tied to this terminology and local scope is required before deciding whether the definition exactly fits the terminal container.

children.title: AC-3 Arc Consistency
children.top_down_role: The classical revision-based arc-consistency family.

assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite, binary, and represented by directed constraint arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output domains are the arc-consistent closure of the input domains, or a domain wipeout certifies inconsistency.

notation.meaning: queue of directed arcs awaiting revision

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical AC-3 for binary extensional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(Q\) with every directed constraint arc. Repeatedly remove \((x,y)\) from \(Q\) and delete each \(a\in D_x\) for which no \(b\in D_y\) satisfies \((a,b)\in R_{xy}\). If \(D_x=\varnothing\), stop with failure. If \(D_x\) changed, insert every \((z,x)\) with \(z\neq y\) into \(Q\). Stop when \(Q=\varnothing\) and output the remaining domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AC-3 repeatedly revises queued arcs and requeues affected neighbors until all values have support or some domain becomes empty.
knowledge_statements.title: AC-3 Arc Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind for AC-3, and the operational description is broadly recognizable. Exact correctness depends on directed-arc orientation, inverse-relation handling, and the precise set of arcs reinserted after a deletion. Those details require an authoritative algorithm citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Queue-Based Revision Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Worklist organization for pending arc revisions.

assumptions_latex: Each revision operator only deletes unsupported values.
The CSP and all domains are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fair queue schedule terminates at the common arc-consistent closure, independently of the fair processing order.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling abstraction for queue-driven arc revision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(Q\) with all directed arcs. Select and remove an arc \((x,y)\), apply \(\operatorname{Revise}_{xy}\), and, whenever \(D_x\) shrinks, enqueue each arc whose support status may thereby change. A schedule is fair when every arc that remains enabled is eventually processed. Stop on domain wipeout or when \(Q\) is empty; in the latter case output \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queue scheduling processes revisions fairly and requeues exactly those arcs whose supports may have been invalidated by a deletion.
knowledge_statements.title: Queue-Based Revision Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic scheduling abstraction fits the leaf, but the statement says only to enqueue arcs whose support status may change and does not define that dependency set exactly. The assumptions and conclusion also assert order-independent convergence to a common closure, which is not established by the uncited operational statement. A source specifying the revision system, fairness condition, and fixed-point result is required.

children.title: Queue-Discipline Variants
children.top_down_role: Ordering policies and their operational consequences for revision worklists.

assumptions_latex: Every variant enqueues all initially relevant arcs and is fair.
Revisions and dependency-triggered reinsertions are identical across variants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: FIFO, LIFO, priority, and duplicate-suppressing disciplines compute the same closure, although their work and memory usage may differ.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares fair worklist disciplines for the same revision system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each discipline repeatedly chooses an element of \(Q\), applies the same contracting revision operators, and fairly processes every revision enabled by a domain deletion. Because the domains form a finite product lattice and the operators delete exactly unsupported values, every such discipline terminates at the same greatest common fixed point below the initial domains. The disciplines can nevertheless perform different numbers of redundant revisions and attain different maximum queue sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair FIFO, LIFO, priority, and duplicate-suppressing queues reach the same arc-consistent closure but may require different work and storage.
knowledge_statements.title: Queue-Discipline Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is an appropriate content kind for comparing queue disciplines. However, contraction and fairness alone are not a sufficiently explicit general basis for the stated greatest-common-fixed-point conclusion; the required monotonicity, revision semantics, and triggering conditions need authoritative support. The listed queue disciplines also require precise fairness and duplicate-suppression conventions.

children.title: AC-4 Support Maintenance
children.top_down_role: The AC-4 family viewed through explicit support maintenance.

assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite, binary, and extensional.
Support lists and counters are initialized from the current domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination without wipeout yields arc-consistent domains maintained by explicit support counts.

notation.meaning: number of current supports for value \(a\) across arc \((x,y)\)
reverse list of value-arc pairs supported by \((y,b)\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational AC-4 support-counting formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every directed arc \((x,y)\) and \(a\in D_x\), initialize \(c_{xy}(a)=|\{b\in D_y:(a,b)\in R_{xy}\}|\), and place the corresponding dependency in each \(S(y,b)\). Delete and enqueue every \((x,a)\) having a zero counter. While \(Q\neq\varnothing\), dequeue \((y,b)\), decrement every still-relevant counter indexed by \(S(y,b)\), and enqueue any newly unsupported value. Stop on domain wipeout or output the remaining domains when \(Q\) empties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AC-4 stores all supports, counts them, and propagates each value deletion by decrementing the counters that depended on that value.
knowledge_statements.title: AC-4 Support Maintenance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct role for AC-4 Support Maintenance, and the support-counting outline matches the intended family. The exact reverse-list entries, initialization propagation, duplicate-deletion handling, and decrement conditions are not specified with enough precision to validate this as classical AC-4 without a cited algorithm definition.

children.title: Support-Counting Methods
children.top_down_role: Arc-consistency approaches organized around maintained support counts.

assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite and binary.
Each allowed support pair is represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deleting a value updates precisely the counters of values for which it was a recorded support.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic support-counting invariant behind AC-4-type methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\operatorname{Supp}_{xy}(a)=\{b\in D_y:(a,b)\in R_{xy}\}\), store \(c_{xy}(a)=|\operatorname{Supp}_{xy}(a)|\), and record \((x,a,x,y)\) in \(S(y,b)\) for each \(b\in\operatorname{Supp}_{xy}(a)\). When \(b\) is deleted from \(D_y\), decrement exactly the counters referenced by \(S(y,b)\). Delete \(a\) as soon as some required counter \(c_{xy}(a)\) reaches zero; stop at a fixed point or domain wipeout.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support-counting methods store forward counts and reverse dependencies so each deletion updates exactly the values that used the deleted support.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Counting Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the Support-Counting Methods leaf and algorithm is a defensible content kind. The stored tuple (x,a,x,y) contains a repeated x and is neither defined nor clearly sufficient to identify the counter c_xy(a), making the exact update rule unreliable. An authoritative source is needed to resolve the dependency representation before mathematical revision.

children.title: Support-Storage Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Memory and revision-work consequences of explicit support information.

assumptions_latex: There are \(e\) binary constraints and every domain has size at most \(d\).
Constraints are represented extensionally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full support storage permits incremental constant-time counter updates per stored dependency but may require \(\Theta(ed^2)\) auxiliary entries.

notation.meaning: number of allowed support pairs stored over directed arcs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case auxiliary-space tradeoff for explicit support dependencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Explicitly storing every support and its reverse dependency uses \(\Theta(M)\) auxiliary entries, where \(M\leq 2ed^2\), hence \(O(ed^2)\) worst-case space. Each stored dependency is invalidated at most once as values are deleted, enabling direct counter updates. Storing only one current support per value-arc pair reduces support memory toward \(O(ed)\), but loss of that support can require searching the corresponding relation for a replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Storing all supports costs quadratic domain space per constraint but makes deletion updates direct; storing one support saves space but requires replacement searches.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Storage Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound is the correct role for this tradeoff leaf. The stated O(ed^2) full-support space and O(ed) single-support space are plausible under directed-arc and auxiliary-entry conventions, but the use of Theta(M), the bound M at most 2ed^2, and the replacement-search tradeoff require a cited complexity model and specific locator.

children.title: AC-6 Support Maintenance
children.top_down_role: Support-oriented arc consistency associated with the AC-6 family.

assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite, binary, and extensional.
Each domain has a fixed order used when searching for supports.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm terminates with arc-consistent domains or detects a domain wipeout while storing one current support per value-arc pair plus reverse dependencies.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-reuse description of classical binary AC-6.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \((x,y)\) and \(a\in D_x\), choose the least current \(b\in D_y\) satisfying \((a,b)\in R_{xy}\), set \(s_{xy}(a)=b\), and add \((x,a,x,y)\) to \(L(y,b)\); delete \(a\) if none exists. When \((y,b)\) is dequeued from \(Q\), seek for every dependent value its next valid support after \(b\), move its dependency if found, and otherwise delete and enqueue that value. Stop at queue exhaustion or domain wipeout.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AC-6 keeps one ordered current support per value and searches forward for a replacement only when that support is deleted.
knowledge_statements.title: AC-6 Support Maintenance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the appropriate content kind for AC-6 Support Maintenance, but the description is not sufficiently sourced to distinguish classical AC-6 from a generic one-current-support scheme. Exact AC-6 initialization, ordered support search, reverse dependency maintenance, symmetry assumptions, and deletion propagation must be checked against an authoritative algorithm statement.

children.title: AC-2001 Support Reuse
children.top_down_role: Last-support reuse within the AC-2001 family.

knowledge_statements.title: AC-2001 Support Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary finite-domain AC-2001 with one remembered support per directed arc and value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given binary constraints and finite current domains, store for every directed constraint arc \((x,y,C_{xy})\) and value \(a\in D(x)\) a residue \(r[x,a,y]\in D(y)\) previously satisfying \((a,r[x,a,y])\in C_{xy}\). To revise \(D(x)\), retain \(a\) when its residue remains in \(D(y)\); otherwise search \(D(y)\) for \(b\) with \((a,b)\in C_{xy}\), replace the residue by such a \(b\), and delete \(a\) if none exists. Whenever deletion changes \(D(x)\), schedule every neighboring revision that may have lost support. Stop when the revision queue is empty or some domain is empty; the nonempty result is arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AC-2001 validates each remembered support, searches only when it has become invalid, deletes unsupported values, and repeats affected revisions to an arc-consistent fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(D(x)\) is finite for every variable \(x\).
Each binary relation \(C_{xy}\subseteq D_0(x)\times D_0(y)\) is fixed while propagation runs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(x)\neq\varnothing\) for all \(x\) implies every remaining directed-arc value has a current support.

notation.meaning: Remembered support in the current or a former domain of y.
Binary constraint relation on x and y.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The procedure is a sound queue-based residue-revalidation algorithm, but the record does not establish the AC-2001-specific support-ordering and last-support behavior that distinguishes this leaf from generic residue methods. An authoritative AC-2001 algorithm locator is required before the exact algorithmic identity can be accepted.

children.title: Residue Methods
children.top_down_role: Cached support witnesses used across repeated propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Residue Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct reuse of cached witnesses by propagators over shrinking finite domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constraint \(C\) with current domains \(D\), a residue for a literal \(x=a\) is a previously found tuple \(t\in C\) satisfying \(t_x=a\). A propagator may accept the residue without a new support search exactly when \(t_y\in D(y)\) for every \(y\in\operatorname{scope}(C)\). If that test fails, the residue is only a search hint: the propagator must find a current supporting tuple or delete \(a\). Thus residues may be stale but cannot compromise correctness when every reuse is validated against all current domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cached support may justify retaining a value only after every component is checked against current domains; otherwise a fresh support search is required.
assumptions_latex: Domains only shrink between creation and reuse of a residue.
The constraint relation \(C\) does not change during propagation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validated residue reuse preserves the same supported values as a complete current-domain support test.

notation.meaning: Cached supporting tuple, called a residue.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residue-validation principle is mathematically coherent, properly scoped to shrinking domains, and uses an appropriate content kind, but no inspectable source is supplied for the claimed equivalence with a complete current-domain support test.

children.title: Support-Reuse Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases affecting the usefulness or validity checking cost of cached supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Reuse Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by treating an unvalidated cached support as a current witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(x)=D(y)=\{0,1\}\) and let \(C_{xy}=\{(0,0),(1,1)\}\). Suppose the cached support for \(x=0\) is \(y=0\). After another propagator deletes \(0\) from \(D(y)\), the cached pair still belongs to \(C_{xy}\) but is no longer a current support. Any reuse procedure that retains \(x=0\) without testing membership of the cached witness in \(D(y)\) terminates with a non-arc-consistent domain. Support reuse is therefore sound only across changes known not to invalidate the witness, or after explicit current-domain validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cached tuple ceases to support a value when any component leaves its domain; blindly reusing it can leave an unsupported value.
assumptions_latex: Propagation may delete values after a residue is stored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure to validate the residue can leave \(0\in D(x)\) although no \(b\in D(y)\) satisfies \((0,b)\in C_{xy}\).

notation.meaning: Equality relation restricted to two Boolean values.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Generic Generalized-Arc Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Queue-driven generalized-arc consistency for arbitrary extensional finite-domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a queue with every constraint. When \(C\) is removed, inspect each \(x\in\operatorname{scope}(C)\) and \(a\in D(x)\). Delete \(a\) unless there exists \(t\in C\) such that \(t_x=a\) and \(t_y\in D(y)\) for every \(y\in\operatorname{scope}(C)\). If \(D(x)\) changes, enqueue every constraint containing \(x\) whose support status may change. Report inconsistency if a domain becomes empty; otherwise stop when the queue is empty. Because domains are finite and only shrink, the algorithm terminates, and its nonempty fixed point is generalized-arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly delete values lacking a compatible tuple in each incident constraint and reschedule affected constraints until failure or a generalized-arc-consistent fixed point.
assumptions_latex: Every variable domain and every extensional constraint relation is finite.
Queued constraints are eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At successful termination, every \(a\in D(x)\) has a supporting tuple in every constraint containing \(x\).

notation.meaning: Component of tuple t assigned to x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The queue-driven generalized-arc algorithm and its finite-domain termination conclusion are standard and internally consistent, but the cited general constraint-programming section is not demonstrated to contain this exact algorithm, fairness condition, or fixed-point conclusion. A dedicated GAC algorithm locator is required.

children.title: Matching-Based Propagators
children.top_down_role: Global filtering organized around matching structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Based Propagators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain consistency criterion for the finite all-different constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\), form the bipartite value graph \(G=(X,V,E)\), where \(V=\bigcup_i D(x_i)\) and \((x_i,a)\in E\) exactly when \(a\in D(x_i)\). The all-different constraint is feasible exactly when \(G\) has a matching covering every vertex of \(X\). Moreover, a value \(a\in D(x_i)\) has support exactly when some matching covering \(X\) contains \((x_i,a)\). Hence a matching-based domain-consistency propagator reports failure when no covering matching exists and otherwise removes precisely the edges belonging to no covering matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All-different is feasible exactly when its variable–value graph has a variable-covering matching; a value survives exactly when such a matching uses its edge.
assumptions_latex: All domains \(D(x_i)\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) is retained in \(D(x_i)\) if and only if \((x_i,a)\) belongs to a matching covering \(X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variable-value matching representation and support criterion are correctly formulated for finite all-different, and representation is suitable for this leaf. No source with a theorem or section locator is supplied for the matching characterization and exact edge pruning.

children.title: Flow-Based Propagators
children.top_down_role: Global filtering organized around capacitated network-flow structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Based Propagators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact propagation through an integral network-flow encoding of a finite-domain constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a constraint \(C\) admit a directed capacitated network \(N(D)\) whose integral feasible flows are in projection-preserving correspondence with tuples of \(C\) compatible with the current domains \(D\). Then \(C\) is feasible exactly when \(N(D)\) has an integral feasible flow. If the assignment \(x=a\) is represented by a designated arc or arc set \(A_{x,a}\), the value \(a\) is supported exactly when an integral feasible flow uses the prescribed assignment structure. A flow-based domain propagator deletes \(a\) when no such flow exists and reports failure when the network itself is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under an exact integral-flow encoding, constraint feasibility equals network feasibility, and a value survives exactly when some feasible flow realizes its assignment arcs.
assumptions_latex: The network encoding preserves feasible tuples in both directions.
Integral feasible flows can be distinguished from merely fractional flows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Network feasibility and assignment-constrained network feasibility provide exact failure and value-support tests for \(C\).

notation.meaning: Network induced by the current domains.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim is valid conditional on the asserted projection-preserving integral-flow correspondence, but that strong encoding assumption and the assignment-support test require a specific flow-propagation source. Without one, the intended scope and exactness cannot be independently verified.

children.title: Network-Structure Selection
children.top_down_role: Constraint characteristics favoring matching or flow representations.

assumptions_latex: The intended consistency level requires exact support tests.
The selected flow model is integral or explicitly enforces integrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated predicates, network infeasibility certifies constraint failure and assignment-restricted network infeasibility certifies absence of support.

notation.meaning: Constraint tuples compatible with all current domains.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for choosing an exact network representation for propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network structure is sufficient for exact propagation of a constraint \(C\) over domains \(D\) when three predicates hold: every integral feasible network flow projects to a tuple in \(C\cap\prod_x D(x)\); every tuple in that set lifts to an integral feasible flow; and, for every assignment \(x=a\), flows realizing \(x=a\) are identifiable by an exact arc restriction or flow condition. Under these predicates, network infeasibility certifies constraint failure and restricted-network infeasibility certifies absence of support. If the two-way correspondence fails, network feasibility alone is only a relaxation and does not establish exact domain consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network representation supports exact pruning when integral flows and feasible tuples correspond in both directions and each assignment has an exact flow-feasibility test; without that correspondence, network feasibility alone is only a relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Network-Structure Selection
Dynamic-Programming Propagators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation using an exact layered state-transition representation of feasible tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent the constraint by a finite layered acyclic graph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and one layer per decision position; an arc labeled \(a\) at layer \(i\) represents choosing \(x_i=a\). Remove arcs whose labels are absent from current domains. Compute states reachable from \(s\) and states from which \(t\) is reachable. Report failure if \(t\) is unreachable. Otherwise delete \(a\in D(x_i)\) exactly when no arc labeled \(a\) in layer \(i\) has a reachable tail and a co-reachable head. Repeat after domain changes when the graph representation is maintained incrementally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an exact layered dynamic program, retain a value exactly when one of its transitions lies on a surviving source-to-sink path.
assumptions_latex: Source-to-sink paths correspond exactly to feasible tuples.
The layered state graph is finite and acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After filtering, every retained value labels a transition on at least one feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) path.

notation.meaning: Source and sink states of the dynamic program.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-filtering algorithm is correct under the exact layered-graph correspondence, and algorithm fits the leaf. The cited general dynamic-programming chapter is not shown to support constraint-propagator pruning by reachable and co-reachable transitions, so a dedicated locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Propagators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compulsory-part timetable propagation for a single cumulative resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonpreemptive activity \(i\), let its start domain be finite, its duration be \(p_i>0\), and its resource demand be \(r_i>0\), with capacity \(C\). Define \(EST_i=\min D(S_i)\), \(LST_i=\max D(S_i)\), and \(ECT_i=EST_i+p_i\). Activity \(i\) is compulsory on \([LST_i,ECT_i)\) when \(LST_i<ECT_i\). Form the compulsory profile \(P(t)\). Report failure if \(P(t)>C\) for some \(t\); delete a candidate start \(s\) when executing \(i\) on \([s,s+p_i)\), excluding its own compulsory contribution, would exceed capacity at some time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Timetable propagation builds a compulsory resource profile, detects overloads, and removes starts whose execution would exceed capacity alongside other compulsory activity.
assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive and use one renewable resource.
Start-time domains are finite integer sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every retained start passes the compulsory-profile capacity test, and any profile overload certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: Sum of demands compulsory at time t.
Earliest start, latest start, and earliest completion of activity i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compulsory-part profile, overload test, and candidate-start pruning rule are coherent for a single renewable resource with nonpreemptive activities. The algorithmic claim requires a scheduling-propagation source with a specific section, theorem, or algorithm locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Driven Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental propagation driven by subscribed domain-change events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate each propagator \(p\) with a subscription set \(S_p\) of events, such as value deletion, bound change, or variable fixation. Initialize the event queue with changes induced by model posting. When an event \(e\) occurs, enqueue each nonqueued \(p\) with \(e\in S_p\). Executing \(p\) may delete domain values and emit further events; each emitted event schedules its subscribers. A propagator may be omitted only when the event abstraction guarantees that no unreported change can invalidate its local fixed point. Stop with failure on an empty domain, or successfully when no scheduled propagator remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain changes emit events that wake subscribed propagators; processing continues until a domain empties or the event and propagator queues become empty.
assumptions_latex: Each subscription covers every change capable of invalidating the propagator's fixed point.
Scheduled propagators are eventually executed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful quiescence is a common local fixed point of all correctly subscribed propagators.

notation.meaning: Events to which propagator p subscribes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The event-subscription algorithm and quiescence conclusion are valid only with complete wake-up subscriptions and fair execution, which the record states. The cited general CP section is not demonstrated to support these event-engine details or the common-fixed-point conclusion.

children.title: Propagator Scheduling Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies governing selection of pending propagator work.

assumptions_latex: \(L\) is finite.
Every \(p\in P\) is monotone and contracting.
A propagator \(p\) is enabled at \(D\) exactly when \(p(D)\neq D\).
Every enabled propagator is eventually executed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal store equals the greatest \(D\subseteq D_0\) satisfying \(p(D)=D\) for every \(p\in P\).

notation.meaning: Finite lattice of domain stores ordered by componentwise inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order independence under fair chaotic iteration of monotone contracting propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the finite lattice of domain stores ordered by componentwise inclusion, let \(P\) be a finite family of monotone, contracting propagators on \(L\), and call \(p\in P\) enabled at store \(D\) when \(p(D)\neq D\). Starting from \(D_0\), repeatedly choose an enabled propagator and replace \(D\) by \(p(D)\). If every enabled propagator is eventually executed, the sequence terminates at the greatest common fixed point of \(P\) contained in \(D_0\). Consequently, FIFO, LIFO, and priority policies produce the same closure whenever their scheduling and wake-up mechanisms ensure this fairness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair execution of monotone contracting propagators over a finite domain-store lattice terminates at the same greatest common fixed point regardless of queue order.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagator Scheduling Policies

children.title: Propagator Priority Classes
children.top_down_role: Priority strata based on propagator cost, expected pruning, or event type.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagator Priority Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dispatcher representation using ordered classes and fair queues within each class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=P_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}P_k\) be priority classes, where a smaller index denotes higher priority, and maintain one fair queue \(Q_i\) per class. A strict-priority dispatcher selects the least \(i\) with \(Q_i\neq\varnothing\), removes one propagator from \(Q_i\), executes it, and enqueues newly enabled propagators in their assigned queues. This representation changes execution order, not propagator semantics. It is globally fair only if higher classes eventually quiesce or the dispatcher includes aging, quotas, or another mechanism ensuring that every continuously enabled lower-priority propagator is eventually selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Priority classes use separate ordered queues; strict priority is globally fair only when high-priority work quiesces or an anti-starvation mechanism is added.
assumptions_latex: Each propagator belongs to exactly one priority class.
Each class queue is internally fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Priority dispatch preserves fixed-point semantics under global fairness but otherwise may indefinitely postpone lower-priority propagators.

notation.meaning: Propagators assigned to priority class i.
Ready queue for priority class i.

children.title: Fairness–Starvation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Execution-balance risks created by scheduling and priority choices.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is finite and each propagator is monotone and contracting.
The domain-state lattice is finite.
A propagator \(p\) is enabled at \(D\) exactly when \(p(D)\subsetneq D\), and dispatch updates the current state to its image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fair execution terminates at a state \(D^*\) satisfying \(p(D^*)=D^*\) for every \(p\in P\); without fairness, an execution may starve an enabled propagator and either run indefinitely or stop under an incomplete scheduler criterion before reaching a common fixpoint.
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses fair propagator scheduling or starvation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when dispatch scheduling reaches the common propagation fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite set of monotone, contracting propagators on a finite domain-state lattice, and repeatedly dispatch enabled members of \(P\). If the schedule is fair—every propagator that is enabled is eventually dispatched—then every execution terminates at a common fixpoint of \(P\). Without fairness, an enabled propagator may be starved: for \(P=\{p,q\}\), an execution that repeatedly selects only an idempotent \(p\) while \(q(D)\subsetneq D\) does not reach a common fixpoint. A dispatcher that treats this unfair state as quiescent may also stop prematurely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair scheduling reaches a common propagation fixpoint; an unfair dispatcher may starve an enabled propagator, causing nontermination or premature scheduler-level quiescence.

children.title: Trailing-Based Restoration
children.top_down_role: State restoration through recorded reversible changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Trailing-Based Restoration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restores mutable finite-domain state by undoing logged changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a mutable search state \(S\) and a trail \(T\). On entering decision level \(k\), record marker \(m_k=|T|\). Before destructively changing a restorable location \(u\) for the first time at level \(k\), append its previous value \((u,S[u])\) to \(T\), then perform the update and propagation. To backtrack from level \(k\), pop entries in reverse order while \(|T|>m_k\), assigning each saved value back to its location. Remove the marker and output the state that existed on entry to level \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trail records overwritten state once per level; backtracking reverses the log to reconstruct the state at that level’s entry.
assumptions_latex: Every mutable component affecting propagation is trailed before its first level-local change.
Trail entries are undone in last-in, first-out order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Undoing to marker \(m_k\) restores exactly the search state present when level \(k\) was entered.

notation.meaning: trail marker for decision level k

review_flags: No supplied locator supports constraint-solver trailing.

children.title: Copying-Based Restoration
children.top_down_role: State restoration through retained search-state copies.

knowledge_statements.title: Copying-Based Restoration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restores search state from a complete snapshot at each retained node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a search state \(S_k\) at decision level \(k\). Before exploring a child, create a complete snapshot \(C_k=\operatorname{copy}(S_k)\) containing every mutable component relevant to propagation. Apply the child decision and propagate on the working state. When that child finishes or fails, discard the working state and replace it by \(\operatorname{copy}(C_k)\) before exploring another child. When leaving level \(k\), discard \(C_k\). The restored output is observationally identical to \(S_k\) for every subsequent propagator and branching operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver snapshots all mutable state before a branch and restores the snapshot before exploring a sibling branch.
assumptions_latex: \(C_k\) is a deep copy of all mutable search and propagation state.
No mutable object is unintentionally shared between the snapshot and working state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing the working state by \(\operatorname{copy}(C_k)\) restores the state at entry to decision level \(k\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports copying-based constraint-solver restoration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits copying-based restoration, and the deep-copy assumptions support observational restoration. No cited source or inspectable locator supports this solver-state restoration method.

children.title: Recomputation-Based Restoration
children.top_down_role: State restoration through reconstruction from an earlier retained state.

knowledge_statements.title: Recomputation-Based Restoration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstructs a search state by replaying decisions from a retained checkpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Retain a checkpoint state \(S_j\) and the ordered decisions \((d_{j+1},\ldots,d_k)\) leading to level \(k\). To restore level \(k\), copy \(S_j\); then, for each \(i=j+1,\ldots,k\), impose \(d_i\) and run the prescribed propagation procedure to quiescence. Output the resulting state \(\widehat S_k\). If propagation is deterministic, or has a schedule-independent common fixpoint, and the same propagators and decisions are replayed, then \(\widehat S_k=S_k\), the state originally reached at level \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver restores a node by loading an earlier checkpoint and replaying the intervening decisions and propagation.
assumptions_latex: The checkpoint \(S_j\) and decision sequence are preserved.
Replayed propagation is deterministic or reaches a schedule-independent common fixpoint.
Propagators have no unrecorded history-dependent effects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replay reconstructs \(\widehat S_k=S_k\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports recomputation-based constraint-solver restoration.

children.title: Restoration-Strategy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Memory, runtime, and implementation consequences across restoration strategies.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration-Strategy Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares asymptotic storage and restoration work for three standard strategies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Along a search path of depth \(h\), let the complete mutable state have size \(M\), let \(\Delta_k\) be the data changed at level \(k\), and let \(R_k\) be the work required to replay from the retained checkpoint to level \(k\). Full copying uses \(O(hM)\) stored data and restores a level in \(O(M)\) time. Trailing uses \(O(M+\sum_{k=1}^{h}|\Delta_k|)\) space and restores changes in time proportional to the number undone. Recomputation reduces stored intermediate state but may require \(O(R_k)\) restoration work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Copying favors predictable restoration, trailing stores changes, and recomputation trades lower retained state for replay time.
assumptions_latex: State copies require time and space linear in \(M\).
Each trail entry and undo operation has constant overhead.
Replay work is measured by \(R_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No strategy uniformly minimizes both retained memory and restoration work for all \(M\), \(\Delta_k\), and \(R_k\).

notation.meaning: replay work to restore level k

knowledge_statements.title: Explanation-Producing Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attaches a checkable logical reason to every propagated value deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constraint set \(C\), current decision literals \(A\), and deletion \(x\ne a\), an explanation is a finite set \(E\subseteq C\cup A\) such that \(E\models x\ne a\). An explanation-producing propagator may delete \(a\) from the domain of \(x\) only while returning such an \(E\). The certificate is independently checkable by verifying the entailment, equivalently the unsatisfiability of \(E\cup\{x=a\}\). If every emitted explanation is valid, every explained deletion is sound relative to \(C\cup A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each propagated deletion carries constraints and decisions whose conjunction logically excludes the deleted value.
assumptions_latex: All variables have finite domains.
The explanation checker decides satisfiability or entailment for the explanation language.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\models x\ne a\) certifies that deleting \(a\) from \(D(x)\) preserves every solution of \(C\cup A\).
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses explanation-producing propagation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is an appropriate role for the checkable explanations produced by propagation, and the entailment and unsatisfiability formulations agree. No cited source or locator supports this explanation model.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Local Inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that local consistency need not detect global inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y,z\) have domains \(\{0,1\}\) and impose the binary constraints \(x=y\), \(y=z\), and \(x\ne z\). Every value of every variable has a supporting value across each incident constraint, so the network is arc consistent and no domain value is removed by arc-consistency propagation. Nevertheless, the equalities imply \(x=z\), contradicting \(x\ne z\); hence the conjunction has no solution. Thus reaching a local-consistency fixpoint does not generally decide satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary network can remain arc consistent although its constraints are jointly unsatisfiable.
assumptions_latex: Propagation enforces binary arc consistency only.
Constraint supports are checked separately rather than jointly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Arc consistency does not imply satisfiability, even for three Boolean variables.
review_flags: The supplied locators do not cover local-consistency incompleteness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and Boolean arc-consistent unsatisfiable example fit the leaf and are internally correct. No authoritative local-consistency source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Loss Under Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demonstrates weaker pruning after decomposing a global all-different constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) with \(D(x_1)=D(x_2)=\{1,2\}\) and \(D(x_3)=\{1,2,3\}\). Generalized arc consistency on the global constraint detects the Hall set \(\{x_1,x_2\}\) with values \(\{1,2\}\), and therefore reduces \(D(x_3)\) to \(\{3\}\). Replace the global constraint by the three pairwise disequalities \(x_i\ne x_j\). Each value of \(x_3\), including \(1\) and \(2\), has a separate support in every disequality, so arc consistency on the decomposition performs no such deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc consistency on pairwise disequalities can prune less than generalized arc consistency on the equivalent all-different constraint.
assumptions_latex: The global propagator enforces generalized arc consistency.
The decomposition contains only pairwise disequalities enforced to arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition is solution-equivalent but propagation-weaker: it retains \(1,2\in D(x_3)\) while global propagation deletes them.

notation.meaning: constraint requiring pairwise distinct assigned values

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role exactly fits the decomposition-loss leaf, and the all-different Hall-set example is mathematically coherent. No cited source or specific locator supports the comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagator Complexity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locates an NP-completeness boundary for generalized arc-consistency support testing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a finite-domain constraint \(C\) is represented intensionally by a Boolean circuit whose satisfaction on a complete tuple is decidable in polynomial time. Given \(C\), current domains \(D\), a variable \(x\), and \(a\in D(x)\), deciding whether \(a\) has a support—a tuple \(t\in\prod_y D(y)\) satisfying \(C\) with \(t(x)=a\)—is NP-complete. Membership follows because a supporting tuple is a polynomially checkable certificate; hardness follows by encoding a Boolean satisfiability instance and fixing an auxiliary variable. Consequently, enforcing generalized arc consistency for arbitrary intensionally represented constraints is NP-hard unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For arbitrary circuit-represented constraints, testing whether a value has support is NP-complete, making full generalized arc consistency NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Constraint satisfaction for a complete tuple is polynomial-time decidable.
Circuit size and explicit domain descriptions determine input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Support testing is NP-complete, and generalized arc-consistency enforcement is NP-hard unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
review_flags: General complexity locators supplied do not specifically establish this propagator support-testing result.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the terminal container, but the candidate includes proof-style membership and hardness commentary, which this layer forbids. More importantly, the NP-completeness claim depends on the precise circuit and domain encoding model; the generic complexity inventory locators do not establish it, so an authoritative specific source is required before revision.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Propagator Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes semantic redundancy from propagation redundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) and \(R\) be constraints with \(C\models R\), and let \(p_C,p_R\) be sound, monotone, contracting propagators. Adding \(R\) does not change the solution set, but it may strengthen propagation because \(p_R(D)\subsetneq D\) can hold at a state fixed by \(p_C\). On a finite domain-state lattice, fair iteration of both propagators terminates at their greatest common fixpoint below the initial state. If every \(p_C\)-fixpoint is also a \(p_R\)-fixpoint, then \(p_R\) is propagation-redundant and cannot improve the final closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logically redundant constraint may still improve pruning; it is propagation-redundant only when it leaves every base-propagator fixpoint unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(C\models R\).
Both propagators are sound, monotone, and contracting on a finite lattice.
The joint dispatch schedule is fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Semantic redundancy preserves solutions, whereas propagation redundancy additionally requires \(p_R(D)=D\) at every \(p_C\)-fixpoint \(D\).
review_flags: The supplied redundant-inequalities locator does not establish finite-domain propagator interaction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the distinction between semantic and propagation redundancy, and the fixpoint qualification is internally coherent under the finite-lattice and fairness assumptions. children.title: Constraint-Solving Search Calculus

knowledge_statements.title: Chronological Backtracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth-first constraint search that retreats to the immediately preceding decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite-domain constraint problem. At a node, propagate to a fixpoint; if a domain is empty, report failure for that node, and if every variable is assigned, output the assignment. Otherwise choose an unassigned variable \(x\), partition its current domain into nonempty branches \(B_1,\ldots,B_r\), and explore each child obtained by imposing \(x\in B_i\). After a child fails or is exhausted, restore the parent state and try the next branch. If all branches fail, return failure only to the immediately preceding decision level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chronological backtracking explores a depth-first branch partition and, after failure, returns to the most recent unresolved decision.
assumptions_latex: Every branching partition is finite, exhaustive, and disjoint.
Propagation is sound and restoration reconstructs the parent state.
The initial variable domains are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates and enumerates every solution exactly once when all branches are explored.
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses chronological constraint backtracking.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits chronological backtracking, and the finite exhaustive disjoint branching assumptions support termination and nonduplicated enumeration. No relevant constraint-search source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Backjumping Search
children.top_down_role: Nonchronological return strategies based on implicated search decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Backjumping Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a sound conflict set to skip irrelevant decision levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain decisions \(d_1,ldots,d_k\) and, after propagation failure, derive a conflict set \(E\subseteq\{d_1,ldots,d_k\}\) such that the constraints together with \(E\) are inconsistent. If \(E\) is empty, declare the problem unsatisfiable. Otherwise let \(j<k\) be the greatest level whose decision occurs in \(E\), or the root when none exists. Undo every level above \(j\), record the conflict information needed to forbid the failed combination, and resume search at level \(j\). Soundness of \(E\) ensures that skipped levels cannot repair the conflict while the retained conflicting decisions remain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backjumping derives a conflict and returns directly to its deepest relevant earlier decision, skipping decisions absent from the conflict.
assumptions_latex: Every reported conflict set is logically inconsistent with the problem constraints.
Restoration correctly reconstructs the selected jump level.
The resumed search excludes the already refuted decision combination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Jumping to the deepest earlier decision in \(E\) preserves completeness while possibly skipping multiple chronological levels.
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses conflict-directed backjumping.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the backjumping leaf, but the decision sequence contains the malformed text \(d_1,ldots,d_k\), and completeness depends on the exact conflict-recording and resumed-search rule. children.title: Conflict-Directed Search
children.top_down_role: Search control guided by recorded conflict information.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(X,D,C)\) is a finite-domain constraint satisfaction problem.
Search decisions form a partial assignment \(\alpha\), and propagation detects failure soundly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a solution of \(P\), or failure after the finite search space has been exhausted.

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict-directed search with learned nogoods and nonchronological backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every propagation failure under \(\alpha\), derive a conflict scope \(S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)\) such that no solution extends \(\alpha|_S\). Add the sound nogood \(\neg\bigwedge_{x\in S}(x=\alpha(x))\). If \(S=\varnothing\), return failure. Otherwise backtrack to the deepest decision level containing an assignment from \(S\) whose alternative remains relevant, undo later decisions, propagate the learned nogood, and continue branching. Return the first complete assignment satisfying every constraint; return failure only when the root conflict is derived or all alternatives are exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On failure, derive and record a sound conflicting partial assignment, jump over irrelevant decisions, propagate the learned restriction, and continue until finding a solution or exhausting the search.

children.title: Conflict-Scope Selection
children.top_down_role: Granularity of conflict information used to redirect search.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(X,D,C)\) is a finite-domain constraint satisfaction problem.
\(\alpha\) is a partial assignment at which sound propagation reports failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A selected scope \(S\) yields a sound nogood forbidding \(\alpha|_S\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard semantic condition for a CSP conflict scope
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic validity condition for selecting variables responsible for a failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)\) is a valid conflict scope for the failed state \(\alpha\) exactly when \[\{s\in\operatorname{Sol}(P):s|_S=\alpha|_S\}=\varnothing.\] Thus the conjunction \(\bigwedge_{x\in S}(x=\alpha(x))\) may be forbidden without removing any solution. An inclusion-minimal conflict scope additionally satisfies, for every \(x\in S\), \[\{s\in\operatorname{Sol}(P):s|_{S\setminus\{x\}}=\alpha|_{S\setminus\{x\}}\}\ne\varnothing.\] Selection need not be minimal for soundness; smaller scopes generally permit longer backjumps and stronger reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conflict scope is any subset of current assignments that no solution can extend. It is inclusion-minimal when removing any one assignment restores extendibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-Scope Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic conflict-scope and inclusion-minimality conditions are coherent and the condition content kind fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: The finite search tree has an ordered list of branches at each decision node.
A nonpreferred branch at a node contributes one discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The search enumerates exactly the leaves having discrepancy count at most \(L\); iterative unbounded limits make it complete for a finite tree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-cost version in which every nonpreferred branch costs one discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the root path with \(\delta=0\). At a node, visit its preferred branch without changing \(\delta\), and visit each nonpreferred branch with update \(\delta\leftarrow\delta+1\); prune a path as soon as \(\delta>L\). Apply propagation after every decision, discard failed nodes, and output the first solution reached, or report that no solution occurs within the limit after all admissible paths are exhausted. Iterative limited-discrepancy search repeats this procedure for \(L=0,1,2,\ldots\), optionally avoiding duplicate work. On a finite tree of maximum depth \(h\), reaching \(L\ge h\) explores every leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search first along heuristic-preferred branches, allowing at most a fixed number of deviations. Increasing the limit eventually explores every leaf of a finite search tree.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For runs \(r=1,2,\ldots\), begin from the root domains, retain only constraints or statistics whose retention preserves soundness, and execute the underlying search until it finds a solution, proves failure, or consumes cutoff \(B_r\). \(x=a\) is the newly made search decision.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical forward checking for binary constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After assigning \(x=a\), process every unassigned variable \(y\) constrained with \(x\) by replacing \[D(y)\leftarrow\{b\in D(y):(a,b)\in C_{xy}\}.\] Record all deletions for restoration on backtracking. If some \(D(y)=\varnothing\), reject the current branch; otherwise choose another unassigned variable and continue. Forward checking tests only constraints joining the newly assigned variable to a future variable: it does not require every value of one unassigned variable to have support in another unassigned variable. A complete branching scheme combined with restoration remains a complete CSP solver.

assumptions_latex: \(P=(X,D,C)\) is a binary finite-domain constraint satisfaction problem.
Branching is exhaustive and every domain deletion is restored on backtracking.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintaining arc consistency for binary finite-domain CSPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initially enforce arc consistency. After each decision, repeatedly delete \(a\in D(x)\) whenever some neighbor \(y\) has no supporting value, that is, whenever \[\{b\in D(y):(a,b)\in C_{xy}\}=\varnothing,\] until a fixed point is reached. If any domain becomes empty, backtrack; if all domains are singleton and satisfy the constraints, output the assignment; otherwise branch and repeat arc-consistency enforcement. Because only unsupported values are deleted, propagation preserves every solution extending the current decisions. Exhaustive branching therefore returns failure only when the original instance is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enforce arc consistency initially and after every decision. Backtrack on an empty domain; otherwise branch until a complete satisfying assignment or exhaustive failure is obtained.

A sound procedure enforces a fixed local consistency level \(K\) after each decision.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic propagation-search scheme parameterized by a stronger local consistency property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a consistency property \(K\) stronger than the baseline propagation, such as path consistency or strong \(k\)-consistency for fixed \(k\ge3\). Enforce \(K\) on the root problem. At a search state \(P_\alpha\), reject the branch if enforcement derives inconsistency; output \(\alpha\) if it is complete and satisfies all constraints; otherwise select a branching decision, impose each alternative in turn, and re-enforce \(K\) to a fixed point. All reductions must be solution preserving. Consequently, exhaustive branching remains complete, while stronger \(K\) can reduce the search tree at the cost of more expensive propagation.
