children.title: Fail-First Heuristics
children.top_down_role: Variable selection emphasizing early exposure of likely failure.

assumptions_latex: The current CSP state has a finite set \(U\) of unassigned variables.
A score \(q(x)\) estimates how likely branching on \(x\) is to expose failure early.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fail-first rule selects an element of \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in U}q(x)\), with minimum remaining domain as its standard operational form.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-ordering principle, with minimum remaining values as the canonical proxy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each nonterminal search state, select a variable predicted to expose inconsistency soonest: \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in U}q(x).\] When no explicit failure model is available, use domain scarcity as the proxy \(q(x)=-|D(x)|\), equivalently \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in U}|D(x)|.\] The rule changes only the order in which an exhaustive search tree is explored; it does not authorize deleting values or branches. Hence it preserves soundness and completeness of the underlying search while seeking to reduce work by discovering failed subtrees near their roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the unassigned variable most likely to fail soon, commonly the one with the fewest remaining values. This changes search order, not the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Fail-First Heuristics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fail-first principle and its minimum-domain proxy are coherent, and principle fits the leaf, but the nontrivial heuristic and preservation claims have no inspectable citation.

children.title: Domain-Size Heuristics
children.top_down_role: Variable scoring based on current domain cardinality or related domain measures.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is the nonempty set of unassigned variables.
Each \(x\in U\) has a current finite domain \(D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected variable has minimum current domain cardinality among all unassigned variables.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-current-domain variable selection, also called minimum remaining values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute the current cardinality \(|D(x)|\) for every \(x\in U\), and select \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in U}|D(x)|.\] If several variables attain the minimum, apply a fixed or separately specified tie-breaking rule. Branch on values of \(x^*\), applying the solver's usual propagation after each branch. The cardinalities must be recomputed or maintained after domain changes, so the rule is dynamic. Because it selects only the next branching variable and leaves all alternatives available, it preserves completeness whenever the underlying branching scheme is exhaustive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select an unassigned variable with the smallest current domain, resolve ties separately, and branch using the solver's ordinary value ordering and propagation.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Size Heuristics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-remaining-values algorithm is precise and locally appropriate, but no source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Fail-First Tie-Breaking
children.top_down_role: Secondary criteria used when primary fail-first scores coincide.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is the nonempty set of unassigned variables.
\(d(x)=|D(x)|\), and \(t(x)\) is a secondary fail-first score.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected variable lexicographically minimizes \((d(x),-t(x),\iota(x))\), where \(\iota\) is a deterministic final ordering.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard lexicographic tie-breaking refinement of fail-first selection
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic refinement of minimum-domain selection by a secondary failure indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First form the minimum-domain candidate set \[M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in U}d(x).\] Among variables in \(M\), maximize a specified secondary score \(t(x)\), such as the number or total weight of constraints linking \(x\) to unassigned variables. Resolve any remaining tie by a fixed rank \(\iota(x)\). Equivalently, choose \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in U}^{\mathrm{lex}}\bigl(d(x),-t(x),\iota(x)\bigr).\] The primary minimum-domain ordering must not be displaced by the secondary score; the latter acts only when primary scores are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a smallest-domain variable, then break ties by a secondary failure-related score, with a fixed ordering for any remaining tie.
knowledge_statements.title: Fail-First Tie-Breaking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lexicographic tie-breaking rule is internally consistent and algorithm is an appropriate content kind, but it lacks an inspectable source supporting this exact formulation.

children.title: Degree Heuristics
children.top_down_role: Variable selection based on constraint-graph connectivity.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is the set of unassigned variables.
The current constraint hypergraph contains each variable and each constraint involving it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The heuristic selects an unassigned variable of maximum current unassigned degree.

notation.meaning: constraints containing x and another unassigned variable

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic degree measured by constraints connecting the candidate to future variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in U\), let \(C_U(x)\) be the set of active constraints whose scope contains \(x\) and at least one other variable in \(U\), and define \(\deg_U(x)=|C_U(x)|\). Select \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in U}\deg_U(x).\] Break ties by a fixed rule or another declared heuristic. Recompute the degree after assignments or constraint entailment changes the active subproblem. The rule seeks a variable interacting with the largest number of future constraints, but it changes only branching order and therefore preserves completeness under exhaustive branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select the unassigned variable participating in the most active constraints with other unassigned variables. Update this degree as the residual problem changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree Heuristics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied. Because degree can count neighboring variables or incident residual constraints, especially in a hypergraph, the chosen active-constraint definition requires explicit source support.

children.title: Weighted-Degree Heuristics
children.top_down_role: Variable selection based on conflict-weighted constraint incidence.

assumptions_latex: Every active constraint \(c\) has a positive weight \(w(c)\), initially one.
When propagation attributes a failure to \(c\), its weight is increased by a positive amount.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The domain-over-weighted-degree rule selects a variable minimizing \(|D(x)|/\operatorname{wdeg}(x)\), with zero weighted degree treated separately.

notation.meaning: weighted degree of x over active future constraints

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard conflict-weighted degree and dom/wdeg heuristic
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic conflict-weighted degree with the common domain-over-weighted-degree score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain \(w(c)>0\) for each constraint, increasing \(w(c)\) whenever the declared attribution rule identifies \(c\) as causing a propagation failure. For each unassigned \(x\), compute \[\operatorname{wdeg}(x)=\sum_{c\in C_U(x)}w(c).\] Among variables with positive weighted degree, select \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}\frac{|D(x)|}{\operatorname{wdeg}(x)}.\] Variables with zero weighted degree receive score \(+\infty\), unless all scores are infinite, in which case use a fixed fallback. After each attributed conflict, update the weights before the next variable selection. The heuristic affects ordering only.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increase weights of constraints implicated in failures, sum incident active weights for each variable, and usually select the smallest ratio of domain size to weighted degree.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Degree Heuristics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dom/wdeg formulation is plausible and algorithm fits the leaf, but no source supports the exact incident-constraint set, failure-attribution update, zero-degree convention, or selection formula.

children.title: Conflict-Weight Evidence
children.top_down_role: Failure information used to distinguish weighted-degree scoring from static degree scoring.

assumptions_latex: The current finite-domain CSP state has variables \(X\), domains \(D(x)\), and active constraints \(C\).
Each constraint \(c\in C\) has a nonnegative weight \(w(c)\), initially fixed and subsequently updated after conflicts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accumulated weights constitute conflict evidence used to prioritize variables incident to repeatedly failing constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of conflict weights in conflict-weighted-degree search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the dynamic evidence underlying conflict-weighted-degree variable selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever propagation detects a failure attributed to a constraint \(c\), update \(w(c)\leftarrow w(c)+\delta\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\); weights of constraints not implicated in that failure remain unchanged. For an unassigned variable \(x\), its conflict-weight evidence is summarized by \[\operatorname{wdeg}(x)=\sum_{c\in C:\,x\in\operatorname{scope}(c),\ c\text{ active}}w(c).\] Thus larger \(\operatorname{wdeg}(x)\) records greater accumulated involvement of constraints incident to \(x\) in earlier propagation failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint weights increase when their propagation causes failure; summing active incident weights gives each variable evidence of its historical involvement in conflicts.
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-Weight Evidence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Conflict-Weight Evidence leaf and is internally coherent, but no inspectable source is cited for the failure-attribution rule, update convention, or active-constraint weighted-degree formula.

children.title: Impact Heuristics
children.top_down_role: Variable selection based on estimated domain-reduction effects.

assumptions_latex: The current search state has finite domains \(D(x)\) for all unassigned variables \(x\).
A trial decision \(x=a\), followed by propagation, produces residual domains \(D_{x=a}(y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selecting a decision with large estimated impact favors branches predicted to remove a large fraction of the remaining search space.

notation.meaning: Residual domain after trial decision and propagation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard product-of-domain-reductions formulation of impact-based search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses propagated domain-volume reduction as a dynamic decision signal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the impact of a feasible trial decision \(x=a\) by \[I(x=a)=1-\frac{\prod_{y\text{ unassigned}}|D_{x=a}(y)|}{\prod_{y\text{ unassigned}}|D(y)|}.\] A failed trial has impact \(1\). Estimate unavailable impacts by probing or by an implementation-specified prior, and update observed estimates from later propagations. For each candidate variable aggregate its value impacts, for example by their mean, select a variable maximizing the chosen aggregate, and then apply the solver's value-selection rule. Stop when every variable is assigned or propagation proves failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Impact search selects a variable whose trial assignments are estimated to cause the greatest proportional reduction in remaining domain volume.
knowledge_statements.title: Impact Heuristics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Impact Heuristics, but no source supports the particular impact formula or aggregation rule. The numerator and denominator also quantify over an unspecified common set of unassigned variables even though assigning x changes that set; an authoritative formulation is needed to fix the convention.

children.title: Activity Heuristics
children.top_down_role: Variable selection based on accumulated participation in propagation or conflict.

assumptions_latex: Each unassigned variable \(x\) has a nonnegative activity score \(A_t(x)\) at search event \(t\).
A conflict or propagation event identifies a set \(S_t\) of participating variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next variable is chosen from the unassigned variables by maximizing its current activity score.

notation.meaning: Activity of x after event t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic event-bump activity heuristic shared by finite-domain solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States an event-driven activity heuristic independently of a particular solver's conflict analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(A_0(x)\ge 0\). After event \(t\), update every variable by \[A_{t+1}(x)=\rho A_t(x)+\beta_t\mathbf{1}_{\{x\in S_t\}},\] where \(0<\rho\le 1\) controls aging and \(\beta_t>0\) is the event increment. At a decision point choose \(x_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\text{ unassigned}}A_t(x)\), breaking ties by a fixed secondary rule, and choose a value using a separate value heuristic. Terminate at a solution or a propagation failure requiring backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Activity search bumps variables involved in important propagation or conflict events, optionally decays old scores, and branches on a currently most active variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Activity Heuristics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits Activity Heuristics, but the generic recurrence blends conflict activity, propagation activity, multiplicative decay, and arbitrary event increments without a source identifying a specific finite-domain heuristic variant.

children.title: Signal-Aging Regimes
children.top_down_role: Persistence and decay choices for dynamic heuristic evidence.

assumptions_latex: Dynamic signals are nonnegative scores \(s_t(u)\) attached to selectable objects \(u\).
Aging factors satisfy \(0<\rho_t\le 1\), and event increments satisfy \(b_t(u)\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aging geometrically discounts old evidence relative to recent increments while preserving nonnegative scores.

notation.meaning: Signal of object u after event t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard exponential aging recurrence for dynamic heuristic scores
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers multiplicative score aging and the no-aging boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under multiplicative aging, signals obey \[s_{t+1}(u)=\rho_t s_t(u)+b_t(u).\] Hence \[s_T(u)=\left(\prod_{j=0}^{T-1}\rho_j\right)s_0(u)+\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\left(\prod_{j=k+1}^{T-1}\rho_j\right)b_k(u).\] For constant \(\rho_t=\rho<1\), an increment of age \(m\) is weighted by \(\rho^m\); for \(\rho=1\), evidence never ages. Periodic global rescaling gives an equivalent ranking whenever it multiplies all current scores by the same positive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative aging discounts older signal increments geometrically; setting the factor to one retains all accumulated evidence without decay.
knowledge_statements.title: Signal-Aging Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence and its expansion are mathematically consistent and the property kind fits Signal-Aging Regimes, but no source is supplied. The rescaling statement also preserves ranking only at the instant of common positive rescaling; equivalence under subsequent additive updates requires corresponding scaling of increments or update parameters.

assumptions_latex: A branching variable \(x\) has a finite nonempty current domain \(D(x)\).
A scoring function \(q(x,a)\) is defined for every \(a\in D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chosen value optimizes the specified score, with deterministic tie-breaking, without altering the set of values represented by the branch.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: abstract formulation encompassing min-value, max-value, promise, and impact value ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes value ordering after a branching variable has already been selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the selected variable \(x\), compute \(q(x,a)\) for each \(a\in D(x)\). For a minimization-oriented score choose \[a^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a\in D(x)}q(x,a),\] and for a maximization-oriented score replace \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}\) by \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}\). Resolve ties by a fixed total order. Use \(a^*\) as the first value in the applicable branching scheme, then retain every untried value in another branch or later alternative. Recompute scores after backtracking whenever the heuristic is dynamic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After selecting a variable, a value heuristic scores its remaining values, chooses an optimum with fixed tie-breaking, and preserves all alternatives for completeness.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Selection Heuristics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind matches Value-Selection Heuristics and the completeness qualification is appropriately separated from value ordering, but no inspectable source supports this abstract formulation and its dynamic recomputation prescription.

assumptions_latex: The current domain \(D(x)\) is finite and contains a selected value \(a\).
The parent search state is represented by a constraint store \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two children are disjoint and their feasible assignments form exactly the feasible assignments of the parent.
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: cited locator covers general branch-and-bound rather than finite-domain constraint programming specifically
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard value-versus-remainder form of finite-domain binary branching.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Binary branching replaces \(P\) by two child stores \[P_1=P\cup\{x=a\},\qquad P_2=P\cup\{x\ne a\}.\] Equivalently, their domains for \(x\) are \(\{a\}\) and \(D(x)\setminus\{a\}\). These domain subsets are disjoint and have union \(D(x)\); consequently every solution of \(P\) satisfies exactly one branch predicate. After propagation, an inconsistent child may be discarded, while complete search explores every remaining child unless pruning is justified independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary branching splits a selected value from the rest of its variable's domain, producing two disjoint children whose union covers the parent.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Branching

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The value-versus-remainder split is precise and representation is a suitable kind for Binary Branching. However, the cited locator concerns general branch-and-bound and is explicitly identified as indirect; it does not inspectably support the stated finite-domain constraint-store construction and completeness conditions.

assumptions_latex: The selected variable \(x\) has finite domain \(D(x)=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}\).
The parent constraint store is \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(k\) children are pairwise disjoint and exactly cover the parent assignments with respect to \(x\).
review_flags: source_scope_indirect: cited locator covers general branch-and-bound rather than finite-domain constraint programming specifically
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States full enumeration branching on one finite-domain variable.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Multiway branching creates one child for every current value: \[P_i=P\cup\{x=a_i\},\qquad i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.\] Since the singleton sets \(\{a_i\}\) are pairwise disjoint and their union is \(D(x)\), each parent solution belongs to exactly one child. The children may be explored in heuristic order. Propagation is applied separately in each child, and complete search retains every consistent unexplored child unless an independent sound pruning rule removes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiway branching creates one equality branch per current value; the branches are disjoint, exhaustive, and may be explored in heuristic order.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiway Branching

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singleton-child representation is mathematically coherent and fits Multiway Branching. The only citation is an indirect general branch-and-bound section and does not inspectably support the finite-domain equality-branch construction or the stated completeness qualification.

children.title: Set Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching choices over membership or subset decisions.

assumptions_latex: The selected variable \(x\) has a finite domain \(D(x)\).
Nonempty subsets \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\) form a partition of \(D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restricting \(x\) to each partition block yields mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive branches.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary partition-based formulation of set branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General domain-subset branching with an arbitrary finite partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Require \[D(x)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}S_i,\qquad S_i\cap S_j=\varnothing\ \text{ for }i\ne j.\] Set branching creates child stores \[P_i=P\cup\{x\in S_i\},\qquad i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.\] Every solution of \(P\) assigns \(x\) to exactly one block and therefore belongs to exactly one child before propagation. Singleton blocks recover multiway branching, while two complementary blocks recover binary domain partitioning. Search completeness requires retaining every consistent block unless sound pruning excludes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set branching partitions a finite domain into nonempty blocks and creates one membership branch per block, giving disjoint and exhaustive alternatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Set Branching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Set Branching, but no source is cited. In addition, the statement uses the parent store P although the assumptions do not introduce P, so the record is not self-contained.

children.title: Interval Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching choices that partition ordered domains into intervals.

assumptions_latex: The finite domain \(D(x)\) is contained in a totally ordered set.
Cut points induce nonempty consecutive blocks \(I_1,\ldots,I_k\) covering \(D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interval-restriction children are disjoint and exhaustive over the current values of \(x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: ordered-domain specialization of exhaustive set branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes set branching to consecutive blocks of an ordered finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose consecutive blocks satisfying \[D(x)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}I_i,\qquad I_i\cap I_j=\varnothing\ \text{ for }i\ne j,\] where each \(I_i\) is the intersection of \(D(x)\) with an interval of the ambient order. Create \(P_i=P\cup\{x\in I_i\}\). For a binary split at a cut \(m\), the blocks are \(D(x)\cap(-\infty,m]\) and \(D(x)\cap(m,\infty)\), provided both are nonempty. Every parent solution enters exactly one child.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval branching partitions an ordered finite domain into consecutive nonempty blocks and branches on membership in each block.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Branching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordered-partition representation fits Interval Branching, but no source is supplied and P is used without being introduced in the assumptions. The assumptions mention cut points generically without defining their domains or how they induce the displayed blocks.

children.title: Branch-Partition Granularity
children.top_down_role: Search-tree consequences of coarse or fine domain partitions.

assumptions_latex: A branching step partitions a finite domain \(D(x)\) into nonempty blocks \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\).
The block count satisfies \(2\le k\le |D(x)|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Granularity ranges from binary partitioning to singleton multiway branching and controls the immediate branching factor and block sizes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary quantitative characterization of domain-partition granularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies partition coarseness without asserting a universal performance ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the branch count as \(k\) and the maximum block size as \[g_{\max}=\max_{1\le i\le k}|S_i|.\] Binary partitioning has \(k=2\); singleton multiway branching has \(k=|D(x)|\) and \(g_{\max}=1\). Refining a partition replaces blocks by smaller disjoint subblocks, weakly increases \(k\), and weakly decreases \(g_{\max}\). This changes the immediate branching factor and the amount of domain restriction per child, but by itself implies no universal reduction in total search effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition granularity measures how many domain blocks become branches and how large they are, ranging from two coarse blocks to singleton alternatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Partition Granularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits Branch-Partition Granularity, and the refinement monotonicity claims are correct for finite partitions. An inspectable source is still required for inclusion as candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Constraint Learning Calculus
children.top_down_role: Constraint-level learning interfaces; Boolean clause derivation and CDCL proof machinery remain cross-part material.

assumptions_latex: A finite-domain search state is described by decision literals and propagated literals.
A conflict analysis derives a finite set \(N\) of literals that cannot hold simultaneously in any solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recording the nogood soundly excludes every future search state containing all literals in \(N\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard nogood semantics in constraint and clause-learning search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines semantic validity and pruning action for recorded finite-domain nogoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nogood is a finite set \(N\) of literals such that the original constraint model entails \[\neg\bigwedge_{\ell\in N}\ell,\] equivalently \(\bigvee_{\ell\in N}\neg\ell\). Nogood recording adds this entailed constraint to the search store. Whenever propagation determines that all but one literal of \(N\) hold, the remaining literal must be false; if every literal in \(N\) holds, the state fails. Because the recorded constraint is entailed by the original model, it removes no solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recorded nogood is an entailed combination of literals that cannot all hold; it propagates against or rejects any future state recreating that combination.
knowledge_statements.title: Nogood Recording

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Nogood Recording and the semantic nogood formula is standard, but no source is cited. The assertion that propagation determines the remaining literal false whenever all others hold presumes a propagator enforcing unit-style propagation for the recorded nogood, which must be stated or sourced rather than presented as unconditional semantics.

assumptions_latex: A propagation or failure conclusion \(p\) is produced under a current set \(A\) of decision and domain literals.
The solver can return a finite subset \(E\subseteq A\) sufficient to entail \(p\) under the model constraints \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implication from \(E\) to \(p\) is a checkable explanation and can support sound learning or backjumping.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard entailment certificate underlying explanation-based constraint learning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats explanations as entailment certificates for propagation and failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explanation for a propagated literal \(p\) is a finite set \(E\subseteq A\) satisfying \[C\models\left(\bigwedge_{\ell\in E}\ell\right)\Rightarrow p.\] For failure, take \(p=\bot\), so \(C\models\neg\bigwedge_{\ell\in E}\ell\). The certificate is verified by checking the stated entailment for the responsible constraint or propagator. The failure explanation yields the sound nogood \(E\); a propagation explanation yields the clause \(\bigvee_{\ell\in E}\neg\ell\lor p\). Combining explanations through inference preserves entailment and supports learned constraints and nonchronological backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explanation is a subset of current literals that, with the model, entails a propagation or contradiction and therefore certifies sound learning.
knowledge_statements.title: Explanation-Based Learning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the explanation and learning claims. The selected certificate kind describes an explanation object but does not fully match the broader Explanation-Based Learning leaf, which is a learning method or principle. Moreover, semantic entailment is not automatically checkable without specifying an explanation language and verification procedure.

knowledge_statements.title: Lazy Clause Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain propagation integrated with clause learning through Boolean explanations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let finite-domain variables be represented by Boolean literals encoding domain facts. Initialize a clause database with the encoded constraints. Whenever a propagator infers a literal \(p\) from currently true literals \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}\), require an explanation clause \((\neg e_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg e_k\lor p)\). On conflict, resolve explanation clauses to derive an asserting nogood, add it to the database, backjump to the highest level at which that clause becomes unit, and propagate its asserting literal. Return a satisfying assignment when all variables are fixed, or infeasibility when conflict analysis derives the empty clause at decision level zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode domain facts as literals, explain every propagation by a clause, and use clause resolution, learning, and nonchronological backtracking to conduct finite-domain search.
assumptions_latex: All variable domains are finite.
Every propagated literal and detected conflict admits a sound clausal explanation.
The Boolean encoding preserves feasibility of the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a feasible assignment or a level-zero empty-clause certificate of infeasibility.

notation.meaning: set of literals explaining one propagation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the Lazy Clause Generation container, but no citation supports the exact explanation, conflict-analysis, backjumping, and termination formulation. Completeness also requires an explicit finite, exhaustive search discipline.

knowledge_statements.title: Learned-Constraint Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retention, activity adjustment, and deletion of constraints learned during search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a learned-constraint database \(L\) and an activity score \(a(C)\) for each \(C\in L\). Insert every sound learned constraint, increase \(a(C)\) when \(C\) participates in conflict analysis, and periodically decay all activities. At a reduction event, retain every locked constraint currently justifying a propagation and every constraint satisfying the prescribed protection rule; delete only unprotected constraints selected by a ranking based on activity, size, or literal-block distance. Clause deletion removes search guidance but not logical consequences required for soundness, because every retained or deleted learned constraint is entailed by the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Score learned constraints, protect those currently needed or judged useful, and periodically delete low-value constraints without changing the model’s solution set.
assumptions_latex: Every learned constraint is logically entailed by the original model.
A locked constraint is not deleted while it serves as a propagation reason.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Database reduction preserves soundness while controlling learned-constraint storage.

notation.meaning: activity score of learned constraint C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role and local topic fit, but the activity, locking, protection, and deletion policy has no cited source. The claimed storage control also depends on a sufficiently restrictive reduction policy.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-consistent propagation of a finite-domain minimization objective under an incumbent cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization model with feasible set \(F\), objective variable \(z=f(x)\), and incumbent value \(U\), post the strict-improvement constraint \(z<U\). Each objective propagator computes a valid lower bound \(L(D)\) over the current domains \(D\). If \(L(D)\ge U\), fail the node. Otherwise remove every domain value whose conditional objective lower bound is at least \(U\), propagate the resulting domain changes to a fixpoint, and repeat whenever \(D\) or \(U\) changes. A maximization problem uses the reversed inequalities and a lower incumbent cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the incumbent and valid objective bounds to reject nonimproving nodes and remove values that cannot participate in a better solution.
assumptions_latex: The optimization direction is fixed and the incumbent is feasible.
Every propagated objective bound is valid for the current domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No assignment capable of strictly improving the incumbent is removed.

notation.meaning: valid objective lower bound over current domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement describes sound objective-bound filtering, but the scope calls it bound-consistent propagation while the stated valid lower-bound procedure does not establish bound consistency. A source is needed to fix the intended propagation strength.

children.title: Incumbent Management
children.top_down_role: Retention, replacement, and sharing of the best known feasible solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintenance of the best feasible solution found in single-objective minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the incumbent pair to \((x^I,U)=(\bot,+\infty)\). Whenever search produces a feasible solution \(x\in F\) with value \(f(x)<U\), atomically replace the pair by \((x,f(x))\); otherwise leave it unchanged. After every replacement, notify all bound-control components of the new value. On termination, return \(x^I\) if it exists. If the search has exhaustively eliminated every assignment with value below \(U\), then \(x^I\) is optimal; if no feasible assignment was ever accepted and the search is exhaustive, report infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store the best feasible solution encountered, update it only on strict improvement, and expose its value to pruning components.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem over feasible set \(F\).
Every candidate accepted as incumbent has been checked for feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every search state, \(U\) equals the smallest objective value among all accepted feasible solutions.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

children.title: Cutoff Management
children.top_down_role: Control of objective thresholds used to restrict subsequent search.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutoff Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of incumbent improvements into strict objective cutoffs for minimization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a cutoff \(c\) defining the admissible improving region \(f(x)<c\). Initially set \(c=+\infty\), or use a valid user-supplied upper cutoff. When a feasible incumbent of value \(U<c\) is accepted, replace \(c\) by \(U\) and post or strengthen the objective constraint \(f(x)<c\). Never increase \(c\) during a monotone minimization run. If objective values are integral, the strict cutoff may equivalently be represented by \(f(x)\le c-1\). Reject any node whose valid lower bound is at least \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a monotonically tightening objective threshold and reject any search region unable to improve on it.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
Each incumbent value used to tighten the cutoff comes from a feasible solution.
Node lower bounds are valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every rejected node contains no feasible solution strictly improving the active cutoff.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

children.title: Bound Synchronization
children.top_down_role: Coordination between incumbent improvements, objective bounds, and active search state.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound Synchronization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone sharing of incumbent cutoffs among concurrent minimization workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let worker \(i\) hold a local cutoff \(c_i\), and let the shared cutoff be \(c^\star=\min_i c_i\). When worker \(i\) verifies a feasible solution of value \(U<c^\star\), it atomically updates \(c^\star\leftarrow U\). Each worker periodically imports the shared value by setting \(c_i\leftarrow\min\{c_i,c^\star\}\), then reruns affected objective propagation. Messages may be delayed or duplicated, but an imported cutoff must never be weakened. Search terminates only after all workers have incorporated every final bound update and their remaining regions are exhausted or pruned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concurrent workers share feasible incumbent bounds monotonically, repropagate tighter cutoffs, and terminate only after final updates are globally accounted for.
assumptions_latex: Every shared upper bound is obtained from a verified feasible solution.
Updates and imports use an atomic or otherwise race-safe minimum operation.
The distributed termination test accounts for messages in transit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No synchronized worker prunes a solution better than the best verified shared incumbent.

notation.meaning: objective value of a newly verified solution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotone minimum synchronization rule is plausible and locally appropriate, but no source supports the concurrent update and global termination conditions. Those conditions are essential to the exact algorithmic claim.

children.title: Lexicographic Search
children.top_down_role: Multiobjective search governed by a fixed priority ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Lexicographic Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential exact optimization of ordered objectives over a finite feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be finite and let \((f_1,\ldots,f_m)\) be minimization objectives ordered by priority. Set \(F_1=F\). For \(k=1,\ldots,m\), solve \(v_k=\min\{f_k(x):x\in F_k\}\), then set \(F_{k+1}=\{x\in F_k:f_k(x)=v_k\}\). If any stage is infeasible, report that \(F\) is infeasible. Otherwise return any \(x^\star\in F_{m+1}\). Equivalently, \(x^\star\) minimizes the objective vector under lexicographic order, with earlier components taking absolute priority over later components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize objectives by priority, fixing each attained optimum before optimizing the next objective.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(F\) is finite and nonempty unless infeasibility is reported.
Each scalar optimization stage is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned solution is lexicographically minimal in \(F\) for the ordered objective vector.

notation.meaning: feasible solutions preserving all earlier optimal objective values
optimal value of objective k at its stage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential exact procedure correctly characterizes lexicographic minimization over a finite feasible set and fits the algorithm container, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Pareto Search
children.top_down_role: Multiobjective search organized around nondominated solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration of nondominated objective vectors for finite multiobjective minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be finite and \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be minimized componentwise. Maintain an archive \(A\) of mutually nondominated feasible solutions, initially empty. Whenever search finds \(x\in F\), discard it if some \(a\in A\) satisfies \(f(a)\le f(x)\) componentwise. Otherwise remove every \(a\in A\) dominated by \(x\), insert \(x\), and add a constraint excluding the region weakly dominated by \(f(x)\). Continue until the remaining objective region is proved empty. Return \(A\), retaining one representative for each attained nondominated objective vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate feasible solutions while maintaining a nondominated archive and excluding objective regions already dominated by discovered points.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(F\) is finite.
Dominance exclusions remove only points weakly dominated by archived feasible points.
Search exhaustively proves the residual objective region empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned archive represents exactly the nondominated objective vectors attained on \(F\).

notation.meaning: archive of mutually nondominated feasible solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite exhaustive archive procedure fits Pareto Search, but no citation supports the exact dominance-exclusion and completeness formulation.

children.title: Objective-Order Regimes
children.top_down_role: Priority structures and order sensitivity in lexicographic optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Order Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order relations that determine comparison and optimality for vector-valued objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible set \(F\) and objective map \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}^m\), an objective-order regime is a specified preorder \(\preceq\) on \(f(F)\). A feasible point \(x^\star\) is globally least when \(f(x^\star)\preceq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\), and is minimal when no \(x\in F\) satisfies \(f(x)\preceq f(x^\star)\) without also satisfying \(f(x^\star)\preceq f(x)\). Lexicographic order typically yields a least objective vector on finite sets, whereas componentwise order generally yields a set of Pareto-minimal vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective-order regime specifies how objective vectors are compared and thereby defines whether optimization seeks a least vector or all minimal vectors.
assumptions_latex: The comparison relation \(\preceq\) is reflexive and transitive on the attainable objective vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality is defined relative to \(\preceq\) as leastness or minimality of the attained objective vector.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct content kind and distinguishes least from preorder-minimal objective vectors correctly, but the terminology and claims about lexicographic and componentwise regimes lack a source.

children.title: Dominance-Frontier Management
children.top_down_role: Representation and maintenance concerns for nondominated solution frontiers.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance-Frontier Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental maintenance of a finite archive representing the current Pareto frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an archive \(A\subseteq F\) whose members have pairwise incomparable objective vectors under componentwise minimization. Given a newly verified feasible point \(x\), reject \(x\) if some \(a\in A\) satisfies \(f(a)\le f(x)\) componentwise. Otherwise set \(A\leftarrow\{a\in A: f(x)\not\le f(a)\}\cup\{x\}\). Optionally merge points with identical objective vectors by retaining one representative. Each archive update may generate dominance cuts excluding objective vectors weakly worse than \(f(x)\); such cuts remain valid because \(x\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insert an undominated feasible point, delete archive members it dominates, and optionally add valid exclusions for its dominated objective region.
assumptions_latex: Every inserted point is feasible.
Objective vectors are compared componentwise for minimization.
The archive is initially empty or pairwise nondominated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After each update, \(A\) is pairwise nondominated and represents all nondominated vectors among the feasible points processed so far.

notation.meaning: objective vector of feasible point x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The archive update is mathematically consistent and fits frontier management, but no source supports the algorithm or the optional generation of dominance cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Destroy–Repair Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-neighborhood search defined by relaxing part of an incumbent assignment and reoptimizing it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible incumbent \(x^I\) over variables \(V\), choose a destroy set \(R\subseteq V\) and fix every variable \(v\in V\setminus R\) to \(x^I_v\). The repair subproblem optimizes the original objective subject to the original constraints and these fixings, either exactly or within a declared limit. If repair returns a feasible solution \(y\) satisfying the acceptance rule, update the incumbent; otherwise retain \(x^I\). Repeat with newly selected destroy sets until the stopping budget is exhausted. The induced neighborhood is \(N_R(x^I)=\{y\in F:y_v=x^I_v\text{ for all }v\notin R\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relax selected incumbent variables, reoptimize the resulting restricted model, and accept repaired feasible solutions according to a stated rule.
assumptions_latex: The incumbent \(x^I\) is feasible.
Repair enforces every original constraint and all nondestroyed variable fixings.
The acceptance and stopping rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted repair is feasible and belongs to the destroy-set neighborhood of the preceding incumbent.

notation.meaning: set of variables relaxed by the destroy step
neighborhood induced by fixing variables outside R

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The destroy–repair algorithm and induced neighborhood are stated consistently and fit the Large Neighborhood Search leaf, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Adaptive Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood choices revised using observed search performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online selection of large-neighborhood operators using observed search performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{H}=\{H_1,\ldots,H_q\}\) be destroy–repair operators with positive weights \(w_i\). At iteration \(t\), sample operator \(H_i\) with probability \(p_i(t)=w_i(t)/\sum_j w_j(t)\), apply it to the current incumbent, and observe a bounded reward \(r_t\) computed from declared signals such as improvement, feasibility, or repair cost. Update the selected weight by \(w_i(t+1)=(1-\alpha)w_i(t)+\alpha\max\{\varepsilon,r_t\}\), leaving other weights unchanged or applying a stated common decay. Preserve \(\varepsilon>0\) so every operator remains selectable, and stop at the prescribed budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select neighborhood operators probabilistically, reward successful operators from observed search signals, and retain positive exploration probability for every operator.
assumptions_latex: The operator family \(\mathcal{H}\) is finite.
Rewards are bounded and computed consistently from declared observations.
Parameters satisfy \(0<\alpha\le 1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure defines a valid adaptive distribution over neighborhoods while preserving nonzero probability for every operator.

notation.meaning: selection weight of operator i at iteration t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines a valid positive-weight adaptive selection scheme, but the particular reward and smoothing update is only one parametric variant and has no citation establishing it as the intended Adaptive Neighborhoods formulation.

children.title: Explanation-Guided Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood choices informed by explanations, conflicts, or failure evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Explanation-Guided Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-neighborhood search using recorded conflict explanations to select relaxed variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite-domain constraint optimization problem, an incumbent assignment \(x\), and a multiset \(E\) of explanations, assign each variable the score \(s_i=\sum_{e\in E:i\in e}w_e\), where \(w_e\ge 0\). Select a relaxation set \(R\) from the variables with largest scores, fix every \(i\notin R\) to \(x_i\), and solve the resulting subproblem within a prescribed resource limit. Replace \(x\) by the returned feasible assignment when it improves the objective; otherwise retain \(x\), update \(E\) and the weights, and construct another neighborhood. Stop under the specified global budget and return the best incumbent found.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Score variables by their participation in conflict explanations, relax highly scored variables, solve the induced subproblem, and retain the best feasible incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(D_i\) is finite for every decision variable \(x_i\).
Each explanation \(e\in E\) identifies variables jointly responsible for a conflict or bound.
The neighborhood subproblem has a specified solver and resource limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns the best feasible incumbent encountered; it does not by itself certify global optimality.

notation.meaning: Set of variables relaxed in the neighborhood.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports explanation-guided neighborhood construction.
Exact explanation scoring and selection policy are parametrized.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, and the variables and stopping behavior are stated coherently. However, no citation supports the particular explanation score, relaxation-set selection rule, or weight-update template, so the mathematical algorithm variant cannot be accepted as candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Neighborhood Adaptation Signals
children.top_down_role: Performance and inference evidence used to alter neighborhood selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood Adaptation Signals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable feedback used to adapt neighborhood selection during large-neighborhood search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For neighborhood type \(k\) at iteration \(t\), represent its adaptation signal by \(z_{k,t}=(\Delta_{k,t},q_{k,t},\tau_{k,t},d_{k,t})\), where \(\Delta_{k,t}\) is objective improvement, \(q_{k,t}\in\{0,1\}\) records whether a feasible solution was produced, \(\tau_{k,t}>0\) is computational effort, and \(d_{k,t}\) measures search novelty. An adaptive controller may update a score by \(S_{k,t+1}=(1-\alpha)S_{k,t}+\alpha U(z_{k,t})\), with \(0<\alpha\le 1\), and use the scores to choose subsequent neighborhoods. The utility function and selection rule must be fixed as part of the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptation signals combine improvement, feasibility, effort, and novelty; a controller converts them into updated neighborhood scores.
assumptions_latex: All compared objective improvements use the same optimization direction and normalization.
The utility function \(U\) and smoothing parameter \(\alpha\) are fixed or updated by an explicit rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector \(z_{k,t}\) provides a measurable basis for updating the selection score \(S_{k,t}\).

notation.meaning: Feedback vector for neighborhood type k at iteration t.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports this feedback representation.
Signal components vary among adaptive large-neighborhood-search formulations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits a leaf about adaptation signals, and the displayed update is internally consistent. No source is supplied for the specific four-component signal vector or exponential score update, both of which are formulation-dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Min-Conflicts Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard min-conflicts local search for finite-domain constraint satisfaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) with finite domains, constraints \(C\), and an initial complete assignment \(a\), repeat until \(a\) satisfies every constraint or a stopping limit is reached: select a variable \(x_i\) occurring in a constraint violated by \(a\); for each \(v\in D_i\), compute the number of constraints violated by \(a[x_i\leftarrow v]\); and assign \(x_i\) a value attaining the minimum, breaking ties by a specified rule. Return \(a\) if it satisfies all constraints; otherwise report only that the run terminated without finding a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly choose a variable in a violated constraint and give it a value minimizing the number of resulting violations.
assumptions_latex: Every variable domain \(D_i\) is finite.
The state is a complete assignment, possibly infeasible.
Violation counts can be evaluated for each candidate value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A returned satisfying assignment solves the CSP; unsuccessful termination does not establish unsatisfiability.

notation.meaning: Assignment obtained by changing x_i to v.

review_flags: The supplied local-search locator concerns integer programming rather than the min-conflicts CSP algorithm.
A direct authoritative min-conflicts source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and mathematical description match standard finite-domain min-conflicts search, including the important limitation that unsuccessful termination does not prove unsatisfiability. A direct authoritative min-conflicts citation with a specific locator is nevertheless required.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Weighting Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local search that increases penalties on persistently violated constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each constraint \(c\in C\) have weight \(w_c>0\), initially \(w_c=1\), and define \(F_w(a)=\sum_{c\in C}w_c\mathbf{1}[a\not\models c]\) for complete assignments \(a\). At each iteration, move to an assignment in the prescribed neighborhood minimizing \(F_w\), subject to the stated tie-breaking rule. If no accepted move improves the weighted violation score, increase by a positive amount the weights of constraints currently violated, optionally followed by a specified normalization. Stop upon finding \(F_w(a)=0\) or reaching the resource limit; return a satisfying assignment only in the former case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize weighted constraint violations, increasing weights on currently violated constraints when search stalls.
assumptions_latex: The CSP has finitely many variables and finite domains.
Every constraint has a positive weight.
The move neighborhood and weight-update rule are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(F_w(a)=0\) certifies that \(a\) satisfies every constraint; other termination does not certify unsatisfiability.

notation.meaning: Indicator that assignment a violates c.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports constraint-weighting search.
Weight normalization and plateau handling are algorithm-dependent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf and the weighted-violation formulation is coherent. The plateau trigger, accepted-move rule, weight increment, and optional normalization describe a family of weighting algorithms, but no specific source supports this template.

children.title: Random-Walk Search
children.top_down_role: Stochastic movement through neighboring assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Walk Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic local search mixing improving moves with random moves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite CSP, a complete initial assignment \(a_0\), a move neighborhood \(N(a)\), a violation score \(V(a)\), and \(p\in(0,1]\), iterate as follows. If \(V(a_t)=0\), return \(a_t\). With probability \(p\), sample \(a_{t+1}\) from a specified distribution supported on \(N(a_t)\); with probability \(1-p\), choose an element of \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{b\in N(a_t)}V(b)\), using a specified tie rule. Stop at the resource limit if no satisfying assignment has appeared. Such termination supplies no unsatisfiability certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each step, either take a random neighboring assignment or choose one minimizing violations; accept success only when all constraints hold.
assumptions_latex: The assignment space and every neighborhood \(N(a)\) are finite.
The random-move distribution and tie rule are specified.
\(V(a)=0\) exactly when \(a\) satisfies all constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any state returned with \(V(a_t)=0\) is a satisfying assignment, but bounded random-walk search is incomplete.

notation.meaning: Probability of taking a random move.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports random-walk CSP search.
Transition distributions differ across named random-walk variants.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits Random-Walk Search, and the stochastic transition rule is mathematically well specified. The named leaf can cover several random-walk variants, while no citation supports this particular mixture of random and minimum-violation moves.

children.title: Metaheuristic Search
children.top_down_role: Higher-level stochastic control strategies for constraint local search.

knowledge_statements.title: Metaheuristic Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-domain search template controlled by memory, acceptance, and diversification rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite assignment space \(X\), objective or violation score \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}\), initial state \(x_0\), and controller state \(m_0\), generate candidates \(Y_t\subseteq X\) using the neighborhood and diversification rule encoded by \(m_t\). Select \(y_t\in Y_t\) by the prescribed selection rule, set \(x_{t+1}=y_t\) when the acceptance predicate \(A(x_t,y_t,m_t)\) holds and otherwise set \(x_{t+1}=x_t\), then update \(m_{t+1}\). Record the best feasible state encountered and return it at the stopping limit. Completeness requires an additional exhaustive or probabilistically complete control condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metaheuristic generates candidates, applies an acceptance rule, updates memory, diversifies search, and returns its best feasible state.
assumptions_latex: The assignment space \(X\) is finite.
Candidate generation, acceptance, memory update, and stopping rules are specified.
Feasibility and score \(F\) are evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The template returns the best feasible state encountered but provides no general optimality or infeasibility certificate.
review_flags: Metaheuristic search is a family rather than a unique algorithm.
No supplied locator supports this abstract CSP-specific template.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Metaheuristic search is a broad method family rather than one canonical algorithm. The record gives a plausible abstract template, but the selected algorithm kind is too specific for the exact leaf and no source establishes this CSP-specific abstraction or its completeness qualification.

children.title: Diversification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms controlling exploration beyond repeatedly visited local regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Diversification Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions ensuring stochastic search retains access to unexplored regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the finite assignment space and \(P_t(x,y)\) the possibly history-dependent transition probability. A persistent global-diversification regime satisfies: there exist an integer \(L\ge 1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, from every state and every search history, each target \(y\in X\) can be reached within the next \(L\) transitions with conditional probability at least \(\varepsilon\). Under indefinitely repeated transitions, every nonempty subset of \(X\), including the solution set when nonempty, is then reached with probability one. A finite stopping budget removes this asymptotic guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diversification is persistent when every target remains uniformly reachable within bounded steps; indefinite search then reaches any nonempty solution set almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite.
The uniform reachability constants \(L\) and \(\varepsilon\) hold after every possible history.
The process is allowed to continue indefinitely for the asymptotic conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every nonempty \(S\subseteq X\), the hitting time \(T_S\) satisfies \(\Pr(T_S<\infty)=1\).

notation.meaning: Conditional transition probability at iteration t.
First hitting time of subset S.

review_flags: No supplied source supports the stated uniform-reachability formulation.
The condition is sufficient rather than a taxonomy of all diversification regimes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform bounded-horizon reachability condition is a coherent sufficient condition, but the almost-sure hitting conclusion is theorem-like rather than merely a condition. It also describes only one sufficient diversification regime, and no source is supplied for the stated history-uniform formulation or conclusion.

children.title: Complete Search Components
children.top_down_role: Systematic components responsible for exhaustive coverage or certification.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Search Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Components that preserve exhaustive finite-domain search and its certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite CSP, a complete search component is a procedure operating on a search region \(R\) that terminates and returns exactly one of: a satisfying assignment in \(R\), or a verifiable certificate that no assignment in \(R\) satisfies all constraints. Branching is complete when its children cover \(R\); pruning is sound when every removed assignment is infeasible or cannot improve the incumbent under the declared objective. A finite composition of terminating complete branching, sound propagation or pruning, and complete leaf resolution is itself a complete search component for its input region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete component either finds a solution in its finite search region or certifies none exists there, using covering branches and sound pruning.
assumptions_latex: All variable domains and the represented search region are finite.
Branching children cover their parent region.
Every pruning inference is sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The component terminates with either a satisfying assignment in \(R\) or a certificate excluding all such assignments from \(R\).

notation.meaning: Finite search region handled by the component.

review_flags: The locator may discuss CP generally rather than this component-level completeness definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf and the record clearly distinguishes covering branching and sound pruning. The cited general constraint-programming section does not specifically support the component-level certificate definition or the finite-composition completeness claim, so the claim needs a more direct source.

children.title: Local Search Components
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood-based components responsible for rapid exploratory improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Search Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heuristic components that navigate complete assignments without exhaustive coverage obligations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite CSP, a local search component consists of a state space \(X\) of complete assignments, a neighborhood map \(N:X\rightrightarrows X\), a score \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}\) measuring violations or objective quality, and rules for move selection, acceptance, restart, and termination. Starting from \(x_0\in X\), it generates a trajectory using candidates in \(N(x_t)\) and returns the best feasible assignment encountered. Unless its control rule guarantees exhaustive coverage or almost-sure hitting, failure to find a solution is not evidence of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local-search component navigates neighboring complete assignments using a score and control rules, but ordinarily cannot certify that no solution exists.
assumptions_latex: The CSP has finite domains.
The neighborhood, scoring, acceptance, and stopping rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible returned assignment is valid, whereas unsuccessful termination generally supplies no infeasibility certificate.

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Primal Bounds: Greedy and Local Search p. 34

review_flags: The locator concerns integer-programming local search and may not state the CSP component abstraction.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Primal Bounds: Greedy and Local Search p. 34

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role is reasonable and the statement correctly limits what unsuccessful local search establishes. The cited integer-programming section on primal bounds and local search does not directly support this finite-CSP component abstraction, its complete-assignment state space, or its almost-sure-hitting qualification.

children.title: Hybrid Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Control structures governing transitions or information exchange between components.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Control Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Control rules interleaving heuristic local search with certificate-producing complete search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a complete-search frontier \(Q\), an incumbent \(x^*\), and a local-search state. Repeatedly choose, by a specified scheduler, either a complete step or a local step. A complete step removes a region from \(Q\), applies sound propagation and covering branching, updates \(Q\), and records any improved feasible assignment. A local step searches heuristically from an incumbent or frontier-derived state and may update \(x^*\), branching priorities, or bounds, but may delete a frontier region only through a sound certificate. Terminate with a completeness claim only when \(Q\) is empty; resource-limited termination returns merely the best incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scheduler alternates complete and local-search steps; heuristic feedback may guide search but cannot remove regions without a sound certificate.
assumptions_latex: The original finite search region is represented by the initial frontier \(Q\).
Complete-step branching covers its processed region and pruning is sound.
Local steps cannot uncertifiably delete complete-search obligations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every frontier obligation is eventually processed and \(Q\) becomes empty, the final incumbent or infeasibility conclusion is certified.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports hybrid CP local-search control.
Fair scheduling requirements depend on the complete-search implementation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits a control-regime leaf, and the separation between heuristic guidance and certified frontier deletion is coherent. No citation supports this particular frontier-based hybrid controller or the scheduling conditions required for its completeness claim.

children.title: Hybrid Completeness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which hybridization preserves or forfeits completeness guarantees.

assumptions_latex: The original CSP has a finite search space.
Complete steps use covering branching and sound pruning.
A completeness claim is made only after all search obligations are discharged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uncertified deletion or indefinite starvation of a feasible unresolved region invalidates completeness; certified coverage together with fair finite processing preserves it.
review_flags: No supplied locator states the completeness boundary for hybrid search.
The corrupted mathematical statement has been reconstructed from the matching plain statement, assumptions, conclusion, and notation; direct source support remains required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact mechanisms by which heuristic hybridization can destroy finite-search completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a hybrid solver for a finite CSP whose complete component maintains a set \(Q\) of unresolved search regions. Completeness is lost if heuristic control may delete from \(Q\) a region \(R\) without a sound certificate excluding every feasible assignment in \(R\), or if the scheduler may leave such a region unprocessed indefinitely. Completeness is preserved when every deletion is justified by a sound certificate, branching children cover each processed region, and the scheduler processes every unresolved region after finitely many steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hybrid completeness is lost when heuristic control can discard unresolved regions or starve them forever; preserving certified coverage and fair processing retains completeness.
knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Completeness Boundaries
