knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Relation Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional representation of finite-domain constraints by allowed or forbidden tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a constraint have ordered scope \((x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\) with finite domains \(D_{i_1},\ldots,D_{i_r}\). An explicit allowed-tuple encoding stores a relation \(R\subseteq D_{i_1}\times\cdots\times D_{i_r}\), and an assignment satisfies the constraint exactly when \((x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\in R\). Equivalently, a forbidden-tuple encoding stores \(F\) and requires the scope tuple not to belong to \(F\). The representation length is proportional to the listed tuples times their arity, in addition to domain and symbol encodings; therefore complexity is measured relative to this explicit input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extensional constraint lists allowed or forbidden tuples, and satisfaction is tuple membership or nonmembership in that finite relation.
assumptions_latex: Every scope domain \(D_{i_j}\) is finite.
Tuples and domain values use a fixed finite encoding.
The scope order is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Allowed-table satisfaction is equivalent to membership in \(R\), while forbidden-table satisfaction is equivalent to nonmembership in \(F\).
review_flags: The supplied locator may not explicitly discuss extensional relation size.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits Explicit Relation Encoding, and the allowed- and forbidden-tuple semantics are precise. The cited general constraint-programming section is not sufficiently specific to support both extensional table semantics and the asserted proportional representation-length bound.

children.title: Succinct Relation Encoding
children.top_down_role: Compact representations of relations that avoid full tuple enumeration.

assumptions_latex: \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) has finite domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\).
The encoding has a specified decoding algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=\{a\in D_1\times\cdots\times D_k:\operatorname{Dec}(E,a)=1\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard definition of an implicitly represented finite relation; an authoritative CSP-specific source remains desirable.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circuit-or-string encoding with membership semantics, not an extensional tuple list.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A succinct encoding of a \(k\)-ary relation is a finite object \(E\), together with a decoding algorithm \(\operatorname{Dec}\), such that for every tuple \(a\in D_1\times\cdots\times D_k\), \(\operatorname{Dec}(E,a)\in\{0,1\}\) and
\[
R=\{a\in D_1\times\cdots\times D_k:\operatorname{Dec}(E,a)=1\}.
\]
The representation size is \(|E|\), including numerical parameters in binary unless another convention is stated; it need not be proportional to \(|R|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A succinct relation encoding represents tuple membership by a finite decoder, potentially using far less space than listing every allowed tuple.
knowledge_statements.title: Succinct Relation Encoding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The membership-decoder formulation is plausible, but it does not distinguish a merely implicit encoding from a formally succinct encoding by a size or encoding-class condition. A CSP-specific source is needed to settle the intended definition.

children.title: Global-Constraint Encoding
children.top_down_role: Named or intensional representations preserving global constraint structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) has finite domains.
The global constraint type supplies a polynomial-time membership predicate for its parameter encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\theta=\{a:\mathcal P(\theta,a)=1\}\).

notation.meaning: Encoded parameters of the global constraint

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard semantic definition of a parameterized global constraint; propagator complexity is deliberately excluded.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic encoding of one parameterized global constraint over an arbitrary-size scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A global-constraint encoding consists of a constraint type with a finite parameter string \(\theta\) and a predicate \(\mathcal P\). On a scope \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), it denotes
\[
R_\theta=\{a\in D_1\times\cdots\times D_k:\mathcal P(\theta,a)=1\}.
\]
Its input size is the bit length of \(\theta\), the scope description, and the encoded domains. The definition requires efficient recognition of a complete tuple, but does not by itself require polynomial-time consistency enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global constraint denotes a parameterized relation over a whole scope; recognizing complete assignments may be easy even when propagation is hard.
knowledge_statements.title: Global-Constraint Encoding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relation semantics are coherent, but polynomial-time complete-tuple recognition is not universally part of the definition of a global constraint. A source is needed to justify this restriction for the intended encoding family.

children.title: Representation-Size Effects
children.top_down_role: Complexity consequences of measuring input through compact rather than explicit encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Size Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity is representation-relative when implicit and extensional encodings differ exponentially.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Complexity claims are relative to representation length. If an implicit encoding of length \(L_{\mathrm{imp}}\) denotes a relation whose extensional table has length \(L_{\mathrm{ext}}\), then \(L_{\mathrm{ext}}\) may be exponential in \(L_{\mathrm{imp}}\). Consequently, a bound \(T=\operatorname{poly}(L_{\mathrm{ext}})\) can be exponential in \(L_{\mathrm{imp}}\). A generic transfer of a polynomial complexity bound between two encodings is justified when the encoding-size bound required in the relevant direction is polynomial; transferring bounds in both directions is justified when the two encoding lengths are polynomially related.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial time under a tuple-table encoding may become exponential under a succinct encoding; transferring a bound requires an appropriate polynomial relation between the representation sizes.
assumptions_latex: Two encodings describe the same finite-domain feasibility relation.
Running time is measured against the chosen encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial bound in one representation need not be polynomial in another unless an appropriate polynomial size relation is established in the direction of transfer.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.3.1, Problems, Instances, Encoding Size, p. 17

review_flags: source_scope_indirect: The cited section supports representation-relative encoding size generally; CSP-specific support remains desirable.

source_witnesses.locator: Section 1.3.1, Problems, Instances, Encoding Size, p. 17

children.title: Domain-Size Parameters
children.top_down_role: Input restrictions and complexity regimes indexed by domain cardinality.

assumptions_latex: A CSP instance has variables \(V\) with nonempty finite domains \(D_v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\max}=\max_{v\in V}|D_v|\) and \(d_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{v\in V}|D_v|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: These are standard finite-domain CSP size parameters.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality parameters for explicitly represented finite variable domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite-domain CSP with variable set \(V\), define
\[
n=|V|,\qquad d_{\max}=\max_{v\in V}|D_v|,\qquad d_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{v\in V}|D_v|.
\]
A uniform domain-size bound \(d\) means \(|D_v|\le d\) for every \(v\in V\). If domain values or domain sets are represented succinctly, their bit length is an additional input parameter and is not determined by these cardinalities alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain-size parameters record the number of variables, the largest domain, and the total number of available variable values.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Size Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cardinality parameters are precise, standard, and appropriate for the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Constraint-Arity Parameters
children.top_down_role: Input restrictions and complexity regimes indexed by relation arity.

assumptions_latex: A CSP instance has constraint set \(C\), and each constraint \(c\) has scope \(S_c\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\max}=\max_{c\in C}|S_c|\) and \(r_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{c\in C}|S_c|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Maximum arity and total scope incidence are standard CSP structural parameters.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arity measures distinct variables in constraint scopes, independently of relation representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a CSP with constraint set \(C\), where constraint \(c\) has scope \(S_c\subseteq V\), define
\[
r_{\max}=\max_{c\in C}|S_c|,
\qquad
r_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{c\in C}|S_c|.
\]
The instance has bounded arity when a constant \(r\) exists such that \(r_{\max}\le r\) throughout the instance class. Repeated syntactic occurrences of a variable do not increase \(|S_c|\); arity counts distinct scoped variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint-arity parameters measure the largest scope and total variable-constraint incidence, counting distinct variables in each scope.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Arity Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum arity and total scope-incidence definitions are internally consistent and fit the leaf, but they lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Scope-Structure Parameters
children.top_down_role: Input restrictions based on the composition or overlap of constraint scopes.

assumptions_latex: A CSP has variable set \(V\) and constraint scopes \((S_c)_{c\in C}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal graph, dual graph, and scope hypergraph are determined solely by \((S_c)_{c\in C}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: These three scope-derived structures are standard CSP representations.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical graph and hypergraph representations induced only by constraint scopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scope hypergraph is \(H=(V,\{S_c:c\in C\})\). The primal graph \(G_P\) has vertex set \(V\) and edge \(\{u,v\}\) exactly when distinct variables \(u,v\) occur together in some \(S_c\). The dual graph \(G_D\) has vertex set \(C\) and edge \(\{c,c'\}\) exactly when \(S_c\cap S_{c'}\ne\varnothing\). Width, acyclicity, degree, and separator parameters must specify which of these structures they measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint scopes induce a hypergraph, a variable-interaction graph, and a constraint-intersection graph; structural parameters must identify the chosen representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Scope-Structure Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph and hypergraph definitions are standard, but the record is chiefly a representation rather than an explicit account of scope-structure parameters. A source is needed before determining whether this treatment is adequate for the parameter leaf.

children.title: Parameter-Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Combined effects of domain size, arity, and scope structure.

assumptions_latex: A class of CSP instances fixes a relation representation and parameter vector.
Input length includes all encoded domains, scopes, relations, and numerical parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A tractability statement must bound running time as a function of the full encoding length and identify which parameters are fixed or variable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard parameterized-complexity discipline applied to CSP encoding and structure.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint interpretation of domain, arity, structural-width, and representation parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the complete encoding length and let \(\kappa\) collect designated parameters such as \(d_{\max}\), \(r_{\max}\), or a width measure. A uniform polynomial-time regime requires \(T\le L^{O(1)}\) with constants independent of every varying parameter. A fixed-parameter regime requires \(T\le f(\kappa)L^{O(1)}\). Bounds such as \(L^{g(\kappa)}\) describe parameter-dependent polynomial degree and do not establish fixed-parameter tractability. Every classification must also fix the relation-encoding model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CSP tractability depends jointly on encoding length, domain size, arity, and structure; the classification must state which parameters vary.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Interaction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinctions among polynomial time, fixed-parameter tractability, and parameter-dependent polynomial degree are precise and fit the leaf, but no authoritative parameterized-complexity or CSP source is supplied.

assumptions_latex: All constraints are binary and given extensionally.
The primal graph is a tree or forest.
Every domain has size at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Satisfiability and a satisfying assignment can be computed in \(O(|C|d^2+n d)\) time.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard leaf-to-root dynamic program for binary CSPs on a tree; source certification is pending.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional binary CSP with an acyclic primal graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Root each component of the primal forest. Process every directed child-parent edge \(u\to p\) bottom-up, retaining \(b\in D_p\) exactly when some \(a\in D_u\) satisfies the constraint on \(\{u,p\}\) and is compatible with all messages from children of \(u\). The instance is satisfiable exactly when each root retains a value. A top-down choice of stored supporting values constructs a solution. With table lookup in constant time, the computation uses \(O(|C|d^2+n d)\) time and \(O(|C|d)\) message space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bottom-up support messages solve an extensionally represented binary CSP on a forest in quadratic time per edge and can reconstruct a solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Structured Binary CSPs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity bound and dynamic-programming idea are plausible, but the recurrence refers to a single constraint per primal edge and does not state how multiple binary constraints on the same variable pair are combined. A source is required for the exact algorithm and bound.

assumptions_latex: A CSP has scope hypergraph \(H=(V,E)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is alpha-acyclic exactly when its hyperedges admit a join tree satisfying connected occurrence of every variable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Join-tree characterization is the standard alpha-acyclicity notion intended by acyclic database and CSP processing.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alpha-acyclic scope hypergraphs characterized by a join tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A scope hypergraph \(H=(V,E)\) is alpha-acyclic when there exists a tree \(T\) whose nodes are the hyperedges in \(E\) and such that, for every variable \(v\in V\), the set
\[
E_v=\{e\in E:v\in e\}
\]
induces a connected subtree of \(T\). Such a tree is a join tree. A finite-domain CSP is alpha-acyclic when the hypergraph formed by its constraint scopes has this property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CSP is alpha-acyclic when its constraint scopes form a join tree in which every variable occurs on a connected subtree.
knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic Hypergraph CSPs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The join-tree characterization of alpha-acyclicity is standard, precise, and appropriate for the leaf, but it has no inspectable citation.

assumptions_latex: Each constraint relation is an explicit finite table.
The constraint scopes admit a join tree.
Semijoin and projection operations use the common separator variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After two directional passes, the CSP is satisfiable exactly when no reduced relation is empty, and compatible tuples reconstruct a solution.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard semijoin processing algorithm for alpha-acyclic CSPs; source certification is pending.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semijoin reduction on an explicit-table join tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose a root of the join tree. For every child-parent edge \(e\to f\), in postorder replace
\[
R_f\leftarrow R_f\ltimes \pi_{S_{ef}}(R_e),
\]
where tuples of \(R_f\) without a matching separator tuple are deleted. Then traverse edges from root to leaves and replace each child relation analogously using its parent. Stop with failure if any relation becomes empty; otherwise choose a root tuple and recursively choose matching child tuples. The running time is polynomial in the total explicit relation-table size under standard indexed relational operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two semijoin passes along a join tree remove unsupported tuples; nonempty reduced relations permit a satisfying assignment to be assembled.
knowledge_statements.title: Join-Tree Processing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-pass semijoin algorithm fits the container and is mathematically plausible for explicit relations on a join tree. Its global-consistency conclusion and polynomial-time claim require an authoritative source specifying the relational-operation model.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Bucket elimination, cycle cutsets, and tree clustering

assumptions_latex: A finite-domain CSP and an elimination ordering \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) are given.
Relations support join and projection over finite tables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The final nullary relation is nonempty exactly when the original CSP is satisfiable.

notation.meaning: Bucket of relations whose latest variable is x_i
Join of relations in bucket i
Maximum induced width of the ordering

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard relational bucket-elimination formulation; source certification is pending.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-form variable elimination using joins and projections of finite relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign every input relation to the bucket of its latest scoped variable in the ordering. For \(i=n,n-1,\ldots,1\), form \(J_i=\Join_{R\in B_i}R\), stop as inconsistent if \(J_i=\varnothing\), and insert \(\pi_{\operatorname{scope}(J_i)\setminus\{x_i\}}(J_i)\) into the bucket of its latest remaining variable. The final nullary relation decides satisfiability; stored supporting tuples permit reconstruction. If domains have size at most \(d\) and induced width is \(w\), intermediate tables contain at most \(d^{w+1}\) tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bucket elimination joins all relations involving the next eliminated variable, projects that variable away, and passes the resulting relation to an earlier bucket.
knowledge_statements.title: Bucket Elimination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elimination step and induced-width table bound are standard, but empty buckets, projected nullary relations, and disconnected components are not explicitly handled. A source is needed to certify the exact decision algorithm and width convention.

assumptions_latex: A binary CSP has primal graph \(G=(V,E)\) and maximum domain size \(d\).
A set \(S\subseteq V\) is chosen so that \(G-S\) is a forest.
Binary relations are available by constant-time lookup.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Satisfiability can be decided in \(O(d^{|S|}(|E|d^2+|V|d))\) time.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard conditioning algorithm parameterized by a cycle cutset; source certification is pending.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning a binary CSP on a vertex set whose deletion leaves a forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Enumerate every assignment \(a\in\prod_{v\in S}D_v\). Reject \(a\) if it violates a constraint internal to \(S\). Otherwise restrict each remaining domain by constraints between its variable and \(S\), then solve the residual forest CSP by tree processing. Return the first combined satisfying assignment, or unsatisfiable if every \(a\) fails. Since at most \(d^{|S|}\) assignments are examined, the running time is
\[
O\bigl(d^{|S|}(|E|d^2+|V|d)\bigr),
\]
up to linear-time checking of constraints incident to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign the cycle-cutset variables exhaustively, reduce the remaining instance to a forest, and solve each residual CSP by tree processing.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Cutset Decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Conditioning on a cycle cutset and solving the residual forest fits the algorithm leaf. The exact runtime, including checks of constraints internal or incident to the cutset, needs an authoritative citation.

assumptions_latex: A finite-domain constraint network has variables \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\), domains of size at most \(d\), and constraint relations over subsets of \(X\).
A tree decomposition \((T,\{B_t\}_{t\in V(T)})\) of the primal graph is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm decides consistency and supports recovery of the network's solutions by tree-structured relational message passing over the clusters.

notation.meaning: Cluster bag at tree node t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard join-tree clustering algorithm for finite-domain constraint networks
conclusion restricted to the relational constraint-network setting introduced by the assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Join-tree clustering on a supplied primal-graph tree decomposition for extensional finite-domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign every constraint to a tree node whose bag contains its scope. Root \(T\). For each directed edge \(t\to p\), form a message on the separator \(S_{tp}=B_t\cap B_p\) by joining the relations assigned to \(t\) with incoming messages from neighbors other than \(p\), then projecting onto \(S_{tp}\). Compute messages from leaves to the root and, if complete solution recovery is required, from the root toward the leaves while recording compatible extensions. The root relation obtained after incorporating its assigned constraints and all incoming messages is empty exactly when the network is inconsistent. With table relations and \(w=\max_t|B_t|-1\), each cluster table has at most \(d^{w+1}\) tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign constraints to decomposition bags, pass projected relations across separators, and recover consistency or solutions. Each cluster table is exponential in the largest bag size.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree Clustering

assumptions_latex: A finite-domain constraint network and an elimination ordering \(\pi=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) are given.
Relations are represented extensionally and support join and projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting network is directionally consistent along \(\pi\), and inconsistency is detected when an eliminated relation becomes empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional adaptive consistency for extensional finite-domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Process variables in reverse order. When processing \(x_i\), join all current relations whose latest variable under \(\pi\) is \(x_i\), obtaining \(R_i\); project \(R_i\) onto its variables other than \(x_i\), and insert that projection as a new relation. If \(R_i\) or its required projection is empty, stop and report inconsistency. Otherwise continue to \(x_1\); compatible values may then be selected in forward order to construct a solution. If \(w(\pi)\) is the induced width and domains have size at most \(d\), intermediate relations involve at most \(w(\pi)+1\) variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate variables in reverse order by joining their current constraints and projecting them away; empty intermediate relations certify inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and directional variable-elimination formulation are plausible for adaptive consistency, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the exact update scheme, directional-consistency conclusion, or solution-recovery claim.

children.title: Treewidth Measures
children.top_down_role: Width quantities associated with primal-graph tree structure.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The treewidth of \(G\) is the least possible maximum number of earlier filled neighbors over all elimination orderings.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard elimination-order definition of graph treewidth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination-order formulation of primal-graph treewidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an ordering \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), eliminate vertices from \(v_n\) to \(v_1\), adding edges that make the remaining neighbors of each eliminated vertex a clique. Let \(w_G(\pi)\) be the maximum, over eliminated vertices, of the number of their remaining neighbors at elimination. The treewidth measure is
\[
\operatorname{tw}(G)=\min_{\pi} w_G(\pi).
\]
Equivalently, \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is one less than the minimum possible largest clique size among chordal completions produced by elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treewidth is the minimum, over vertex elimination orders, of the largest number of remaining neighbors encountered during filled elimination.
knowledge_statements.title: Treewidth Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the treewidth-measure container, and the elimination-width formulation is standard and internally consistent. No source reference with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Tree Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Tree-organized bag structures used for width-based reasoning.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(T\) is a finite tree and each \(B_t\) is a subset of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((T,\{B_t\})\) is a tree decomposition precisely when vertex coverage, edge coverage, and running intersection hold.

notation.meaning: Bag indexed by tree node t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical definition of a graph tree decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard tree decompositions of finite primal graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A tree decomposition of \(G\) is a pair \((T,\{B_t\}_{t\in V(T)})\) satisfying
\[
\bigcup_{t\in V(T)}B_t=V,
\]
every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\) has \(\{u,v\}\subseteq B_t\) for some \(t\), and for every \(v\in V\), the set \(\{t:v\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree of \(T\). Its width is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\). The connectedness condition is also called the running-intersection property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree decomposition covers all vertices and edges with bags arranged so that the bags containing each vertex form a connected subtree.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the container, and the three tree-decomposition conditions and width convention are stated consistently. No source reference with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Width–Decomposition Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between decomposition quality and the resulting width.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum tree-decomposition width equals the minimum induced elimination width and hence equals \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical equivalence of tree decompositions, chordal completions, and elimination width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-graph treewidth correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every finite undirected graph \(G\),
\[
\operatorname{tw}(G)
=\min_{(T,\{B_t\})}\left(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\right)
=\min_{\pi}w_G(\pi),
\]
where the first minimum ranges over all tree decompositions of \(G\), and the second ranges over all vertex orderings, with fill edges added during elimination. Thus an ordering of induced width \(k\) yields a tree decomposition of width at most \(k\), while a tree decomposition of width \(k\) yields an elimination ordering of induced width at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph's optimal tree-decomposition width and optimal filled-elimination width are equal; each representation can be converted into the other without increasing width.
knowledge_statements.title: Width–Decomposition Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role is correct for the correspondence leaf, and the equality and two conversion directions are appropriately stated for finite undirected graphs. The theorem has no cited authoritative source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Induced Width
children.top_down_role: Width associated with variable elimination on the primal graph.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph and \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) is a vertex ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The induced width \(w_G(\pi)\) is the largest number of uneliminated neighbors encountered during filled elimination according to \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: Filled graph immediately before eliminating v_i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard induced-width definition for variable elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Filled-elimination width of a fixed ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Eliminate vertices in the order \(v_n,v_{n-1},\ldots,v_1\). Immediately before eliminating \(v_i\), add every missing edge between its neighbors that remain in \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}\). If \(N_i^+(v_i)\) denotes those remaining neighbors after fill, define
\[
w_G(\pi)=\max_{1\le i\le n}|N_i^+(v_i)|.
\]
The added edges form the induced graph associated with \(\pi\). For a constraint network, this width bounds the number of other variables co-occurring with an eliminated variable in an intermediate relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Induced width is the maximum number of still-active neighbors of a vertex when fill edges are added and vertices are eliminated in a fixed order.
knowledge_statements.title: Induced Width

children.title: Elimination Orderings
children.top_down_role: Variable orders used to organize elimination and graph fill.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) is the variable set of a finite-domain constraint network with primal graph \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An elimination ordering fixes the sequence of variable removal and thereby the fill graph, induced scopes, and induced width.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable orderings for primal-graph elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An elimination ordering is a bijection \(\pi:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to X\), written \(\pi=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), together with the convention that variables are eliminated from \(x_n\) down to \(x_1\). When \(x_i\) is eliminated, all of its currently uneliminated neighbors are joined pairwise by fill edges before \(x_i\) is removed. Equivalently for constraint elimination, all current relations containing \(x_i\) are combined, and their projection after removing \(x_i\) becomes a relation over those remaining neighbors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elimination ordering is a variable permutation that determines removal order, fill edges, intermediate constraint scopes, and ultimately computational width.
knowledge_statements.title: Elimination Orderings

children.title: Ordering-Quality Effects
children.top_down_role: Consequences of ordering choice for induced width and intermediate structure.

assumptions_latex: A finite-domain constraint network has \(n\) variables, \(m\) input relations, domain size at most \(d\), and primal graph \(G\).

Bucket-style variable elimination uses extensional tables, an ordering \(\pi\) of induced width \(w_G(\pi)\), constant-time indexed relation lookups, and produces at most one projected table per eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordering controls the exponential factor: intermediate joined tables have size at most \(d^{w_G(\pi)+1}\), and under the stated implementation assumptions elimination takes \(O((m+n)d^{w_G(\pi)+1})\) time and \(O(nd^{w_G(\pi)})\) additional table space.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard table-based variable-elimination width bound
aggregate bounds require the stated table-access and bucket-processing assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case table growth and bucket-elimination resource bounds under a fixed ordering and explicit extensional-table model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the elimination of any variable, the combined intermediate relation contains that variable and at most \(w_G(\pi)\) remaining neighbors. Hence its table contains at most \(d^{w_G(\pi)+1}\) assignments, and the projected table contains at most \(d^{w_G(\pi)}\) assignments. Under the stated indexed-table and bucket-processing assumptions, total elimination time is \(O\!\left((m+n)d^{w_G(\pi)+1}\right)\), and the projected tables require \(O\!\left(nd^{w_G(\pi)}\right)\) additional entries. Consequently, different orderings of the same graph can yield exponentially different worst-case resource bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For indexed extensional tables, elimination is exponential in the chosen ordering's induced width; different orderings can therefore have exponentially different worst-case time and additional-space bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Quality Effects

assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,E)\) is a finite hypergraph.
A rooted tree \(T\) indexes vertex bags \(\chi(t)\subseteq V\) and hyperedge guards \(\lambda(t)\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hypertree width \(\operatorname{hw}(H)\) is the minimum, over hypertree decompositions, of \(\max_t|\lambda(t)|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical hypertree width, including the special condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hypertree decomposition is \((T,\chi,\lambda)\) such that every \(e\in E\) is contained in some \(\chi(t)\); for every \(v\in V\), the nodes whose bags contain \(v\) form a connected subtree; \(\chi(t)\subseteq\bigcup_{e\in\lambda(t)}e\) for every \(t\); and, writing \(T_t\) for the subtree rooted at \(t\),
\[
\left(\bigcup_{e\in\lambda(t)}e\right)\cap\left(\bigcup_{u\in V(T_t)}\chi(u)\right)\subseteq\chi(t).
\]
Its width is \(\max_t|\lambda(t)|\), and \(\operatorname{hw}(H)\) is the minimum such width.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hypertree width minimizes the maximum number of guarding hyperedges per bag in a rooted decomposition satisfying coverage, connectedness, and the special condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypertree Width

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, and the record includes the guard condition and rooted special condition needed for classical hypertree decompositions. Because hypertree-decomposition variants differ in exactly these conditions, an authoritative source with a precise definition or page locator is required before accepting this formulation.

assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,E)\) is a finite hypergraph.
\((T,\{B_t\})\) ranges over tree decompositions of the primal graph of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fractional hypertree width is \(\operatorname{fhw}(H)=\min_T\max_t\rho_H^*(B_t)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard bag-based definition of fractional hypertree width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional edge-cover width over primal-graph tree decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subseteq V\), define its fractional edge-cover number by
\[
\rho_H^*(S)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}\gamma_e:\gamma_e\ge0,\ \sum_{e\ni v}\gamma_e\ge1\text{ for every }v\in S\right\}.
\]
The fractional hypertree width of \(H\) is
\[
\operatorname{fhw}(H)=\min_{(T,\{B_t\})}\max_{t\in V(T)}\rho_H^*(B_t),
\]
where the minimum ranges over all tree decompositions of the primal graph of \(H\). Thus integral guard cardinality is replaced by the optimum fractional hyperedge-cover weight of each bag.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional hypertree width minimizes, over tree decompositions, the largest fractional hyperedge-cover number of any bag.
knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Hypertree Width

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, and the fractional edge-cover linear program and bag-width minimization are internally consistent. No source reference with a specific definition, section, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,E)\) is a finite hypergraph.
Functions considered are normalized, monotone, submodular, and edge-dominated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The submodular width is the largest, over all admissible \(f\), of the least possible maximum bag value in a tree decomposition.
review_flags: normalization conventions require authoritative source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-dominated submodular width of finite hypergraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) satisfy \(f(\varnothing)=0\), monotonicity, and submodularity
\[
f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B),
\]
and be edge-dominated, meaning \(f(e)\le1\) for every \(e\in E\). Define
\[
f\text{-}\operatorname{width}(H)=\min_{(T,\{B_t\})}\max_{t\in V(T)}f(B_t),
\qquad
\operatorname{subw}(H)=\sup_f f\text{-}\operatorname{width}(H),
\]
where decompositions are tree decompositions of the primal graph and the supremum ranges over all such \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Submodular width maximizes, over normalized edge-dominated submodular functions, the minimum achievable largest bag value of a tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Width

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, and the formula states the normalized, monotone, submodular, edge-dominated convention explicitly. A precise source is needed to confirm the admissible-function convention and the use of a supremum for this version of submodular width.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite undirected graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\).
Running time is measured in the standard deterministic Turing-machine model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact unrestricted decomposition discovery is NP-complete as a decision problem, while fixed-width discovery is fixed-parameter tractable in \(k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical NP-completeness and fixed-parameter tractability of treewidth
exact algorithmic bound and citation required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discovery cost for primal-graph tree decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The decision problem
\[
\text{given }(G,k),\text{ decide whether }\operatorname{tw}(G)\le k
\]
is NP-complete when \(k\) is part of the input. Nevertheless, there exists a computable function \(f\) and an algorithm running in \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\) time that either constructs a tree decomposition of width at most \(k\) or correctly reports that none exists. Thus tractability conditional on a supplied low-width decomposition does not make unrestricted optimal decomposition discovery polynomial-time, although bounded width remains algorithmically exploitable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finding an optimal tree decomposition is NP-hard, but deciding and constructing one at fixed width is fixed-parameter tractable in the width.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Discovery Cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the discovery-cost leaf, and the NP-completeness/FPT distinction is standard. The exact decision and constructive FPT assertions require authoritative theorem-level citations with inspectable locators; none are supplied, and the local inventory is unrelated to graph treewidth discovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Separator State-Space Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Table-size boundary for separator-based dynamic programming on finite-domain CSPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a separator in a decomposition of a finite-domain CSP, and let every variable \(x\in S\) have finite domain \(D_x\). A dynamic-programming state that records every assignment on \(S\) has
\[N_S=\prod_{x\in S}|D_x|\]
possible configurations. If \(|S|\le s\) and \(|D_x|\le d\) for every \(x\in S\), then \(N_S\le d^s\). Thus the state space is exponential in the separator-size bound \(s\). When \(s\) is fixed and domains are represented explicitly, this table size is polynomial in the input length; with succinctly represented domains, polynomiality additionally depends on the representation and supported constraint operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separator of size at most s over domains of size at most d has at most d^s assignment states. This is polynomial for fixed s with explicitly represented domains, but succinct domain representations require additional assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a separator whose complete assignments index the dynamic-programming states.
Every \(D_x\) is finite.
The polynomial-input-size conclusion assumes that domains are represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_S=\prod_{x\in S}|D_x|\le d^s\) when \(|S|\le s\) and \(|D_x|\le d\); for fixed \(s\), this is polynomial under explicit domain representation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct counting of assignments in a separator table

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Constraint Width Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of primal-graph width for constraints represented globally rather than extensionally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a CSP with variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and one global constraint whose scope is \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\). Its primal graph is the clique \(K_n\), so its treewidth is \(n-1\), even if membership in the global relation and its propagation oracle are computable in polynomial time. Thus primal-treewidth methods can report unbounded width solely because of a large global scope. Conversely, bounded incidence or hypergraph width does not ensure tractability unless the required constraint projections, joins, or extension tests also admit polynomial-time representations and algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomially manageable global constraint may create a primal clique, while generalized width remains useful only when constraint operations are computationally tractable.
assumptions_latex: A primal graph connects every pair of variables occurring in a common constraint scope.
The global constraint has scope \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal treewidth equals \(n-1\); alternative width bounds require tractable access to the global relation.

notation.meaning: number of variables in the global scope

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a constraint scope induces a clique in the primal graph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal-clique observation is standard, but the converse claim about incidence or hypergraph width depends on the representation of global relations and the precise decomposition framework. No inspectable source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Backtrack-Free Orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Freuder’s sufficient consistency condition for backtrack-free search along a fixed ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite CSP and \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) a variable ordering of induced width \(w\). If \(I\) is strongly \((w+1)\)-consistent, then chronological search assigning variables in the order \(\pi\) is backtrack-free: for every \(i\), every consistent assignment to \(v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\) extends to at least one value of \(v_i\). Therefore, unless an empty domain or relation has already established inconsistency, choosing any value that remains consistent with the preceding assignment can be continued through \(v_n\) to obtain a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong (w+1)-consistency makes search backtrack-free along any ordering of induced width w.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is strongly \((w+1)\)-consistent.
The ordering \(\pi\) has induced width \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Chronological search along \(\pi\) extends every consistent prefix and requires no backtracking.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed Freuder condition is standard under an appropriate induced-width convention, but ordering direction and the applicable CSP consistency framework must be checked against an exact source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Induced-Width Consistency Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency level sufficient for search under a variable ordering of bounded induced width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite CSP and an ordering \(\pi\) of induced width \(w\), strong \(k\)-consistency with \(k\ge w+1\) is a sufficient regime for backtrack-free search along \(\pi\). The threshold depends on the ordering: changing \(\pi\) may change \(w\), and hence the required consistency level. If a family of instances admits orderings with \(w\le c\) for a fixed constant \(c\), enforcing strong \((c+1)\)-consistency followed by ordered assignment yields a polynomial-time decision procedure, provided consistency enforcement at that fixed level is polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordering of induced width w requires strong consistency through level w+1; bounded width therefore gives a fixed local-consistency regime.
assumptions_latex: The CSP is finite.
Strong \(k\)-consistency can be enforced in polynomial time for each fixed \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(k\ge w+1\), search along \(\pi\) is backtrack-free; constant \(w\) gives a fixed-level polynomial regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: consequence of the Freuder width-consistency theorem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regime is a plausible consequence of the Freuder theorem, but the ordering convention and the complexity of enforcing fixed-level consistency require a source and an explicit representation model.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Consistency-Solvable Languages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite constraint languages decided uniformly by a fixed level of local consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be finite and let \(\Gamma\) be a constraint language over \(A\). The language \(\Gamma\) is local-consistency-solvable, or has bounded width, if there exist fixed integers \(1\le k\le \ell\) such that, for every finite instance \(I\) over \(\Gamma\), enforcing \((k,\ell)\)-consistency decides satisfiability: the resulting local-consistency closure contains an empty relation exactly when \(I\) is unsatisfiable. The pair \((k,\ell)\) depends only on \(\Gamma\), not on the size or constraint scopes of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite language is local-consistency-solvable when one fixed consistency level detects unsatisfiability for every instance over that language.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(\Gamma\) are finite.
Instances use relations from \(\Gamma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma\) has bounded width precisely when some fixed \((k,\ell)\)-consistency procedure decides every instance over \(\Gamma\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This fits the definition container, but bounded-width definitions vary in their formulation of the canonical (k,l)-consistency procedure and rejection condition. An authoritative locator is required to fix the convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Relational Width
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pair-valued width defined through completeness of the relational consistency procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite constraint language and let \(1\le k\le\ell\). The relational width of \(\Gamma\) is at most \((k,\ell)\) if every \((k,\ell)\)-minimal instance over \(\Gamma\) in which every constraint relation is nonempty has a solution. Here every set of at most \(\ell\) variables is contained in a constraint scope, and the constraint relations have identical projections on every common variable set of size at most \(k\). Equivalently, the canonical \((k,\ell)\)-consistency procedure rejects every unsatisfiable instance over \(\Gamma\) and does not reject a satisfiable one. The language has bounded relational width if such a fixed pair \((k,\ell)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relational width at most (k,l) means that every nonempty instance stabilized by the corresponding scope and projection-consistency conditions is satisfiable.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma\) is a finite constraint language.
\(1\le k\le\ell\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relational width at most \((k,\ell)\) is equivalent to completeness of the \((k,\ell)\)-consistency test for \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard relational-width characterization via minimal instances

children.title: Relational Closure
children.top_down_role: Closure organization for relations generated within a constraint language.

knowledge_statements.title: Relational Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primitive-positive closure of a finite-domain constraint language.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be a finite domain and \(\Gamma\) a set of finitary relations on \(A\). The relational closure \(\langle\Gamma\rangle\) is the set of all relations \(R\subseteq A^m\), over all finite arities \(m\), definable by a primitive-positive formula
\[R(\mathbf{x})\iff \exists\mathbf{y}\;\bigwedge_{j=1}^{q}\alpha_j,\]
where each atomic formula \(\alpha_j\) applies a relation from \(\Gamma\) to variables or is an equality atom. Thus the allowed closure operations are conjunction, introduction of existentially quantified variables, identification of variables, and equality; negation and disjunction are not allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relational closure consists exactly of relations definable from the language using conjunction, existential quantification, variable identification, and equality.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is finite.
Every member of \(\Gamma\) is a finitary relation on \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle\Gamma\rangle\) is the primitive-positive closure of \(\Gamma\) with equality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primitive-positive closure definition is mathematically standard and fits the container, but no source verifies the stated equality convention and closure operations.

children.title: Polymorphism Invariance
children.top_down_role: Preservation-based organization of relations under polymorphism operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Polymorphism Invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise preservation of relations by operations on the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\subseteq A^m\) and let \(f:A^r\to A\). The relation \(R\) is invariant under \(f\), and \(f\) is a polymorphism of \(R\), if for every \(r\) tuples \(\mathbf{a}^{1},\ldots,\mathbf{a}^{r}\in R\), the coordinatewise tuple
\[f(\mathbf{a}^{1},\ldots,\mathbf{a}^{r})=\bigl(f(a^{1}_1,\ldots,a^{r}_1),\ldots,f(a^{1}_m,\ldots,a^{r}_m)\bigr)\]
also belongs to \(R\). For a language \(\Gamma\), \(\operatorname{Pol}(\Gamma)\) contains the operations preserving every relation in \(\Gamma\), while \(\operatorname{Inv}(F)\) contains the relations preserved by every operation in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operation preserves a relation when applying it coordinatewise to any member tuples produces another tuple in the relation.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq A^m\) is finitary.
\(f:A^r\to A\) is a total operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in\operatorname{Pol}(R)\) exactly when \(R\) is closed under coordinatewise application of \(f\).

notation.meaning: operations preserving every relation in Gamma
relations invariant under every operation in F

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of relational invariance and polymorphism

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise preservation definition is precise and appropriate, but it has no inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Closure–Invariance Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The organizing relationship between relational closure and preservation.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure–Invariance Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain polymorphism theorem for primitive-positive definability with equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be finite and let \(\Gamma\) be a constraint language on \(A\). A finitary relation \(R\) on \(A\) is primitive-positive definable from \(\Gamma\), with equality allowed, if and only if every polymorphism of \(\Gamma\) preserves \(R\). Consequently,
\[\langle\Gamma\rangle=\operatorname{Inv}(\operatorname{Pol}(\Gamma)).\]
Thus two finite-domain constraint languages having the same polymorphisms have the same primitive-positive relational closure, and algebraic preservation may be used to test or characterize relational expressibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over a finite domain, a relation is primitive-positive definable from a language exactly when all polymorphisms of the language preserve it.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is finite.
\(\Gamma\) consists of finitary relations on \(A\), and equality is available in primitive-positive definitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle\Gamma\rangle=\operatorname{Inv}(\operatorname{Pol}(\Gamma))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-domain closure–invariance correspondence is stated in its standard form, but this nontrivial theorem requires an exact authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Tractable Polymorphism Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical polymorphism conditions sufficient for polynomial-time finite-domain CSP algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite constraint language on a finite domain \(A\). Each of the following is an independent sufficient condition for polynomial-time solvability of \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\): \(\Gamma\) admits a semilattice polymorphism; \(\Gamma\) admits a majority polymorphism \(m\) satisfying \(m(x,x,y)=m(x,y,x)=m(y,x,x)=x\); or \(\Gamma\) admits a Mal'tsev polymorphism \(p\) satisfying \(p(x,x,y)=y\) and \(p(x,y,y)=x\). These families are sufficient examples rather than an exhaustive classification of tractable finite-domain languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semilattice, majority, and Mal'tsev polymorphisms each provide a classical sufficient route to polynomial-time CSP solvability.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(\Gamma\) are finite.
The stated operation preserves every relation of \(\Gamma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any one of the three stated polymorphism conditions implies \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{P}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical algebraic sufficient conditions for CSP tractability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three tractability implications are classical but arise from distinct algorithmic results and need sources for each family. The semilattice operation is also named without stating its associative, commutative, and idempotent identities.

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Tractable Constraint Languages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial side of Schaefer’s dichotomy for finite Boolean constraint languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite set of relations on \(\{0,1\}\). If every relation in \(\Gamma\) is preserved by at least one common operation from the following list, then \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) is polynomial-time solvable: constant \(0\), constant \(1\), conjunction \(x\wedge y\), disjunction \(x\vee y\), Boolean majority, or parity \(x\oplus y\oplus z\). These cases correspond respectively to \(0\)-valid, \(1\)-valid, Horn, dual-Horn, bijunctive, and affine constraint languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite Boolean language is tractable when it is 0-valid, 1-valid, Horn, dual-Horn, bijunctive, or affine.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma\) is a finite Boolean constraint language.
One listed operation preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{P}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: polynomial cases in Schaefer's Boolean dichotomy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The listed Boolean tractable cases and their common-polymorphism formulation are standard, but Schaefer's theorem is nontrivial and no exact source locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Hard Constraint Languages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-complete side of Schaefer’s dichotomy for finite Boolean constraint languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite set of relations on \(\{0,1\}\). Suppose no single operation among constant \(0\), constant \(1\), conjunction, disjunction, Boolean majority, and parity \(x\oplus y\oplus z\) preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\). Equivalently, \(\Gamma\) is neither \(0\)-valid, \(1\)-valid, Horn, dual-Horn, bijunctive, nor affine. Then deciding whether a finite conjunction of constraints using relations from \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite Boolean constraint language outside Schaefer’s six tractable classes has an NP-complete satisfiability problem.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma\) is a finite Boolean constraint language.
\(\Gamma\) belongs to none of Schaefer's six tractable classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: NP-complete case of Schaefer's Boolean dichotomy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hard side of Schaefer's dichotomy is stated appropriately for a finite Boolean language, but the NP-completeness conclusion requires an exact authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Language Tractable Side
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic tractability side of the finite-domain CSP dichotomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be finite and let \(\Gamma\) be a finite constraint language on \(D\). Replace \(\Gamma\) by a core having the same CSP complexity. If this core admits a Taylor polymorphism—equivalently, an idempotent Siggers polymorphism—then the decision problem \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\), whose input is a conjunction of constraints using relations from \(\Gamma\), is solvable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite constraint language is polynomial-time tractable when its core admits a Taylor, equivalently idempotent Siggers, polymorphism.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and \(\Gamma\) are finite.
The selected representative of \(\Gamma\) is a core.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{P}\).

notation.meaning: finite constraint language over the domain
decision CSP restricted to relations in the language

knowledge_statements.title: General CSP Intractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity without structural or language restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unrestricted finite-domain CSP decision problem is in NP and is NP-hard even over the Boolean domain. In particular, fix the finite language containing, for every sign pattern, the ternary Boolean relation satisfying the corresponding three-literal clause. Translating each 3-CNF clause into its matching relation gives a polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT. Consequently, unrestricted finite-domain CSP is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without structural or language restrictions, finite-domain CSP is NP-complete, already for a fixed Boolean constraint language encoding 3-SAT.
assumptions_latex: Constraints are represented explicitly and have polynomially checkable scopes and tuples.
The input asks whether at least one satisfying assignment exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CSP}\) is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.

notation.meaning: unrestricted finite-domain constraint satisfaction decision problem
satisfiability of Boolean formulas in three-literal conjunctive normal form

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-language encoding of 3-SAT is standard

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The NP-completeness claim is standard, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied. The reduction narrative is also proof material and should be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Structural Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes induced by restrictions on instance structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic programming on bounded-treewidth primal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite-domain CSP instance with maximum domain size \(d\), and suppose a tree decomposition of its primal graph of width \(k\) is supplied. Dynamic programming over the bags, indexed by assignments to at most \(k+1\) variables, decides satisfiability in time \(d^{k+1}|I|^{O(1)}\) for extensionally represented constraints. Thus every class of instances with bounded primal treewidth and bounded domain size is polynomial-time tractable independently of its constraint language.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a primal-graph decomposition of width k and maximum domain size d, bag dynamic programming decides an extensionally represented CSP in time d^(k+1) times a polynomial in the input size.
assumptions_latex: All variable domains are finite and have size at most \(d\).
A width-\(k\) tree decomposition of the primal graph is supplied.
Constraint relations are represented extensionally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) is decidable in time \(d^{k+1}|I|^{O(1)}\).

notation.meaning: width of the supplied primal-graph tree decomposition

children.title: Constraint-Language Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes induced by restrictions on allowed constraint languages.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Language Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tractability obtained by fixing the allowed relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed finite domain \(D\) and fixed finite constraint language \(\Gamma\), instance size varies through variables, scopes, and constraint occurrences while every constraint relation belongs to \(\Gamma\). The Bulatov–Zhuk dichotomy states that \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) is polynomial-time solvable when the core of \(\Gamma\) admits a Taylor polymorphism, and is NP-complete otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing the constraint language yields a dichotomy: a Taylor polymorphism of its core gives tractability; its absence gives NP-completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is finite.
\(\Gamma\) is finite and fixed rather than part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{P}\), or \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) is NP-complete, according to the Taylor-polymorphism criterion.

notation.meaning: CSP restricted to relations from the language

children.title: Joint Restriction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Tractability arising only from combined structural and language conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Restriction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance classes restricted simultaneously by structure and allowed relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A joint structure–language restriction regime is a class \(\mathcal C\) of finite-domain CSP instances specified by coupled conditions on each instance's structural representation \(H(I)\), such as its primal graph or constraint hypergraph, and on the relations \(\Gamma(I)\) used by that instance. The regime is polynomial-time tractable if one algorithm decides every \(I\in\mathcal C\) in time polynomial in \(|I|\), with the polynomial uniform over all permitted structure–language pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint regime couples restrictions on an instance's graph or hypergraph with restrictions on its relations and requires one uniform algorithm.
assumptions_latex: Every \(I\in\mathcal C\) has an explicitly represented finite domain and constraints.
Membership in \(\mathcal C\) is fixed as part of the regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is tractable exactly when a uniform polynomial-time decision algorithm exists for all \(I\in\mathcal C\).

notation.meaning: jointly restricted class of CSP instances
chosen structural representation of an instance

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes the standard two-axis restriction regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent and fits the joint-regime leaf, but the proposed coupled-regime formalization and uniformity condition have no cited source with a locator.

children.title: Combined-Tractability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits where separately useful restrictions fail to yield joint tractability.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined-Tractability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why neither structural nor language complexity alone defines the full boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Neither bounded structural width nor a tractable fixed language is individually necessary for polynomial-time CSP classes. Instances whose primal graphs are trees are tractable by dynamic programming even when their binary relations vary with the input. Conversely, instances over a fixed bijunctive Boolean language are tractable by 2-SAT even when their primal graphs have unbounded treewidth. Hence a taxonomy using only one projection—structure or language—cannot characterize every tractable combined regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tractability may come from structure or language: tree-structured arbitrary binary CSPs and unbounded-treewidth 2-SAT exhibit opposite mechanisms.
assumptions_latex: Tree-structured constraints are binary and represented extensionally.
The bijunctive Boolean language is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither bounded primal treewidth nor bounded structural width is a necessary condition for every tractable language-restricted CSP class, and language tractability is unnecessary on tree-structured binary classes.

notation.meaning: satisfiability for conjunctive formulas with clauses of at most two literals

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: tree-CSP dynamic programming and 2-SAT tractability are classical

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two examples plausibly establish the stated failure boundary, and failure_boundary is the appropriate content kind, but neither example nor the resulting taxonomy claim has an authoritative citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized CSP Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-domain CSP parameterized by primal treewidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite domain \(D\), and parameterize a CSP instance \(I\) by the primal-graph treewidth \(k\). Given a width-\(k\) tree decomposition, bag dynamic programming decides satisfiability in time \(|D|^{k+1}|I|^{O(1)}\), provided constraint relations are polynomial-time testable from their representations. Because \(D\) is fixed, this has the form \(f(k)|I|^{O(1)}\) with \(f(k)=|D|^{k+1}\); therefore the regime is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed finite domain, CSP is fixed-parameter tractable by primal treewidth, with parameter dependence |D|^(k+1) and a polynomial input-size factor.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is finite and fixed.
A width-\(k\) primal-graph tree decomposition is supplied.
Relations are polynomial-time testable from their representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CSP}\) is fixed-parameter tractable in \(k\), with running time \(|D|^{k+1}|I|^{O(1)}\).

source_refs.source_title: Complexity of K-Tree Structured Constraint Satisfaction Problems

source_witnesses.source_title: Complexity of K-Tree Structured Constraint Satisfaction Problems

knowledge_statements.title: Counting CSP Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counting assignments rather than deciding their existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite domain \(D\) and constraint language \(\Gamma\), the counting problem \(\#\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) maps an instance \(I=(V,C)\) to \[\#\operatorname{CSP}(I)=\left|\left\{s:V\to D:\ s\text{ satisfies every constraint in }C\right\}\right|.\] The unrestricted counting regime allows the relations to vary with the input; a language-restricted regime fixes \(D\) and \(\Gamma\). Decision tractability does not by itself specify the complexity of computing this exact number.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counting CSP asks for the exact number of satisfying assignments; regimes may be unrestricted or based on a fixed finite language.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and \(D\) are finite.
Every constraint has a finite scope and a relation over \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\#\operatorname{CSP}(I)\) is the cardinality of the satisfying-assignment set.

notation.meaning: CSP instance with variables and constraints
complete assignment of domain values to variables

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical definition of the counting CSP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-counting definition is mathematically standard and the content kind fits, but no authoritative counting-CSP source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Constraint Modeling Systems
children.top_down_role: High-level models, compilation pipelines, interchange formats, solver interfaces, validation, and analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Model–Data Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MiniZinc parameters separate reusable model structure from instance values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A MiniZinc model declares parameter symbols and decision variables, constraints, and an objective without requiring parameter values in the model file. A data assignment \(\delta\) supplies ground, type-compatible values for the parameters. Combining model \(M\) with \(\delta\) produces the instantiated model \(M[\delta]\); parameters are fixed before solving, whereas declared decision variables remain unknown values selected by the solver subject to the instantiated constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reusable MiniZinc model declares parameters; a separate data assignment supplies their ground values before decision variables are solved.
assumptions_latex: Every parameter required by \(M\) receives exactly one type-compatible ground value.
The combined declarations and data assignments are well typed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) and \(\delta\) determine the instantiated solver input \(M[\delta]\).

notation.meaning: MiniZinc model containing declarations and constraints
ground data assignment to model parameters

source_refs.locator: Basic Modelling, model and data files

source_witnesses.locator: Basic Modelling, model and data files

children.title: MiniZinc Type System
children.top_down_role: Scalar, collection, parameter, and decision-variable type categories.

knowledge_statements.title: MiniZinc Type System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static type-inst classification of MiniZinc expressions and declarations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A MiniZinc type-inst records both a value type and an instantiation category. Scalar value types include Boolean, integer, floating-point, string, annotation, and enumerated types; compound types include sets and arrays. The instantiation category distinguishes compile-time parameters \(\mathtt{par}\) from solver decision values \(\mathtt{var}\), with optionality and structural restrictions where supported. An expression is admissible at a declaration or operator position only when its inferred type-inst is compatible with the required type-inst, possibly through a specified coercion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MiniZinc classifies expressions by value type and by whether they are fixed parameters or solver decision values.
assumptions_latex: The program is checked before flattening and solving.
Declarations and operators have specified required type-insts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every well-typed expression has a compatible value type and instantiation category at each use site.

children.title: MiniZinc Domain System
children.top_down_role: Finite value domains, ranges, sets, and enumerated domains.

knowledge_statements.title: MiniZinc Domain System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible-value sets attached to MiniZinc variables and parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a MiniZinc declaration \(T:x\), the declared domain \(\operatorname{dom}(x)\) is the set of values admitted by the type-inst expression \(T\). Once a parameter is assigned a ground value, that parameter is fixed to the assigned value. A finite-domain decision variable may be declared over an integer range, an explicit finite integer set, or an enumerated type; a set-valued decision variable may be bounded by a finite upper-bound set. Constraints can further restrict feasible values or permit propagation to tighten a solver's current domain, but they do not change the declaration syntax. Solving seeks values from the declared domains that satisfy every constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A MiniZinc declaration gives a symbol an admissible value set; parameter data fix values, finite decision domains bound solver choices, and constraints further restrict feasible assignments.
assumptions_latex: \(T:x\) is a valid MiniZinc declaration.
Every decision domain considered in the finite-domain setting is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every solution assignment \(s\) satisfies \(s(x)\in\operatorname{dom}(x)\) for each declared symbol \(x\).

notation.meaning: MiniZinc declaration of symbol x with type-inst expression T
set of values admitted by the declaration of x

source_refs.locator: Basic Modelling, Types and variable declarations

source_witnesses.locator: Basic Modelling, Types and variable declarations

children.title: Type–Domain Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility constraints between declared types and admissible domains.

assumptions_latex: The model is checked under the MiniZinc type-instantiation system.
Every identifier has a declared or inferred type-instantiation and domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An occurrence of an expression is well typed exactly when its type-instantiation is admissible in the required context, possibly after a permitted implicit coercion.

notation.meaning: permitted implicit coercion or compatibility relation

review_flags: Authoritative MiniZinc specification locator required for the exact compatibility and coercion rules.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static compatibility of MiniZinc types, instantiations, and finite domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e\) occur in a context \(C\) requiring type-instantiation \(\rho_C\), and let \(\tau(e)\) be the type-instantiation inferred for \(e\). The occurrence is type-domain compatible precisely when \(\tau(e)\preceq\rho_C\), where \(\preceq\) consists only of MiniZinc's declared compatibility and implicit-coercion rules. In addition, every value admitted by the domain of \(e\), after any coercion, must belong to the value class of \(\rho_C\). Otherwise static checking rejects the occurrence; compatibility does not itself add a constraint that repairs a type or domain mismatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression may appear in a context only when its inferred type-instantiation and domain fit the required one through an explicitly permitted MiniZinc compatibility rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Type–Domain Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the asserted compatibility relation, domain/value-class requirement, and static-error behavior are MiniZinc-specific and have no cited specification locator.

children.title: Coercion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of implicit conversion across MiniZinc type categories.

assumptions_latex: Source and target type-instantiations are well formed MiniZinc type-instantiations.
Only language-defined implicit coercions are available during type checking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Crossing a coercion boundary without an applicable declared coercion is a static error rather than a constraint to be solved.
review_flags: Authoritative MiniZinc specification locator required for the complete coercion table and overload-resolution boundaries.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static failure at MiniZinc implicit-coercion boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an expression of type-instantiation \(\tau_s\) is supplied where \(\tau_t\) is required. The boundary is crossed implicitly only if MiniZinc defines an applicable coercion \(c:\tau_s\to\tau_t\) and the coerced expression satisfies all target structural requirements, including element, set, array-index, optionality, and instantiation requirements that apply. If no such \(c\) exists, or if competing coercions leave overload resolution ambiguous, the model is ill typed. A solver cannot interpret the mismatch as a relation between otherwise incompatible values.
