knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution record denotes reported values induced by at least one constraint-satisfying assignment.

notation.meaning: Solution assignment, objective, outputs, and metadata.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf, but the tuple \(R=(a,z,o,m)\), required assignment coverage, objective treatment, metadata field, and extension-based feasibility semantics are not tied to an official result-reporting format. These fields may describe an abstract proposal rather than the actual interface.

children.title: Solve Status Signaling
children.top_down_role: Backend signals for satisfiability, optimality, exhaustion, or interruption.

knowledge_statements.title: Solve Status Signaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status values and logical claims communicated when solver execution terminates or is interrupted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solve-status signal is a pair \((q,c)\), where \(q\) is a status code and \(c\) is the evidence class supporting it. Its interpretation must distinguish at least: a feasible solution found without an optimality claim; optimality established; infeasibility established; unboundedness established when meaningful; termination with unknown conclusion; and execution error. A conclusive status may be emitted only when its required certificate or complete-search condition is satisfied. Resource-limit termination alone implies an unknown conclusion unless an independently justified conclusive status was already established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Status signaling distinguishes feasible, optimal, infeasible, unbounded, unknown, and error outcomes; limits alone do not justify a conclusive mathematical claim.
assumptions_latex: Status meanings are fixed by the reporting protocol.
The solver reports whether termination followed a limit, normal completion, or error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The signal \((q,c)\) determines the strongest justified solve claim and must not exceed the evidence class \(c\).

notation.meaning: Status code and supporting evidence class.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is acceptable for a status signal, but the pair \((q,c)\), mandatory status categories, unboundedness semantics, and evidence or certificate requirements are not sourced to a reporting protocol. In particular, protocols differ on optimization status, unknown termination, and whether an explicit certificate class is represented.

children.title: Solver Statistics Reporting
children.top_down_role: Runtime, search, propagation, and resource measurements.

assumptions_latex: The backend executes a fixed FlatZinc instance \(I\).
Each reported statistic has a declared key, value domain, and measurement convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every parsed report \(R\), the statistics map is \(\sigma_R:K_R\to V\), where each \(k\in K_R\) occurs at most once unless its declaration permits aggregation. If \(k\) denotes a cumulative counter, then successive reports satisfy \(\sigma_{R_{t+1}}(k)\geq \sigma_{R_t}(k)\). Statistics are observational metadata: deleting all statistic records leaves the reported solve status and every solution assignment unchanged. A consumer shall treat an absent key as unavailable, not as having numerical value \(0\), and shall interpret each present value only according to the convention declared for that key.

notation.meaning: map of reported statistic keys to values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract semantics of machine-readable FlatZinc solver statistics; concrete keys and serialization require specification evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every parsed report \(R\), the statistics map is \(\sigma_R:K_R\to V\), where each \(k\in K_R\) occurs at most once unless its declaration permits aggregation. If \(k\) denotes a cumulative counter, then successive reports satisfy \(\sigma_{R_{t+1}}(k)\geq \sigma_{R_t}(k)\). Statistics are observational metadata: deleting all statistic records leaves the reported solve status and every solution assignment unchanged. A consumer shall treat an absent key as unavailable, not as having numerical value \(0\), and shall interpret each present value only according to the convention declared for that key.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A statistics report maps declared keys to typed values, preserves cumulative-counter monotonicity, and cannot alter solutions or status. Missing statistics mean unavailable, not zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver Statistics Reporting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited evidence supports uniqueness, aggregation, monotonicity, missing-key semantics, or the claimed separation of statistics from status and solutions. These FlatZinc protocol rules require an official specification with a section-level locator. The representation kind fits the container.

children.title: Interface Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency among reported solutions, statuses, and statistics.

assumptions_latex: A solver output stream \(O\) is parsed under one fixed FlatZinc result-reporting protocol.
The stream may contain solution, status, and statistics records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Let \(P(O)=(S,T,\sigma)\), where \(S\) is the ordered solution sequence, \(T\) is the terminal solve status, and \(\sigma\) is statistics metadata. Interface consistency requires that every accepted stream have at most one terminal status, no solution record occur after that status, every solution bind exactly the declared output fields with compatible values, and \(T\) not contradict \(S\). In particular, a status asserting unsatisfiability entails \(S=()\), while a status asserting completion after finding solutions entails \(|S|\geq1\). Statistics records may supplement but may not change \(S\) or \(T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency predicate for a complete FlatZinc solver-result stream, independent of concrete delimiter syntax.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(O)=(S,T,\sigma)\), where \(S\) is the ordered solution sequence, \(T\) is the terminal solve status, and \(\sigma\) is statistics metadata. Interface consistency requires that every accepted stream have at most one terminal status, no solution record occur after that status, every solution bind exactly the declared output fields with compatible values, and \(T\) not contradict \(S\). In particular, a status asserting unsatisfiability entails \(S=()\), while a status asserting completion after finding solutions entails \(|S|\geq1\). Statistics records may supplement but may not change \(S\) or \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent result stream has compatible solution records and one terminal status, forbids solutions after termination, and keeps statistics semantically separate.
knowledge_statements.title: Interface Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stream-order, terminal-status, output-binding, and status/solution compatibility requirements are protocol-specific and uncited. An official FlatZinc reporting specification with a precise locator is needed. The condition kind fits the container.

assumptions_latex: An XCSP3 instance has finite-domain variables \(X\), constraints \(C\), and possibly objectives \(O\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A problem-framework declaration is a value \(F\) attached to an instance and interpreted as a contract on its admissible components and solution criterion. For a satisfaction framework, \(F=\mathrm{CSP}\), the objective collection is empty and a solution is any assignment \(a\in\prod_{x\in X}D_x\) satisfying every constraint in \(C\). For an optimization framework, \(F=\mathrm{COP}\), at least one objective is declared and a solution sought is a feasible assignment ordered by the declared minimization or maximization criterion. The declaration classifies the instance; it does not itself add a constraint or objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core satisfaction-versus-optimization declaration; additional XCSP3 framework values are outside this record.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A problem-framework declaration is a value \(F\) attached to an instance and interpreted as a contract on its admissible components and solution criterion. For a satisfaction framework, \(F=\mathrm{CSP}\), the objective collection is empty and a solution is any assignment \(a\in\prod_{x\in X}D_x\) satisfying every constraint in \(C\). For an optimization framework, \(F=\mathrm{COP}\), at least one objective is declared and a solution sought is a feasible assignment ordered by the declared minimization or maximization criterion. The declaration classifies the instance; it does not itself add a constraint or objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A framework declaration classifies an instance as satisfaction or optimization and determines whether feasible assignments alone or objective-ordered feasible assignments are sought.
knowledge_statements.title: Problem Framework Declarations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asserted CSP/COP values, objective cardinality rules, and interpretation of the declaration are XCSP3-specific and unsupported. A precisely located official XCSP3 source is required before determining whether the definition is complete and accurate.

children.title: Constraint Vocabulary
children.top_down_role: XCSP3 elements representing supported constraint families.

assumptions_latex: Each variable \(x\in X\) has a finite domain \(D_x\).
Every vocabulary symbol has a declared arity, argument sorts, and denotation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An XCSP3 constraint vocabulary is a set \(\mathcal V_C\) of typed constructors. Each constructor \(q\in\mathcal V_C\), applied to well-sorted arguments \(u\), denotes a relation \(\llbracket q(u)\rrbracket\subseteq\prod_{x\in\operatorname{scope}(q(u))}D_x\). An assignment \(a\) satisfies the constructed constraint exactly when its restriction belongs to that relation: \(a\models q(u)\) if and only if \(a|_{\operatorname{scope}(q(u))}\in\llbracket q(u)\rrbracket\). A serialized constraint is vocabulary-conforming only when its constructor is declared, its arguments meet the constructor's syntactic and sorting conditions, and all referenced identifiers are defined.

notation.meaning: relation denoted by a constructed constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Denotational definition of the core constraint vocabulary, not an enumeration of XCSP3 constraint constructors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An XCSP3 constraint vocabulary is a set \(\mathcal V_C\) of typed constructors. Each constructor \(q\in\mathcal V_C\), applied to well-sorted arguments \(u\), denotes a relation \(\llbracket q(u)\rrbracket\subseteq\prod_{x\in\operatorname{scope}(q(u))}D_x\). An assignment \(a\) satisfies the constructed constraint exactly when its restriction belongs to that relation: \(a\models q(u)\) if and only if \(a|_{\operatorname{scope}(q(u))}\in\llbracket q(u)\rrbracket\). A serialized constraint is vocabulary-conforming only when its constructor is declared, its arguments meet the constructor's syntactic and sorting conditions, and all referenced identifiers are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constraint vocabulary consists of typed constructors denoting relations on finite-domain variables; satisfaction means the assignment restricted to the constraint scope belongs to the denoted relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Vocabulary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract relational semantics is plausible, but no source establishes that it accurately characterizes XCSP3 constructor declarations, sorting rules, identifier requirements, or the exact constraint vocabulary. The definition kind fits.

children.title: Objective Vocabulary
children.top_down_role: XCSP3 elements representing optimization criteria.

assumptions_latex: The feasible assignments form \(A\neq\varnothing\).
Every objective expression is well-sorted and has a totally ordered codomain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An XCSP3 objective vocabulary is a set \(\mathcal V_O\) of declarations pairing an optimization direction with a well-sorted objective term. A declaration \((\min,e)\) denotes selection of \(a^*\in A\) satisfying \(\llbracket e\rrbracket(a^*)\leq\llbracket e\rrbracket(a)\) for every \(a\in A\); a declaration \((\max,e)\) reverses the inequality. If a declared aggregate objective applies an operator \(g\) to terms \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), its value is \(g(\llbracket e_1\rrbracket(a),\ldots,\llbracket e_m\rrbracket(a))\). Vocabulary conformance requires a declared direction, supported objective form, well-sorted arguments, and an unambiguous comparison convention.

notation.meaning: value of expression e under assignment a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic core of single or aggregate objectives; XCSP3 multiobjective combination modes require separate specification evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An XCSP3 objective vocabulary is a set \(\mathcal V_O\) of declarations pairing an optimization direction with a well-sorted objective term. A declaration \((\min,e)\) denotes selection of \(a^*\in A\) satisfying \(\llbracket e\rrbracket(a^*)\leq\llbracket e\rrbracket(a)\) for every \(a\in A\); a declaration \((\max,e)\) reverses the inequality. If a declared aggregate objective applies an operator \(g\) to terms \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), its value is \(g(\llbracket e_1\rrbracket(a),\ldots,\llbracket e_m\rrbracket(a))\). Vocabulary conformance requires a declared direction, supported objective form, well-sorted arguments, and an unambiguous comparison convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective declarations pair minimization or maximization with a typed expression or aggregate whose value orders feasible assignments.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Vocabulary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimization and maximization semantics are standard, but the claimed XCSP3 objective vocabulary, aggregate forms, ordering conventions, and restriction to nonempty feasible sets require official specification evidence. The definition kind fits the leaf.

children.title: Shared Expression Vocabulary
children.top_down_role: Expression constructs reused by constraints and objectives.

assumptions_latex: Variables and constants are assigned declared sorts.
Every operator has a declared signature and interpretation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The shared expression vocabulary is a typed term algebra \(\mathcal E\) generated from constants, variable references, and declared operators. If an operator \(f:s_1\times\cdots\times s_m\to s\) is declared and \(e_i\in\mathcal E_{s_i}\) for every \(i\), then \(f(e_1,\\ldots,e_m)\in\mathcal E_s\). Under an assignment \(a\), evaluation is compositional: \(\llbracket f(e_1,\ldots,e_m)\rrbracket_a=f^{\mathcal I}(\llbracket e_1\rrbracket_a,\ldots,\llbracket e_m\rrbracket_a)\). The same term has the same denotation when used in a constraint, objective, or annotation context that admits its sort.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed compositional semantics shared across XCSP3 constraints, objectives, and annotations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The shared expression vocabulary is a typed term algebra \(\mathcal E\) generated from constants, variable references, and declared operators. If an operator \(f:s_1\times\cdots\times s_m\to s\) is declared and \(e_i\in\mathcal E_{s_i}\) for every \(i\), then \(f(e_1,\\ldots,e_m)\in\mathcal E_s\). Under an assignment \(a\), evaluation is compositional: \(\llbracket f(e_1,\ldots,e_m)\rrbracket_a=f^{\mathcal I}(\llbracket e_1\rrbracket_a,\ldots,\llbracket e_m\rrbracket_a)\). The same term has the same denotation when used in a constraint, objective, or annotation context that admits its sort.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared expressions form a typed term algebra with compositional evaluation and retain the same meaning in every context admitting their sort.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared Expression Vocabulary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No evidence establishes that XCSP3 uses one typed term algebra with context-invariant denotation across constraints, objectives, and annotations. In addition, `\\ldots` in the constructor expression is malformed TeX and must be repaired to `\ldots` after the mathematical claim is sourced. The definition kind otherwise fits.

children.title: Vocabulary Extension Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compatibility limits for optional or implementation-specific constructs.

assumptions_latex: The standard vocabulary is \(\mathcal V\) with interpretation \(\mathcal I\).
An extension introduces symbols \(E\) and an extension identifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vocabulary extension is conservative on standard models only if \(E\cap\mathcal V=\varnothing\) and the extended interpretation \(\mathcal I'\) satisfies \(\mathcal I'|_{\mathcal V}=\mathcal I\). Every occurrence of a symbol in \(E\) must carry or inherit enough identification to select its syntax and semantics. An extension crosses the portability boundary when a conforming consumer that implements only \(\mathcal V\) cannot either reject the extended construct explicitly or recover an equivalent standard-vocabulary encoding. Redefining a standard symbol, silently changing its argument rules, or changing its denotation is not a conservative extension.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservative-extension and portability boundary for symbols outside the standard XCSP3 vocabulary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vocabulary extension is conservative on standard models only if \(E\cap\mathcal V=\varnothing\) and the extended interpretation \(\mathcal I'\) satisfies \(\mathcal I'|_{\mathcal V}=\mathcal I\). Every occurrence of a symbol in \(E\) must carry or inherit enough identification to select its syntax and semantics. An extension crosses the portability boundary when a conforming consumer that implements only \(\mathcal V\) cannot either reject the extended construct explicitly or recover an equivalent standard-vocabulary encoding. Redefining a standard symbol, silently changing its argument rules, or changing its denotation is not a conservative extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extension must use identifiable new symbols and preserve all standard meanings; silent redefinition or an extension that cannot be rejected or translated breaches portability.
knowledge_statements.title: Vocabulary Extension Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The disjoint-symbol, conservative-interpretation, explicit-rejection, and standard-encoding conditions appear to be proposed policy rather than established XCSP3 rules. Official extension and conformance documentation is required. The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container.

children.title: Constraint Groups
children.top_down_role: Parameterized collections of structurally similar constraints.

assumptions_latex: A constraint template \(T\) contains placeholders \(p_1,\ldots,p_r\).
Each argument tuple \(u_j\) is well-sorted for those placeholders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A constraint group represents the ordered family \(G=(T[u_1/p],\ldots,T[u_m/p])\), where simultaneous substitution of \(u_j\) for the placeholder tuple \(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)\) yields one ordinary constraint. Its denotation is conjunctive: \(\operatorname{Sol}(G)=\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{Sol}(T[u_j/p])\). Group expansion shall preserve the order and identity of generated constraints whenever these are referenced by annotations or external tooling. A group is well formed only if every substitution produces a vocabulary-conforming constraint and no unbound placeholder remains.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Template-and-arguments representation of repeated XCSP3 constraints with conjunctive model semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint group represents the ordered family \(G=(T[u_1/p],\ldots,T[u_m/p])\), where simultaneous substitution of \(u_j\) for the placeholder tuple \(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)\) yields one ordinary constraint. Its denotation is conjunctive: \(\operatorname{Sol}(G)=\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{Sol}(T[u_j/p])\). Group expansion shall preserve the order and identity of generated constraints whenever these are referenced by annotations or external tooling. A group is well formed only if every substitution produces a vocabulary-conforming constraint and no unbound placeholder remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint group compactly represents an ordered family obtained by substituting argument tuples into one template; its solutions satisfy every expanded constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Groups

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Template substitution and conjunctive semantics are plausible, but ordering, generated-constraint identity, placeholder binding, and annotation-reference behavior are XCSP3-specific and uncited. The representation kind fits.

children.title: Model Blocks
children.top_down_role: Explicit containers for related XCSP3 model content.

assumptions_latex: An XCSP3 instance contains serializable model items with stable document order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A model block is a structural container \(B=(	au,id,M_1,\ldots,M_k)\), where \(\tau\) is its declared block kind, \(id\) is optional identifying metadata, and each \(M_i\) is an admissible model item or nested container. The block's flattened content is defined recursively by \(\operatorname{flat}(B)=\operatorname{flat}(M_1)\mathbin{\|}\cdots\mathbin{\|}\operatorname{flat}(M_k)\), with an atomic item flattening to its singleton sequence. Unless the block kind declares additional semantics, replacing \(B\) by \(\operatorname{flat}(B)\) preserves the feasible assignments and objectives; the block records organization, scope for metadata, and item order.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic structural block semantics; block-specific restrictions and metadata inheritance require XCSP3 specification evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A model block is a structural container \(B=(\tau,id,M_1,\ldots,M_k)\), where \(\tau\) is its declared block kind, \(id\) is optional identifying metadata, and each \(M_i\) is an admissible model item or nested container. The block's flattened content is defined recursively by \(\operatorname{flat}(B)=\operatorname{flat}(M_1)\mathbin{\|}\cdots\mathbin{\|}\operatorname{flat}(M_k)\), with an atomic item flattening to its singleton sequence. Unless the block kind declares additional semantics, replacing \(B\) by \(\operatorname{flat}(B)\) preserves the feasible assignments and objectives; the block records organization, scope for metadata, and item order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model block is an ordered structural container. Unless its kind adds semantics, recursively flattening it preserves feasibility and objectives while discarding organization.
knowledge_statements.title: Model Blocks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes the proposed generic block tuple, admissible nesting, recursive flattening, or the claim that flattening preserves feasibility and objectives. Official XCSP3 block-kind and nesting rules are necessary. The definition kind fits.

children.title: Structure Preservation
children.top_down_role: Retention of source grouping through interchange and processing.

assumptions_latex: Models \(M\) and \(M'\) use the same declared variables and objective convention.
A transformation \(F\) changes only structural containers or group encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformation \(F:M\mapsto M'\) preserves XCSP3 structure when there is a bijection \(\phi\) between the addressable items of \(M\) and \(M'\) that preserves item kind, stable identifier, document order among siblings, and the ancestor relation. Semantic preservation additionally requires \(\operatorname{Sol}(M)=\operatorname{Sol}(M')\) and, for every feasible assignment \(a\), equality of declared objective values in the two models. Mere equality of solution sets is therefore insufficient for structure preservation when grouping, nesting, order, identifiers, or annotation targets are lost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong preservation includes hierarchy and identity in addition to solution and objective equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The transformation \(F:M\mapsto M'\) preserves XCSP3 structure when there is a bijection \(\phi\) between the addressable items of \(M\) and \(M'\) that preserves item kind, stable identifier, document order among siblings, and the ancestor relation. Semantic preservation additionally requires \(\operatorname{Sol}(M)=\operatorname{Sol}(M')\) and, for every feasible assignment \(a\), equality of declared objective values in the two models. Mere equality of solution sets is therefore insufficient for structure preservation when grouping, nesting, order, identifiers, or annotation targets are lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structure preservation requires a bijection retaining item kinds, identifiers, order, and ancestry, together with unchanged solutions and objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Structure Preservation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong bijective criterion involving identifiers, sibling order, ancestry, solutions, and objective values is a substantive proposed definition with no cited XCSP3 basis. A precise source is required to distinguish official preservation requirements from a locally chosen criterion. The property kind is acceptable for this leaf.

children.title: Nesting Identity
children.top_down_role: Identity and scope of elements within nested structural containers.

assumptions_latex: Every addressable structural item has an identifier unique within its prescribed scope.
The model hierarchy is a finite rooted tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The nesting identity of an item \(v\) is its rooted address \(\iota(v)=(id(v_0),id(v_1),\ldots,id(v))\), where \(v_0,
\ldots,v\) is the unique ancestor chain from the root to \(v\). For any items \(u,v\), \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\) if and only if \(\iota(u)\) is a prefix of \(\iota(v)\). Hence two locally named items are globally identical exactly when their full rooted addresses agree. Moving an item to a different parent changes its nesting identity even when its local identifier and mathematical denotation are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract path-based identity for nested structural items; exact XCSP3 identifier scoping remains source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The nesting identity of an item \(v\) is its rooted address \(\iota(v)=(id(v_0),id(v_1),\ldots,id(v))\), where \(v_0,
\ldots,v\) is the unique ancestor chain from the root to \(v\). For any items \(u,v\), \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\) if and only if \(\iota(u)\) is a prefix of \(\iota(v)\). Hence two locally named items are globally identical exactly when their full rooted addresses agree. Moving an item to a different parent changes its nesting identity even when its local identifier and mathematical denotation are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An item's nesting identity is its full root-to-item identifier path; prefix comparison recovers ancestry, and moving the item changes that identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Nesting Identity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rooted-address construction assumes locally scoped identifiers and path-based global identity, neither of which is supported by a cited XCSP3 source. Moreover, the statement introduces a definition of nesting identity, so `definition` is a better mathematical role than `property`. Source evidence is needed before a replacement can be settled.

children.title: Search Annotations
children.top_down_role: XCSP3 guidance for branching, ordering, and exploration.

assumptions_latex: The instance has variables \(X\) and feasible assignments \(A\).
An annotation names only declared variables or well-formed search objects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A search annotation is advisory metadata \(H\) that specifies a search object, such as an ordered variable sequence, and optionally a selection or exploration policy. If \(H\) names variables \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), then each \(x_i\in X\), with repetitions permitted only when explicitly allowed by the annotation kind. The annotation may alter the order in which a solver explores candidate assignments, but it does not alter model semantics: \(A_H=A\), where \(A_H\) is the feasible set when \(H\) is honored. A solver may ignore unsupported advisory annotations unless the applicable conformance profile makes them mandatory.

notation.meaning: feasible sets without and with the annotation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Advisory search-control semantics; exact annotation kinds and mandatory support depend on the XCSP3 specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A search annotation is advisory metadata \(H\) that specifies a search object, such as an ordered variable sequence, and optionally a selection or exploration policy. If \(H\) names variables \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), then each \(x_i\in X\), with repetitions permitted only when explicitly allowed by the annotation kind. The annotation may alter the order in which a solver explores candidate assignments, but it does not alter model semantics: \(A_H=A\), where \(A_H\) is the feasible set when \(H\) is honored. A solver may ignore unsupported advisory annotations unless the applicable conformance profile makes them mandatory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search annotation advises variable ordering or exploration policy without changing feasible assignments; unsupported advisory annotations may be ignored unless a profile requires them.
knowledge_statements.title: Search Annotations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The advisory status, repetition rule, semantic invariance, and permission to ignore unsupported annotations are XCSP3-specific claims without evidence. An official annotation catalogue and conformance section with precise locators are required. The definition kind fits.

children.title: Filtering Annotations
children.top_down_role: XCSP3 guidance for propagation or consistency strength.

assumptions_latex: The XCSP3 instance has finite-domain variables and a finite set of constraints.
The annotation consumer recognizes a declared set of filtering levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A filtering annotation is well formed exactly when every referenced constraint and requested filtering level is recognized by the consumer.

notation.meaning: finite set of constraints in the instance
filtering-level annotation assigned to a constraint
filtering levels supported by the consumer

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses XCSP3 filtering annotations; exact standardized vocabulary and semantics require an XCSP3 specification source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-formedness and advisory interpretation of per-constraint filtering requests in an XCSP3 model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be the finite constraint set of an XCSP3 instance, let \(L\) be the declared vocabulary of filtering levels, and let \(\lambda:C\rightharpoonup L\) be a partial annotation. For a consumer supporting \(L_{\mathrm{sup}}\subseteq L\), the annotation is well formed for that consumer precisely when \(\operatorname{dom}(\lambda)\subseteq C\) and \(\lambda(c)\in L_{\mathrm{sup}}\) for every \(c\in\operatorname{dom}(\lambda)\). Its operational meaning is a request that propagation for \(c\) attain level \(\lambda(c)\); it does not alter the relation defined by \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A filtering annotation validly assigns supported propagation levels to referenced constraints and requests those levels without changing the constraints' solution relations.
knowledge_statements.title: Filtering Annotations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but no XCSP3 specification citation supports the filtering vocabulary, consumer-relative well-formedness rule, or claimed operational semantics.

children.title: Annotation Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined effects of multiple annotation categories.

assumptions_latex: Search and filtering annotations are individually well formed.
Filtering operations are sound: they remove no value occurring in a solution extending the current partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Search annotations may change exploration order and filtering annotations may change pruning, but their interaction preserves the model's solution set.

notation.meaning: set of solutions of the unannotated constraint model
sound filtering policy induced by annotations

review_flags: No supplied source supports the XCSP3 annotation-interaction contract; standardized precedence and unsupported-feature behavior remain unverified.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic interaction between advisory search choices and sound propagation choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite-domain constraint model, \(S\) a search policy induced by search annotations, and \(F\) a filtering policy induced by filtering annotations. Assume every reduction made by \(F\) is sound and the search under \(S\) is complete over every branch not proved inconsistent by \(F\). Then the combined execution enumerates exactly \(\operatorname{Sol}(M)\). Thus \(S\) may determine branching order and \(F\) may determine domain reductions, but neither annotation class changes the satisfaction relation of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When filtering is sound and annotated search remains complete, combining both annotation classes changes execution behavior but not the model's solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Annotation Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically plausible under its explicit soundness and completeness assumptions, but no source establishes that this is the XCSP3 annotation-interaction contract.

children.title: Annotation Portability
children.top_down_role: Backend support and degradation across annotation vocabularies.

assumptions_latex: Two consumers implement the same XCSP3 constraint semantics.
Each consumer either honors an annotation or applies a documented fallback that preserves satisfaction semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The annotation set is solution-portable when all conforming consumers preserve \(\operatorname{Sol}(M)\), even if their search traces differ.

notation.meaning: annotation set attached to the model

review_flags: No supplied source defines XCSP3 annotation portability or mandatory fallback behavior; specification evidence is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic portability across consumers, distinct from reproducibility of search traces or performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-domain model \(M\) with annotation set \(A\), call \(A\) solution-portable over a class \(\mathcal E\) of conforming consumers when, for every \(E\in\mathcal E\), each annotation is either implemented as specified or replaced by a documented semantics-preserving fallback, and \(\operatorname{Sol}_E(M,A)=\operatorname{Sol}(M)\). Portability permits different branching orders, propagation strengths, runtimes, and output orders; it does not require identical execution traces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Annotations are solution-portable when every conforming consumer honors them or uses a safe fallback while preserving exactly the unannotated model's solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Annotation Portability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the portability leaf, but the definition of conforming consumers and the asserted semantics-preserving fallback behavior require specification evidence.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Automatic solution checking, model validation, benchmarking, CP-Profiler, FindMUS, and Mzn-Analyse

assumptions_latex: Every variable has a finite declared domain.
Constraint and objective evaluators implement the instance's declared arithmetic and satisfaction semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The checker accepts exactly assignments satisfying all domain, constraint, and claimed objective conditions.
review_flags: The algorithm is standard but the supplied source hints do not address independent checking of finite-domain constraint solutions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checker for feasibility and claimed objective value; optimality requires a separate certificate or bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite-domain instance \(M=(X,D,C,f)\), a candidate total assignment \(a\), and optionally a claimed objective value \(z\). First reject if some \(a(x)\notin D(x)\). Evaluate every \(c\in C\) independently of the solver and reject if \(c(a)\) is false. If \(f\) and \(z\) are supplied, compute \(f(a)\) under the declared arithmetic semantics and reject unless \(f(a)=z\). Otherwise accept \(a\) as feasible with verified value \(z\); do not infer optimality without an independently checkable bound or proof object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent checker reevaluates domains, constraints, and any claimed objective value; feasibility alone does not certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Solution Checking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly separates feasibility and objective-value checking from optimality certification, but no inspectable source supports the stated independent-checking protocol.

assumptions_latex: The constraint family is finite.
Satisfiability is interpreted over the declared finite variable domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subset \(U\) is minimally unsatisfiable exactly when \(U\) is unsatisfiable and every one-constraint deletion is satisfiable.

notation.meaning: solutions satisfying every constraint in a family

review_flags: Definition is standard, but none of the supplied source locators directly supports minimal unsatisfiable subsets in constraint models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset-minimal unsatisfiable cores, not minimum-cardinality unsatisfiable subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite family of constraints over finite declared domains, and write \(\operatorname{Sol}(U)\) for the assignments satisfying every member of \(U\subseteq C\). A set \(U\subseteq C\) is a minimal unsatisfiable subset if \(\operatorname{Sol}(U)=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{Sol}(U\setminus\{c\})\neq\varnothing\) for every \(c\in U\). Minimality is with respect to set inclusion; consequently, a minimal unsatisfiable subset need not have minimum cardinality among all unsatisfiable subsets of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal unsatisfiable subset is inconsistent, while deleting any one of its constraints makes the remaining set satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Unsatisfiable Subsets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard subset-minimal unsatisfiability definition and the content kind is correct, but the record supplies no authoritative source with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: All tested solvers receive semantically equivalent encodings of the same finite-domain instance.
Reported assignments are checked independently before solution sets are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any unexplained mismatch among checked statuses, feasible assignments, or objective values is a differential-validation failure.
review_flags: The validation procedure is standard software-testing practice, but the supplied sources do not establish a CP-specific differential-validation protocol.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-solver checking after normalization, with timeouts and unsupported features treated as inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite-domain model \(M\) and solvers \(E_1,\ldots,E_k\). Run each solver under declared limits, normalize its status, assignments, and objective values, and independently check every reported assignment against \(M\). Compare the resulting \(R_i(M)\). Flag a failure if two conclusive results disagree on satisfiability, a checked assignment violates \(M\), or proven optimum values differ. Treat timeout, unknown, and unsupported-feature outcomes as inconclusive rather than contradictory. Output the normalized results, checker evidence, and the smallest reproducible instance available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differential validation normalizes several solvers' results, independently checks witnesses, and flags unexplained disagreements while treating resource-limited outcomes as inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.title: Differential Solver Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits differential solver validation and appropriately treats nonconclusive outcomes separately, but its CP-specific comparison and failure criteria lack a supporting source.

children.title: Search Profiling
children.top_down_role: Branching, failure, depth, restart, and exploration measurements.

assumptions_latex: The solver emits timestamped events with stable search-node identifiers.
Counters are updated consistently throughout the profiled run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting per-node and aggregate counters form a search profile of the observed execution.

notation.meaning: counter vector attached to search node \(v\)

review_flags: No supplied source defines a search-profiling event schema or required counters for constraint solvers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-based representation of branching, failure, restart, and node-processing measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a profiled run by an event stream \((e_t)_{t=1}^m\) whose events identify a node \(v\in V\), time, event type, and optional payload. The induced search tree is \(T=(V,E)\), and each node receives a counter vector \(p(v)=(n_{\mathrm{branch}},n_{\mathrm{fail}},n_{\mathrm{solution}},\tau)\), where \(\tau\) is measured processing time. Aggregate values are obtained by componentwise summation over any subtree or depth class. Restarts begin new rooted components while retaining a common run identifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search profiling represents a run as identified events and derives per-node or aggregate counts for branching, failure, solutions, time, and restarts.
knowledge_statements.title: Search Profiling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits search profiling, but the event schema, counter vector, aggregation rules, and restart convention are proposed without an inspectable source.

children.title: Propagation Profiling
children.top_down_role: Propagator activity, pruning, wakeups, and scheduling measurements.

assumptions_latex: Every propagation event identifies its constraint or propagator and measured invocation interval.
Domain-removal counts use one fixed counting convention throughout the run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregating invocation, time, and pruning data by propagator yields a propagation profile of the observed run.

notation.meaning: total measured time and removed values for propagator \(p\)

review_flags: No supplied source defines propagation-profile measurements or a standard value-removal counting convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-propagator execution and pruning measurements under an explicitly declared counting convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each instrumented propagator \(p\in P\), record invocations \(j=1,\ldots,N_p\), elapsed times \(t_{pj}\geq0\), and pruning counts \(r_{pj}\geq0\). Define \(T_p=\sum_{j=1}^{N_p}t_{pj}\) and \(R_p=\sum_{j=1}^{N_p}r_{pj}\). The propagation profile is the family \(\{(N_p,T_p,R_p):p\in P\}\), optionally partitioned by search node or outcome such as fixpoint, failure, or suspension. The profile must state whether \(r_{pj}\) counts removed values, bound changes, or domain updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation profiling aggregates each propagator's calls, elapsed time, and pruning under a fixed convention, optionally partitioned by node or outcome.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Profiling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is internally coherent, but no source supports these particular propagation measurements, outcome classes, or pruning-count conventions.

children.title: Correlated Profile Views
children.top_down_role: Joint interpretation of search events and propagation activity.

assumptions_latex: Search and propagation events share a run identifier, a stable search-node identifier, and a monotone event order.
Every propagation event is assigned to exactly one active search node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Joining events on run and node identifiers produces consistent views relating search outcomes to propagation costs.

notation.meaning: join keys consisting of run and search-node identifiers

review_flags: No supplied source establishes a canonical correlation schema for search and propagation profiles.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relational correlation of search structure with propagator activity and cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) contain search events and \(P\) contain propagation events, with common key \(K=(\text{run},\text{node})\). The correlated profile is the keyed join \(S\bowtie_K P\), followed by aggregation over a declared grouping such as node, depth, branch, restart, constraint, or propagator. Correct correlation requires each propagation event to reference exactly one active node and to lie between that node's activation and closure events. The resulting views may associate failures, solutions, and subtree sizes with propagation invocation, pruning, and time totals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Correlated views join search and propagation events by stable run and node identifiers, then aggregate costs and outcomes over declared groupings.
knowledge_statements.title: Correlated Profile Views

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes the correlation schema, and a raw many-to-many join on run and node can multiply event rows and corrupt aggregates unless event-level keys or preaggregation rules are specified.

children.title: Instrumentation Overhead
children.top_down_role: Runtime or memory distortion introduced by profiling.

assumptions_latex: Instrumented and uninstrumented executions use the same model, solver configuration, hardware class, and workload protocol.
Elapsed time is measured by the same clock and aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Instrumentation overhead is quantified by absolute increase \(T_1-T_0\) and relative factor \(T_1/T_0-1\).
review_flags: The measurement definition is standard, but the supplied source locators do not address profiling overhead or experimental controls.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime overhead under paired, controlled measurements; memory and trace-volume overhead require separate metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under matched experimental conditions, let \(T_0>0\) be aggregate elapsed time for uninstrumented runs and \(T_1\) the corresponding aggregate for instrumented runs, using the same statistic over repetitions. Define absolute overhead \(\Delta T=T_1-T_0\) and relative overhead \(\rho=T_1/T_0-1\). A claimed overhead bound \(\rho\leq\varepsilon\) is supported only for the stated workload and protocol. Changes in peak memory, event count, or trace volume are not represented by \(\rho\) and must be reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime instrumentation overhead compares matched profiled and unprofiled runs through absolute and relative time increases, with other resource costs reported separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Instrumentation Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The runtime formulas are standard and precise, but no experimental-method citation is supplied. The statement primarily defines measurement metrics, so the selected condition kind also requires reconsideration against definition or representation.

children.title: Portfolio-Encoding Backend Interface

children.title: Solver Portfolio Selection for CP Models

assumptions_latex: The model and solver profile use stable identifiers for global-constraint families and variants.
Support levels and admissible decompositions are explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile determines whether each model constraint is native, decomposable, unsupported, or supported only under stated restrictions.

notation.meaning: solver capability map for global constraints

review_flags: No supplied source documents a standard capability-profile schema for global constraints or the semantics of support categories.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver capabilities for global-constraint families, variants, restrictions, and semantics-preserving decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a solver \(E\), a global-constraint support profile is a partial map \(\sigma\) from a constraint family and parameter signature to \(\{\mathrm{native},\mathrm{decomp},\mathrm{none}\}\), augmented by domain, arity, and parameter restrictions. For a model \(M\), coverage holds when every \(g\in G(M)\) matches an entry that is native or has a declared semantics-preserving decomposition. An absent or nonmatching entry is unsupported. A native entry states acceptance and semantic support, not any particular propagation strength or performance guarantee unless separately recorded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global-constraint profile maps constraint variants to native, decomposed, or unsupported status under explicit restrictions and thereby determines model coverage.
knowledge_statements.title: Global-Constraint Support Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf, but the support categories, matching rules, restriction semantics, and decomposition requirements are not tied to a documented capability-profile standard.

children.title: Domain Support Profiles
children.top_down_role: Backend coverage of finite ranges, enumerations, sets, and related domains.

assumptions_latex: Every model variable has a declared finite domain representation.
The solver profile states admissible representations and any numeric or cardinality limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A model is domain-supported exactly when every variable's domain satisfies at least one declared profile entry and all associated limits.

notation.meaning: solver's set of supported domain-profile entries

review_flags: No supplied source defines a standardized domain-support profile or its matching relation for finite-domain solvers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of concrete finite-domain representations and limits, separate from variable-type compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the variables of a model and \(D(x)\) the finite declared domain of \(x\). A domain-support profile \(\mathcal P_E\) for solver \(E\) consists of predicates on domain representations, such as interval, explicit enumeration, or union of intervals, together with numeric and cardinality limits. The model is domain-supported by \(E\) precisely when, for every \(x\in X\), some \(p\in\mathcal P_E\) satisfies \(p(D(x))=\mathrm{true}\). Support of the domain representation alone does not imply support of every constraint using \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver supports a model's domains when every declared finite domain matches a supported representation and all associated numeric and size limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Support Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is internally consistent and distinguishes domain support from constraint support, but its profile schema and matching relation have no supporting source with a specific locator.

children.title: Type Support Profiles
children.top_down_role: Backend coverage of scalar, collection, and decision-variable types.

assumptions_latex: A portfolio contains a finite set of backends \(B\) and the model language has a finite set of declared types \(T\).
Each backend exposes a declared type-support relation, including any restrictions on variable and parameter use.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every backend \(b\in B\), its type support profile is the set \[P_T(b)=\{(t,u)\in T\times U: b\text{ accepts type }t\text{ in usage mode }u\},\] where \(U\) distinguishes at least parameter, decision-variable, array-index, and set-element usage. A model with required type-usage set \(R_T\subseteq T\times U\) is type-compatible with \(b\) exactly when \(R_T\subseteq P_T(b)\). Conditional or bounded support must be represented by refining the corresponding usage mode or attaching its explicit admissibility predicate.

notation.meaning: Finite backend portfolio and declared type set.
Type requirements of a model and support profile of a backend.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines type support as a backend capability relation indexed by usage mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every backend \(b\in B\), its type support profile is the set \[P_T(b)=\{(t,u)\in T\times U: b\text{ accepts type }t\text{ in usage mode }u\},\] where \(U\) distinguishes at least parameter, decision-variable, array-index, and set-element usage. A model with required type-usage set \(R_T\subseteq T\times U\) is type-compatible with \(b\) exactly when \(R_T\subseteq P_T(b)\). Conditional or bounded support must be represented by refining the corresponding usage mode or attaching its explicit admissibility predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A backend supports a model's types when it accepts every required type in each required usage mode, subject to all declared restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Type Support Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Type Support Profiles leaf, and the variables are introduced consistently. However, no inspectable source is cited for the proposed usage-mode taxonomy or the requirement that conditional support be encoded by refined modes or admissibility predicates.

children.title: Cross-Profile Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between supported types and their admissible domains.

assumptions_latex: A model has domain requirements \(R_D\) and type-usage requirements \(R_T\).
Backend \(b\) has domain profile \(P_D(b)\) and type profile \(P_T(b)\), with shared admissibility predicates retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Backend \(b\) is cross-profile compatible with the model when \[R_D\subseteq P_D(b),\qquad R_T\subseteq P_T(b),\] and every pair of jointly used domain and type features satisfies the backend's coupling predicate \(K_b\). Thus marginal coverage of both requirement sets is necessary but not sufficient: compatibility fails if some required pair \((d,t)\in R_D\times R_T\) violates \(K_b(d,t)\), for example when a supported type is unavailable over a supported domain representation.

notation.meaning: Backend domain and type support profiles.
Predicate for jointly admissible domain-type features.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility includes interactions between domain and type capabilities, not only separate set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Backend \(b\) is cross-profile compatible with the model when \[R_D\subseteq P_D(b),\qquad R_T\subseteq P_T(b),\] and every pair of jointly used domain and type features satisfies the backend's coupling predicate \(K_b\). Thus marginal coverage of both requirement sets is necessary but not sufficient: compatibility fails if some required pair \((d,t)\in R_D\times R_T\) violates \(K_b(d,t)\), for example when a supported type is unavailable over a supported domain representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate domain and type coverage is insufficient when a backend restricts which supported domains and types may be combined.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Profile Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A compatibility condition is the correct role for this leaf, but the coupling predicate is not formally sourced or fully specified. In particular, the text alternates between jointly used feature pairs and all pairs in the Cartesian product, which can impose different conditions depending on the model representation.

children.title: Profile Coverage Gaps
children.top_down_role: Model features falling outside declared domain or type support.

assumptions_latex: The model requires a finite capability set \(R\).
Each backend \(b\) declares a capability profile \(P(b)\), including restrictions represented as capabilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For backend \(b\), the profile coverage gap is \[G(b)=R\setminus P(b).\] The backend directly covers the model exactly when \(G(b)=\varnothing\). For a portfolio \(B\), the unavoidable portfolio gap is \[G(B)=R\setminus\bigcup_{b\in B}P(b).\] A nonempty \(G(B)\) identifies requirements unsupported by every backend. The equality \(G(B)=\varnothing\) establishes aggregate capability coverage only; it does not establish that one backend covers all requirements simultaneously or that cross-profile combinations are admissible.

notation.meaning: Coverage gaps for one backend and the portfolio.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-difference measure of missing declared capabilities at backend and portfolio levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For backend \(b\), the profile coverage gap is \[G(b)=R\setminus P(b).\] The backend directly covers the model exactly when \(G(b)=\varnothing\). For a portfolio \(B\), the unavoidable portfolio gap is \[G(B)=R\setminus\bigcup_{b\in B}P(b).\] A nonempty \(G(B)\) identifies requirements unsupported by every backend. The equality \(G(B)=\varnothing\) establishes aggregate capability coverage only; it does not establish that one backend covers all requirements simultaneously or that cross-profile combinations are admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coverage gap is a required capability absent from a backend, or absent from every backend when measured across the portfolio.
knowledge_statements.title: Profile Coverage Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-difference definition and definition content kind fit Profile Coverage Gaps. No source supports the chosen capability-set abstraction or the interpretation of the union-based portfolio gap, so the record cannot yet be accepted as evidence-backed candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Annotation Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Backend acceptance and interpretation of model annotations.

assumptions_latex: A model carries a finite set of annotations \(A_M\).
Backend \(b\) declares recognized annotations \(A_b\) and an interpretation map \(I_b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is annotation-compatible with backend \(b\) when every annotation \(a\in A_M\) is either recognized by \(b\) or is explicitly erasable without changing the model's feasible solutions, objective values, or required output semantics. Formally, if \(E\subseteq A_M\) is the erasable subset, compatibility requires \[A_M\setminus E\subseteq A_b\] and each interpretation \(I_b(a)\) to satisfy the annotation's declared semantic contract. Mere syntactic acceptance is insufficient when \(I_b(a)\) changes a correctness-relevant meaning.

notation.meaning: Model annotations and annotations recognized by the backend.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers solving annotations whose omission or reinterpretation may affect correctness-relevant behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The model is annotation-compatible with backend \(b\) when every annotation \(a\in A_M\) is either recognized by \(b\) or is explicitly erasable without changing the model's feasible solutions, objective values, or required output semantics. Formally, if \(E\subseteq A_M\) is the erasable subset, compatibility requires \[A_M\setminus E\subseteq A_b\] and each interpretation \(I_b(a)\) to satisfy the annotation's declared semantic contract. Mere syntactic acceptance is insufficient when \(I_b(a)\) changes a correctness-relevant meaning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Annotation compatibility requires supported interpretations for all correctness-relevant annotations; only annotations proven semantically erasable may be ignored.
knowledge_statements.title: Annotation Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, and the record correctly distinguishes syntactic recognition from semantic compatibility. The notions of an annotation contract and semantic erasability are interface-language dependent, however, and no authoritative annotation-semantics source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Output Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Backend support for requested solution and presentation formats.

assumptions_latex: The model requests output fields \(O_M\) with declared value domains and formatting contracts.
Backend \(b\) can return fields \(O_b\) through a decoder \(D_b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Backend \(b\) is output-compatible with the model when every required output field is reconstructible from its result: \[O_M\subseteq \operatorname{dom}(D_b).\] For every backend result \(r\) and every \(o\in O_M\), the value \(D_b(r)(o)\) must belong to the declared domain of \(o\), preserve the represented solution or certificate semantics, and satisfy the requested serialization contract. Output compatibility therefore includes status values, objective values, variable assignments, and any required proof or diagnostic fields.

notation.meaning: Required output fields and backend-returnable fields.
Decoder from backend results to model-level output fields.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic and serialization compatibility of solver results with model-level output requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Backend \(b\) is output-compatible with the model when every required output field is reconstructible from its result: \[O_M\subseteq \operatorname{dom}(D_b).\] For every backend result \(r\) and every \(o\in O_M\), the value \(D_b(r)(o)\) must belong to the declared domain of \(o\), preserve the represented solution or certificate semantics, and satisfy the requested serialization contract. Output compatibility therefore includes status values, objective values, variable assignments, and any required proof or diagnostic fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Output compatibility means every required result field can be decoded with the correct value, semantics, status, and serialization.
knowledge_statements.title: Output Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is appropriate for Output Compatibility, but the decoder is described as mapping backend results to fields while the formula treats required fields as elements of its domain. A source and a precise decoder signature are needed to determine the correct formal condition and the supported status, certificate, and serialization obligations.

children.title: End-to-End Interface Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility spanning annotated model input through rendered output.

assumptions_latex: An encoder \(E_b\) translates accepted models to backend \(b\), and a decoder \(D_b\) translates backend results back.
The model satisfies the backend's domain, type, constraint, annotation, and output interface conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface is end-to-end compatible for model \(M\) and backend \(b\) when \(E_b(M)\) is defined and preserves feasibility and objective order, while \(D_b\) is defined on every permitted backend result. If \(x\) is a model assignment and \(y\) its encoded assignment, then \[x\text{ solves }M\quad\Longleftrightarrow\\quad y\text{ solves }E_b(M),\] with corresponding objective values, and decoding any returned \(y\) recovers the required model-level assignment, status, and outputs. All annotation preconditions must also hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint semantic condition for encoding, solving, and decoding one model through one backend.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The interface is end-to-end compatible for model \(M\) and backend \(b\) when \(E_b(M)\) is defined and preserves feasibility and objective order, while \(D_b\) is defined on every permitted backend result. If \(x\) is a model assignment and \(y\) its encoded assignment, then \[x\text{ solves }M\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y\text{ solves }E_b(M),\] with corresponding objective values, and decoding any returned \(y\) recovers the required model-level assignment, status, and outputs. All annotation preconditions must also hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: End-to-end compatibility requires the encoder, backend semantics, annotations, and decoder jointly to preserve solutions, objectives, statuses, and requested outputs.
knowledge_statements.title: End-to-End Interface Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and overall semantic-preservation condition fit the leaf. The assignment correspondence between x and y is not formally defined, and requiring the decoder on every permitted backend result is a substantial interface claim. No source establishes these preservation and totality obligations.

children.title: Compatibility Degradation
children.top_down_role: Silent loss or weakening of annotations or output features.

assumptions_latex: A fully compatible interface satisfies a contract set \(C\).
A degraded translation satisfies only \(C'\subsetneq C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility degradation occurs when a translation remains executable after replacing the required contract \(C\) by a strict subset \(C'\subsetneq C\). It is semantics-preserving only if every omitted clause is observationally irrelevant for the given model and requested outputs. Otherwise there exist a permitted model \(M\) and result observation \(q\) such that \[q(D_b(\operatorname{solve}(E_b(M))))\ne q(\operatorname{solve}(M)).\] Silent deletion of unsupported constraints, correctness-relevant annotations, statuses, or output fields is therefore incompatibility, not a valid degraded mode.

notation.meaning: Full and degraded interface contract sets.
Model, backend encoder, and backend decoder.
An observable query on a solve result.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between declared, observationally harmless degradation and silent semantic incompatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compatibility degradation occurs when a translation remains executable after replacing the required contract \(C\) by a strict subset \(C'\subsetneq C\). It is semantics-preserving only if every omitted clause is observationally irrelevant for the given model and requested outputs. Otherwise there exist a permitted model \(M\) and result observation \(q\) such that \[q(D_b(\operatorname{solve}(E_b(M))))\ne q(\operatorname{solve}(M)).\] Silent deletion of unsupported constraints, correctness-relevant annotations, statuses, or output fields is therefore incompatibility, not a valid degraded mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degradation is valid only when omitted interface guarantees cannot affect requested observations; silent loss of relevant semantics constitutes incompatibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Compatibility Degradation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct role for Compatibility Degradation. The proposed observational-equivalence formula depends on unspecified solve-result semantics, nondeterminism, optimization status, and the domain of q; an authoritative source is required before choosing a reliable formal version.

assumptions_latex: Variables have finite domains and constraints are relations over their scopes.
The backend maintains domains or equivalent finite-domain representations during search.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite-domain constraint-programming backend solves a model \(M=(X,D,C,f)\) by combining sound constraint propagation with systematic search over finite assignments. Here \(X\) is finite, every \(D(x)\) is finite, each \(c\in C\) is a relation on its scope, and \(f\) is optional. Every propagation step may delete a value only if no completion using that value satisfies the propagated constraint. A complete backend returns a satisfying assignment, an optimal one when \(f\) is present, or a correct infeasibility conclusion after exhausting the finite search.

notation.meaning: Variables, domain map, and constraint family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-domain propagation-and-search backend, optionally supporting optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-domain constraint-programming backend solves a model \(M=(X,D,C,f)\) by combining sound constraint propagation with systematic search over finite assignments. Here \(X\) is finite, every \(D(x)\) is finite, each \(c\in C\) is a relation on its scope, and \(f\) is optional. Every propagation step may delete a value only if no completion using that value satisfies the propagated constraint. A complete backend returns a satisfying assignment, an optimal one when \(f\) is present, or a correct infeasibility conclusion after exhausting the finite search.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Domain CP Backends

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section is specific, but the available inventory does not establish that it supports the detailed claims about value deletion, completeness, optimization, and exhaustive finite search. The deletion sentence may also be read as requiring a particular support-consistency strength rather than merely sound propagation. Full-text inspection or a more directly authoritative CP source is needed; the definition content kind otherwise fits the backend-family topic.

children.title: Lazy-Clause-Generation Backends
children.top_down_role: CP backends integrating propagation with learned clauses.

assumptions_latex: The model has finite-domain variables represented by Boolean literals.
Each propagator can explain every inferred literal or conflict by a clause valid for the represented constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A lazy-clause-generation backend interleaves finite-domain propagation with clause learning. When a propagator infers literal \(l\) under antecedent literals \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\), it supplies the valid explanation \[(a_1\land\cdots\land a_k)\Rightarrow l,\] equivalently the clause \(\neg a_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg a_k\lor l\). A detected failure supplies a conflicting clause. The Boolean engine performs conflict analysis, learns a valid clause, backjumps, and resumes propagation. Search terminates with a decoded solution, an optimality result under an objective procedure, or unsatisfiability after the encoded finite search space is refuted.

notation.meaning: Conjunction and disjunction in an explanation clause.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explanation-producing CP propagation integrated with clause learning and nonchronological backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lazy-clause-generation backend interleaves finite-domain propagation with clause learning. When a propagator infers literal \(l\) under antecedent literals \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\), it supplies the valid explanation \[(a_1\land\cdots\land a_k)\Rightarrow l,\] equivalently the clause \(\neg a_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg a_k\lor l\). A detected failure supplies a conflicting clause. The Boolean engine performs conflict analysis, learns a valid clause, backjumps, and resumes propagation. Search terminates with a decoded solution, an optimality result under an objective procedure, or unsatisfiability after the encoded finite search space is refuted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lazy clause generation couples finite-domain propagators with clause explanations, conflict analysis, learned clauses, and nonchronological backtracking.
knowledge_statements.title: Lazy-Clause-Generation Backends

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind for the mechanism described, and the explanation clause is internally consistent. The record has no authoritative LCG citation for explanation-producing propagators, conflict learning, backjumping, or the stated termination and optimization outcomes.

children.title: CP-SAT Backends
children.top_down_role: SAT-centered backends exposing finite-domain CP interfaces.

assumptions_latex: The model uses finitely bounded integer and Boolean variables with constraints accepted by the backend.
Every backend transformation preserves feasible assignments and objective values under decoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A CP-SAT backend is a hybrid finite-domain optimization backend that represents Boolean and bounded-integer reasoning within a clause-learning search and may additionally use constraint propagators and linear relaxations. Given model \(M\), it constructs an internal representation \(E(M)\), repeatedly propagates clauses and supported constraints, branches, analyzes conflicts, learns valid constraints, and maintains objective bounds when optimizing. A complete run returns a decoded feasible or optimal assignment, or a certificate status asserting that no feasible assignment exists within the accepted finite model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementation-family definition emphasizing bounded integer reasoning, clause learning, propagation, and optional relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A CP-SAT backend is a hybrid finite-domain optimization backend that represents Boolean and bounded-integer reasoning within a clause-learning search and may additionally use constraint propagators and linear relaxations. Given model \(M\), it constructs an internal representation \(E(M)\), repeatedly propagates clauses and supported constraints, branches, analyzes conflicts, learns valid constraints, and maintains objective bounds when optimizing. A complete run returns a decoded feasible or optimal assignment, or a certificate status asserting that no feasible assignment exists within the accepted finite model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CP-SAT backend combines bounded integer and Boolean modeling with clause learning, constraint propagation, and possibly linear relaxations and objective bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: CP-SAT Backends

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A family definition is plausible for this leaf, but CP-SAT is not given a standardized mathematical scope here. children.title: Hybrid Backend Overlap
children.top_down_role: Capabilities shared across clause-learning finite-domain backends.

assumptions_latex: Backend families are classified by mathematical mechanisms rather than product names.
Each backend exposes a set of mechanisms used during search.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Let \(L\) be the class of backends with explanation-producing finite-domain propagators integrated into clause learning, and let \(S\) be the class using clause-learning search for Boolean and bounded-integer constraint optimization. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats LCG and CP-SAT as potentially intersecting mechanism-defined backend classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Backend Overlap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is an appropriate role for an overlap leaf, but the displayed intersection is tautological under the record's own predicates and does not independently establish that recognized LCG and CP-SAT families overlap. children.title: Paradigm Selection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Model characteristics limiting interchangeability between backend paradigms.

assumptions_latex: A model \(M\) has required semantic features \(R(M)\).
Each backend paradigm \(p\) has admissible features \(A(p)\), translation \(E_p\), and declared resource limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Paradigm \(p\) is selectable for model \(M\) only if \[R(M)\subseteq A(p)\] and \(E_p\) preserves feasible solutions, objective order, and required outputs within the declared numeric and size limits. If no paradigm satisfies the inclusion and preservation conditions, selection must report an unsupported model or invoke an explicitly declared reformulation whose own preservation obligations are checked.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard semantic compatibility precedes performance-based ranking of backend paradigms.

This compatibility boundary is mandatory. Among compatible paradigms, predicted runtime or memory may rank alternatives but cannot make an incompatible paradigm valid. If no paradigm satisfies the inclusion and preservation conditions, selection must report an unsupported model or invoke an explicitly declared reformulation whose own preservation obligations are checked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A backend paradigm is selectable only after semantic support and translation preservation are established; performance predictions rank only the compatible alternatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Paradigm Selection Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind matches Paradigm Selection Boundaries, and separating hard semantic compatibility from performance ranking is coherent.
