children.title: MIP Backends
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer optimization backends used for finite-domain CP models.

knowledge_statements.title: MIP Backends
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-hot MIP representation of finite-domain constraint models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let variables \(x_i\) have finite domains \(D_i\). Introduce binary variables \(z_{i,a}\) for \(a\in D_i\), impose \(\sum_{a\in D_i}z_{i,a}=1\), and recover \(x_i=\sum_{a\in D_i}a z_{i,a}\). A forbidden tuple \(t\) on scope \(S\) is excluded by \(\sum_{i\in S}z_{i,t_i}\le |S|-1\). If every constraint is represented by all its forbidden tuples, then projection through the recovery equations gives exactly the feasible assignments of the original finite-domain model. A linear objective in the value indicators is consequently preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A MIP backend can represent each domain value by one binary indicator and exclude forbidden tuples using linear inequalities, preserving feasible assignments and linear objectives exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(D_i\) is finite for every variable \(i\).
Each constraint is available extensionally through its forbidden tuples.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(F_{\mathrm{MIP}})=F_{\mathrm{CP}}\).

notation.meaning: indicator that variable i takes value a
feasible set of the MIP encoding
feasible assignments of the finite-domain model

review_flags: exact tuple-encoding support should be checked against a dedicated encoding source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the MIP-backend leaf, and the forbidden-tuple formulation is mathematically plausible, but the cited introductory modeling section does not specifically support this encoding or its exact projection claim. The recovery equation also requires numeric domain values, such as D_i contained in the reals, which is not assumed. A dedicated finite-domain-to-MIP encoding source and the missing domain hypothesis are required.

children.title: SMT Backends
children.top_down_role: Satisfiability-modulo-theories backends used for finite-domain CP models.

knowledge_statements.title: SMT Backends
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier-free SMT representation over integers or finite enumerations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each finite-domain variable \(x_i\) with domain \(D_i\), declare either an enumerated-sort constant or an integer constant constrained by \(\bigvee_{a\in D_i}(x_i=a)\). Translate each constraint relation \(R_j\subseteq\prod_{i\in S_j}D_i\) as \(\bigvee_{t\in R_j}\bigwedge_{i\in S_j}(x_i=t_i)\). The conjunction of the domain and relation formulas is satisfiable exactly when the finite-domain model is feasible, and its satisfying interpretations restricted to the \(x_i\) are precisely the feasible assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SMT backend represents domains and allowed tuples as quantifier-free formulas; satisfying interpretations correspond exactly to feasible finite-domain assignments.
assumptions_latex: Every domain \(D_i\) and relation \(R_j\) is finite.
Equality and Boolean connectives have their standard SMT semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Mod}(\Phi)\vert_{\{x_i\}}=F_{\mathrm{CP}}\).
review_flags: a dedicated authoritative source for finite-domain SMT encodings is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role and extensional quantifier-free translation fit the SMT-backend leaf, and the formulas are internally coherent. No citation is supplied, however, so the exact soundness-and-completeness correspondence requires an authoritative finite-domain SMT encoding source with a specific locator.

children.title: Cross-Paradigm Model Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Model fragments suitable for either backend paradigm.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Paradigm Model Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic compatibility criterion for CP, MIP, and SMT backend translations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite-domain model with feasible assignments \(F(M)\) and objective \(f\), and let \(E_B(M)\) be its encoding for backend \(B\) with feasible objects \(F_B\). The encoding is cross-paradigm compatible when there is a decoding map \(\delta_B:F_B\to F(M)\) such that \(\delta_B(F_B)=F(M)\), every backend-feasible object decodes to a feasible assignment, and \(f_B(y)=f(\delta_B(y))\) for all \(y\in F_B\). For satisfaction models, the objective condition is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A backend is compatible when decoding is sound and complete for feasibility and preserves objective values whenever the model has an objective.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) has finite variable domains.
Backend feasibility and decoding are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_B(F_B)=F(M)\) and \(f_B=f\circ\delta_B\) on \(F_B\).

notation.meaning: feasible assignments of the source model

source_refs.locator: 1.1 The concept of a model p. 3

children.title: Translation Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Semantic or propagation losses arising during backend translation.

knowledge_statements.title: Translation Loss Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite big-M translation without valid variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\), and the implication \(y=0\Rightarrow x=0\). The usual MIP translation \(x\le My\) is exact only when \(M\) is a valid finite upper bound for \(x\) whenever \(y=1\). If no such bound exists, every finite \(M\) removes the source-feasible point \((M+1,1)\). Thus this translation is incomplete, although it still enforces the implication on the retained points; backend compatibility fails at the boundary where required finite bounds are unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite big-M encoding loses feasible solutions when the activated continuous variable has no valid finite upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(x\ge 0\) is unbounded above when \(y=1\).
The translation uses a finite constant \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\in\{0,1\},\ y=0\Rightarrow x=0\}\not\subseteq\{(x,y):x\le My\}\).
review_flags: a dedicated authoritative source for big-M validity boundaries is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate in isolation, and the big-M counterexample is mathematically correct. It is not a boundary of the stated finite-domain source-model context: its essential assumption is an unbounded continuous variable. Finite source domains provide finite value bounds. No source is supplied, and this record belongs under a mixed continuous-discrete or general implication-translation context rather than this immutable finite-domain leaf.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Level Solver Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static portfolio choice using features of the model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a model class \(\mathcal{M}\), portfolio \(\mathcal{S}\), class descriptor \(g(\mathcal{M})\), and estimated class loss \(\widehat L(s,g(\mathcal{M}))\), select \(s^{*}\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\widehat L(s,g(\mathcal{M}))\). Run \(s^{*}\) on every instance in \(\mathcal{M}\) with the prescribed resource limit. Return its verified feasible solution and bound, or its infeasibility or optimality certificate; if the limit expires without a certificate, return the incumbent and an unknown-status flag. The selection is fixed for the class and does not inspect individual-instance features.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one solver from a portfolio using model-class characteristics, then apply that fixed choice to every instance in the class.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{S}\) is a finite solver portfolio.
\(\widehat L\) uses a common loss and resource convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s^{*}\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\widehat L(s,g(\mathcal{M}))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is a suitable role for model-level solver selection, but the cited section titled Portfolio selection is an applications section on mathematical portfolio optimization, not algorithm portfolio selection. It does not support the class-level loss rule or the checker and certificate protocol. The return behavior also does not specify the case in which no incumbent exists at timeout. A dedicated algorithm-selection source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Feature Solver Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-instance portfolio choice from computable instance features.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \(I\), compute a feature vector \(\phi(I)\) within feature budget \(T_f\). For each solver \(s\) in a finite portfolio \(\mathcal{S}\), evaluate a trained predictor \(\widehat L_s(\phi(I))\), and choose \(s^{*}\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\widehat L_s(\phi(I))\), with a fixed tie rule. Run \(s^{*}\) under the remaining resource budget. Return only solutions or certificates accepted by an independent checker; otherwise return the best checked incumbent and unknown status when the budget expires.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute features for each instance, predict every portfolio solver's loss, choose the minimum-predicted-loss solver, and validate its output.
assumptions_latex: Feature computation satisfies \(T_f\) and does not exhaust the solving budget.
All predictors use the same loss convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s^{*}\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\widehat L_s(\phi(I))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and per-instance feature-based argmin fit the leaf. The cited Portfolio selection section concerns an optimization application rather than solver portfolio selection and does not support feature extraction, trained loss predictors, or independent checking. A specific authoritative algorithm-selection source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Portfolio Execution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent execution with shared checked incumbents and certified termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given solvers \(s_1,\ldots,s_p\), launch each on the same instance with assigned resources. Whenever a solver produces a feasible solution, verify it and atomically publish it if its objective improves the shared incumbent. A solver may consume a published incumbent only through its documented interface. Terminate with infeasible or optimal status only after receiving a valid certificate for that claim; otherwise stop at the global limit and return the best verified incumbent with unknown status. For a satisfaction problem, execution may stop at the first verified satisfying assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run portfolio solvers concurrently, share only verified improving incumbents, and claim optimality or infeasibility only with a valid certificate.
assumptions_latex: The portfolio contains \(p\ge1\) solvers.
All solvers use the same model semantics and objective ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{out}}=\min\{z(y):y\text{ is a verified incumbent produced before termination}\}\) for minimization.

notation.meaning: objective value of the returned incumbent

Moreover, the displayed minimum is undefined when no verified incumbent is produced and does not describe certificate-only infeasible termination. children.title: Direct Encodings
children.top_down_role: Boolean representations assigning literals to finite-domain values.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-hot Boolean encoding with conflict clauses for forbidden tuples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each variable \(x_i\) with finite domain \(D_i\), the direct encoding introduces a Boolean atom \(p_{i,a}\) for every \(a\in D_i\), interpreted as \(x_i=a\). It includes one exactly-one constraint \(\sum_{a\in D_i}p_{i,a}=1\) per variable. For a constraint with scope \(S\), every forbidden tuple \(t\in\prod_{i\in S}D_i\) contributes the clause \(\bigvee_{i\in S}\neg p_{i,t_i}\). Boolean models of the complete encoding correspond bijectively to feasible finite-domain assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The direct encoding uses one Boolean per variable-value pair, exactly-one domain constraints, and a conflict clause for each forbidden tuple.
assumptions_latex: Every variable domain and encoded constraint scope is finite.
All forbidden tuples of each encoded constraint are included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Mod}(E_{\mathrm{dir}})\leftrightarrow F_{\mathrm{CP}}\) bijectively.
review_flags: a dedicated authoritative source for direct finite-domain Boolean encodings is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct role for this leaf, and the one-hot atoms, exactly-one constraints, forbidden-tuple clauses, and bijection are coherent under the stated completeness assumption. No source is supplied; an authoritative finite-domain Boolean-encoding reference with a specific definition or section locator is required.

children.title: Support Encodings
children.top_down_role: Boolean representations organized around allowed supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-relation encoding by clauses listing supported neighbor values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq D_x\times D_y\) be a binary constraint and let \(p_{x,a}\) and \(p_{y,b}\) be direct value atoms with exactly-one domain constraints. Its support encoding contains, for every \(a\in D_x\), the clause \(\neg p_{x,a}\vee\bigvee_{b:(a,b)\in R}p_{y,b}\), and symmetrically, for every \(b\in D_y\), the clause \(\neg p_{y,b}\vee\bigvee_{a:(a,b)\in R}p_{x,a}\). An empty support set yields the unit clause negating the unsupported value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support encoding requires every selected value to imply that at least one compatible value is selected for the neighboring variable.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq D_x\times D_y\) is finite.
Value atoms satisfy exactly-one constraints for both variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{x,a}\Rightarrow\bigvee_{b:(a,b)\in R}p_{y,b}\) and symmetrically for \(y\).
review_flags: a dedicated authoritative source for support encodings is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct role, and the bidirectional clauses correctly state the support encoding for a finite binary relation with exactly-one value atoms. No authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Encoding Strength Comparison
children.top_down_role: Relative propagation behavior across direct and support representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Strength Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-propagation comparison for binary direct and support encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary relation \(R\subseteq D_x\times D_y\), equip both encodings with the same exactly-one value constraints. Under any partial assignment representing current domains, unit propagation on the bidirectional support encoding removes every value whose support set in the neighboring current domain is empty. Hence its fixed point realizes arc consistency for \(R\). The direct encoding using only clauses for forbidden pairs need not remove such a value until a particular conflicting neighbor value is selected; therefore support propagation can be strictly stronger while both complete encodings have the same satisfying assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For binary constraints, support clauses can enforce arc-consistency pruning by unit propagation, while forbidden-pair direct clauses may leave unsupported values unpruned.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a finite binary relation.
Both encodings share equivalent exactly-one domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{UP}(E_{\mathrm{sup}})\) enforces arc consistency and may strictly dominate \(\operatorname{UP}(E_{\mathrm{dir}})\).
review_flags: propagation-strength claim requires a dedicated encoding theorem source
exact treatment depends on the chosen exactly-one encoding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is an appropriate role for the propagation-strength comparison. The claim is plausible for the stated domain interpretation, but its exact unit-propagation result depends on how current domains and exactly-one constraints are encoded. A dedicated theorem source and an explicit treatment of that dependence are required.

children.title: Encoding Size Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instance regimes producing unfavorable Boolean representation size.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Size Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clause and literal counts for a finite binary relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq D_x\times D_y\), with \(m=|D_x|\), \(n=|D_y|\), and \(r=|R|\), excluding the shared exactly-one domain constraints. The forbidden-pair direct encoding has exactly \(mn-r\) binary clauses and \(2(mn-r)\) literal occurrences. The bidirectional support encoding has \(m+n\) clauses; counting the antecedent literal in each clause, it has \(m+n+2r\) literal occurrences. Thus support encoding is linear in the number of values plus allowed pairs, whereas direct conflict encoding is linear in the number of forbidden pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one binary relation, direct encoding scales with forbidden pairs; bidirectional support encoding has one clause per value and scales in literals with allowed pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(D_x\) and \(D_y\) are finite.
Shared exactly-one constraints are excluded from both counts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|C_{\mathrm{dir}}|=mn-r\), \(|C_{\mathrm{sup}}|=m+n\), and \(L_{\mathrm{sup}}=m+n+2r\).
review_flags: exact clause counts should be checked against a dedicated Boolean-encoding source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound is the correct role, and the displayed counts follow from the stated binary direct and bidirectional support clause schemes when shared exactly-one constraints are excluded. The cited general section on encoding size does not support these exact Boolean clause and literal counts. A dedicated encoding reference is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Order Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-variable encoding for a totally ordered finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_x=\{d_1<\cdots<d_m\}\). The order encoding introduces Boolean variables \(q_k\) for \(1\le k<m\), with \(q_k\) interpreted as \(x\le d_k\), and imposes \(q_k\Rightarrow q_{k+1}\) for \(1\le k<m-1\). Decoding is \(x=d_1\) when \(q_1\) holds, \(x=d_k\) when \(\neg q_{k-1}\wedge q_k\) for \(1<k<m\), and \(x=d_m\) when \(\neg q_{m-1}\). Consequently each monotone Boolean assignment determines exactly one domain value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order encoding represents an ordered domain using monotone threshold Booleans, with each monotone truth pattern decoding to exactly one value.
assumptions_latex: \(D_x\) is finite and totally ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x=d_k\}_{k=1}^{m}\) is in bijection with monotone assignments to \(q_1,\ldots,q_{m-1}\).
review_flags: a dedicated authoritative source for the order encoding is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct role, and the threshold semantics, monotonicity clauses, decoding cases, and bijection are internally consistent for a finite totally ordered domain with at least two values. No authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Binary Encodings
children.top_down_role: Bit-vector representations of finite-domain values.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical positional encoding of one finite-domain variable by Boolean bits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\}\) with \(m\ge 2\), and set \(k=\lceil\log_2 m\rceil\). Introduce \(b_0,\ldots,b_{k-1}\in\{0,1\}\) and define \(q(b)=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}2^j b_j\). The binary encoding represents \(x=v_i\) by \(q(b)=i\). Its valid code set is \(C=\{b\in\{0,1\}^k:q(b)<m\}\); hence the encoding of \(x\in D\) is exact precisely when assignments outside \(C\) are excluded. On valid assignments, decoding by \(x=v_{q(b)}\) is a bijection between \(C\) and \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite domain is indexed by positional bit patterns; unused patterns must be forbidden so valid bit assignments correspond bijectively to domain values.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite set with \(|D|=m\ge 2\).
Domain values have the fixed indexing \(v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=v_i\iff \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}2^j b_j=i\), with \(k=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) and invalid codes excluded.

notation.meaning: finite domain of the encoded variable
unsigned integer represented by the bits

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical positional encoding follows directly from indexing a finite set by unsigned binary integers
authoritative finite-domain encoding source and exact locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positional binary representation is mathematically precise, matches the leaf context, and uses an appropriate content kind, but no inspectable source and locator are supplied. Standard-field rationale alone is insufficient for this review layer.

children.title: Logarithmic Encodings
children.top_down_role: Compact value representations using logarithmically many Boolean variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General injective Boolean encoding using asymptotically minimal code length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite domain \(D\) of cardinality \(m\), a logarithmic encoding consists of \(k=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) Boolean variables and an injection \(c:D\to\{0,1\}^k\). A bit assignment \(b\) represents \(x=d\) exactly when \(b=c(d)\), and validity requires \(b\in c(D)\). Conversely, every injective encoding of all \(m\) values into \(r\) Boolean variables satisfies \(2^r\ge m\), so \(r\ge\lceil\log_2m\rceil\). Thus logarithmic encodings attain the minimum possible number of Boolean coordinates among fixed-length injective Boolean codes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An injective code uses ceiling log-base-two domain-size bits, and no fixed-length Boolean encoding can use fewer.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is finite with \(|D|=m\ge 2\).
Each domain value must have a distinct fixed-length Boolean code.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) bits suffice, and every injective fixed-length Boolean encoding requires at least \(k\) bits.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the lower bound is the elementary counting inequality for injective Boolean codes
authoritative encoding source and locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The injective-code definition and counting lower bound are correct and fit Logarithmic Encodings, but the record has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Bit-Width Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Representation size and constraint complexity across bit widths.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Width Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-count and literal-complexity comparison between logarithmic and one-hot encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(|D|=m\ge2\). A one-hot representation uses \(m\) Boolean variables \(y_i\) and \(\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}y_i=1\), making the predicate \(x=v_i\) the single literal \(y_i\). A logarithmic representation uses \(k=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) bits, but \(x=v_i\) requires fixing all \(k\) bit literals of its code. Consequently, logarithmic encoding reduces the variable count from \(m\) to \(k\), while equality-to-value predicates expand from one literal to a conjunction of \(k\) literals; propagation strength is therefore not determined by bit width alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logarithmic coding saves Boolean variables, but testing one value requires all code bits; fewer bits alone does not guarantee stronger propagation.
assumptions_latex: The compared encodings are one-hot and injective fixed-length binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The respective Boolean widths are \(m\) and \(\lceil\log_2m\rceil\), whereas a value equality uses respectively one and \(\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) literals.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: variable and literal counts follow directly from the two representations
propagation claim requires a finite-domain encoding reference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variable and literal counts are correct, and content_kind property fits the tradeoff leaf. The statement about propagation is appropriately cautious but still requires an authoritative finite-domain encoding source with a precise locator.

children.title: Invalid-Code Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Unused Boolean codes arising from non-power-of-two domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Invalid-Code Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validity boundary for a contiguous-domain positional binary code.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge2\), \(k=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\), and \(q(b)=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}2^j b_j\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}^k\). The positional code for indices \(\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\) is valid exactly under \(q(b)\le m-1\). If \(m=2^k\), every bit pattern is valid. If \(m<2^k\), the invalid-code boundary is \(q(b)\ge m\), comprising exactly \(2^k-m\) patterns. Omitting the validity inequality introduces assignments that decode to no domain value and therefore destroys equivalence with the original finite-domain variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Codes at least the domain size are invalid; they disappear only when the domain size is a power of two.
assumptions_latex: The domain indices are \(0,\ldots,m-1\).
Bits are interpreted as an unsigned positional integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The code is valid iff \(q(b)\le m-1\); otherwise \(q(b)\in\{m,\ldots,2^k-1\}\) is invalid.

notation.meaning: unsigned value of the bit vector

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the boundary follows from the image of unsigned positional decoding
authoritative finite-domain encoding source and locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The validity boundary and invalid-pattern count are correct for the stated unsigned positional code, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Integer Theory Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Satisfiability-preserving translation of finite integer domains into SMT integer arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite-domain variable \(x\) have domain \(D=\{d_1,\ldots,d_m\}\subset\mathbb Z\). Its integer-theory mapping introduces an SMT integer variable \(X\) and asserts the domain formula \(\bigvee_{i=1}^m X=d_i\). If \(D=\{\ell,\ell+1,\ldots,u\}\), this formula may be replaced by \(\ell\le X\le u\). Each finite-domain arithmetic relation is then translated by replacing \(x\) with \(X\) and interpreting operations in integer arithmetic. Provided every translated variable carries its domain formula, an assignment satisfies the finite-domain model exactly when its integer image satisfies the translated SMT formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Map each finite-domain variable to an SMT integer, assert its exact domain, and translate arithmetic relations; this preserves satisfying assignments.
assumptions_latex: Every finite-domain value is an integer.
Translated operations have their ordinary unbounded-integer semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite-domain model and its integer-theory translation are equisatisfiable under the asserted domain formulas.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact-domain axioms make the variable mapping a bijection on assignments
SMT finite-domain translation source and locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-domain mapping is standard and the representation kind fits the container. An SMT translation source is required to support the equisatisfiability claim and delimit which finite-domain arithmetic operations share the asserted unbounded-integer semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Vector Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsigned fixed-width SMT bit-vector mapping with explicit range and overflow conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-domain variable with indices \(0,\ldots,m-1\), let \(k=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) and introduce an SMT bit-vector \(B\) of width \(k\). Interpret \(B\) as the unsigned integer \(\operatorname{uval}(B)\) and assert \(\operatorname{uval}(B)<m\). Domain value \(v_i\) corresponds to \(\operatorname{uval}(B)=i\). A translated arithmetic constraint preserves integer semantics only when every intermediate result lies in \(\{0,\ldots,2^k-1\}\), or when widening and range constraints prevent modular overflow. Under these conditions, decoding satisfying bit-vector assignments yields exactly the satisfying finite-domain assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a fixed-width unsigned bit-vector plus a range guard; arithmetic is equivalent only when modular overflow is excluded or intentionally modeled.
assumptions_latex: Domain values are represented by indices \(0,\ldots,m-1\).
Arithmetic is unsigned, with overflow excluded by bounds or widening.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The guarded bit-vector translation is equisatisfiable with the finite-domain model when all translated arithmetic preserves its intended integer value.

notation.meaning: unsigned integer value of the bit-vector

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: guarded unsigned decoding and modular bit-vector semantics determine equivalence
SMT bit-vector standard or textbook locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The guarded unsigned mapping and overflow qualification are substantively correct for m at least 2, but the record does not state m>=2; otherwise k can be zero, which is not a valid SMT-LIB bit-vector width. No SMT standard or textbook locator is supplied to support the mapping and arithmetic-equivalence conditions.

children.title: Indicator Encodings
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer formulations using solver-native indicator constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-integer representation of a binary-triggered linear inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(x\in X\), and suppose \(M\) satisfies \(M\ge\max_{x\in X}(a^{\mathsf T}x-\beta)\). Then the indicator implication \(z=1\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is represented by \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta+M(1-z)\). For \(z=1\), this reduces to the indicated inequality; for \(z=0\), validity of \(M\) makes the inequality redundant over \(X\). The formulation is therefore exact for integer \(z\), although its continuous relaxation depends on the tightness of \(M\). A solver-native indicator constraint expresses the same implication without requiring the modeler to display \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary indicator activates a linear inequality; a valid big-M inequality is exact for binary indicators, though its relaxation may be weak.
assumptions_latex: The maximum defining \(M\) is finite over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=1\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is equivalent over \(X\times\{0,1\}\) to \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta+M(1-z)\).

notation.meaning: base feasible region for continuous or integer variables

review_flags: confirm that the cited section explicitly covers binary implication or big-M formulations

children.title: Logical Encodings
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer formulations for Boolean combinations and implications.

knowledge_statements.title: Logical Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear encodings of elementary Boolean connectives over binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z,z_1,\ldots,z_r\in\{0,1\}\). The equivalence \(z\leftrightarrow\bigwedge_{i=1}^r z_i\) is represented by \(z\le z_i\) for every \(i\) and \(z\ge\sum_{i=1}^r z_i-r+1\). The equivalence \(z\leftrightarrow\bigvee_{i=1}^r z_i\) is represented by \(z\ge z_i\) for every \(i\) and \(z\le\sum_{i=1}^r z_i\). Negation \(z\leftrightarrow\neg z_1\) is represented by \(z=1-z_1\). Introducing an auxiliary binary variable for each subformula recursively yields an exact mixed-integer representation of any propositional formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AND, OR, and NOT have exact linear descriptions on binary variables; auxiliary binaries recursively encode arbitrary propositional formulas.
assumptions_latex: All variables representing truth values are binary.
Each auxiliary variable is constrained by the encoding of its defining connective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible binary assignments are exactly the truth-table assignments of the encoded Boolean connectives.

notation.meaning: truth variable for the compound formula

review_flags: confirm exact Boolean-connective formulations in the cited chapter

children.title: Reified Formulation Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of reified CP constructs with mixed-integer interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Reified Formulation Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a two-way reified inequality admits an exact mixed-integer formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the reification \(z=1\leftrightarrow g(x)\le0\) on a bounded set \(X\), with \(z\in\{0,1\}\). An exact mixed-integer encoding by two implications requires formulations for both \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\) and \(z=0\Rightarrow g(x)\ge\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) separates violation from satisfaction. Such an \(\varepsilon\) exists, for example, when \(g(X)\) is finite or lies on a known lattice. For continuous \(g(X)\) accumulating at zero from above, the strict complement \(g(x)>0\) has no fixed positive margin, so this closed two-inequality formulation is not exactly compatible without changing the semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact reification needs encodable forward and reverse implications; the reverse direction requires a positive violation margin or another exact complement representation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is bounded and valid implication bounds are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two-sided big-M reification is exact when \(g(x)>0\) over violating points is equivalent to \(g(x)\ge\varepsilon\) for some known \(\varepsilon>0\).

notation.meaning: truth indicator for the reified inequality

review_flags: strict-complement compatibility claim needs confirmation against a dedicated reification source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-margin boundary is plausible and the condition kind fits the leaf, but the cited general mixed-integer-formulations section has not been shown to support the strict-complement and accumulation-at-zero claims. A dedicated reification source with an exact locator is required before the mathematical compatibility statement can be accepted.

children.title: Relaxation Weakness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Formulation regimes with weak continuous relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Weakness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss of relaxation strength caused by an oversized big-M coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0\le x\le U\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and encode \(z=1\Rightarrow x\le0\) by \(x\le M(1-z)\), where \(M\ge U>0\). The formulation is exact for binary \(z\). Its convex-hull inequality is \(x\le U(1-z)\). If \(M>U\), the linear relaxation contains \((x,z)=(U,1-U/M)\), whereas the convex-hull inequality at that \(z\) permits only \(x\le U^2/M\). Thus every choice \(M>U\) weakens the relaxation, and the discrepancy approaches \(U\) as \(M/U\) grows without bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oversized big-M remains integer-exact but admits fractional indicator points increasingly far from the convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The integrality restriction on \(z\) is relaxed to \(0\le z\le1\) when assessing strength.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(M>U\), the big-M relaxation strictly contains the convex hull described by \(x\le U(1-z)\).

notation.meaning: tight upper bound on the continuous variable

review_flags: confirm that the cited section supports the relaxation-strength interpretation

knowledge_statements.title: Extended Global-Constraint Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tuple-based extended formulation for any finite extensional global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a global constraint on \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) permit exactly the finite tuple set \(T\subset\mathbb Z^n\). Introduce \(\lambda_t\in\{0,1\}\) for each \(t\in T\), impose \(\sum_{t\in T}\lambda_t=1\), and set \(x_j=\sum_{t\in T}t_j\lambda_t\) for every \(j\). The projection of the integer feasible set onto \(x\)-space is exactly \(T\). Relaxing \(\lambda_t\in[0,1]\) projects onto \(\operatorname{conv}(T)\); hence this tuple formulation is ideal with respect to the represented finite relation, although its size is proportional to \(|T|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select one allowed tuple with auxiliary binaries and reconstruct each variable; the integer projection is exact and the relaxation projects to the tuple convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The allowed tuple set \(T\) is finite and explicitly available.
Each tuple contains one value for every constrained variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extended formulation projects to \(T\) integrally and to \(\operatorname{conv}(T)\) after relaxing the tuple selectors.

notation.meaning: component of the represented global-constraint variables

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Disjunctive Programming and Extended Formulations p. 69

review_flags: confirm tuple-selection specialization within the cited extended-formulation chapter

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Disjunctive Programming and Extended Formulations p. 69

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Domain Linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-hot linearization of a univariate function on a finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\subset\mathbb R\) and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\). Introduce \(\lambda_i\in\{0,1\}\) and impose \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\lambda_i\), and \(y=\sum_{i=1}^m f(v_i)\lambda_i\). Exactly one selector is active, so the projection onto \((x,y)\)-space is the graph \(\{(v_i,f(v_i)):i=1,\ldots,m\}\). If the selectors are relaxed to \([0,1]\), the projection is the convex hull of this finite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-hot selectors exactly linearize a function evaluated on a finite domain; relaxing selectors gives the convex hull of its graph points.
assumptions_latex: The domain values \(v_i\) are distinct.
The values \(f(v_i)\) are known constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary formulation represents \(y=f(x)\) exactly for \(x\in D\), and its continuous relaxation projects to the graph's convex hull.
review_flags: confirm finite-domain graph linearization in the cited modeling chapter

children.title: Encoding Size Growth
children.top_down_role: Variable, constraint, clause, or coefficient growth after encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Size Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case bit-length growth for a fixed finite-domain compilation scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a compilation map \(E\), define its output-size function by \(S_E(I)=|E(I)|\) and its worst-case growth function by \[G_E(n)=\sup\{S_E(I): I\text{ is a valid instance and }|I|\le n\}.\] The encoding has polynomial size growth when constants \(c>0\) and \(k\ge 0\) exist such that \(G_E(n)\le c n^k\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); it has exponential size growth when \(G_E(n)\ge 2^{cn}\) for some \(c>0\) and infinitely many \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding-size growth is the largest backend bit length produced from any valid source instance up to a given source bit length. It is polynomial when bounded eventually by a fixed polynomial and exponential in the stated lower-bound sense when it reaches an exponential bound for infinitely many input lengths.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) compiles each finite-domain instance into a finite backend representation.
\(|I|\) and \(|E(I)|\) are bit lengths under fixed source and backend encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_E(n)=\sup\{|E(I)|:|I|\le n\}\) measures worst-case encoding-size growth, with polynomial growth exactly when \(G_E(n)=O(n^k)\) for some constant \(k\).

notation.meaning: Compilation map from source instances to backend representations.
Bit length of an encoded object.
Worst-case output size for inputs of length at most n.

children.title: Compilation Cost
children.top_down_role: Time and memory consumed before backend solving begins.

knowledge_statements.title: Compilation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compiler running cost under an explicitly fixed operation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_E(I)\) be the number of primitive operations executed by compiler \(E\) on valid finite-domain instance \(I\), including generation of backend variables, constraints, and coefficients. Define \[C_E(n)=\sup\{T_E(I): I\text{ is valid and }|I|\le n\}.\] This is the worst-case compilation cost at source size \(n\). If \(W_E(I)\) is the number of emitted symbols, every emitted symbol requires at least one primitive operation, and the output alphabet is fixed and finite, then \(T_E(I)\ge W_E(I)\) and \(W_E(I)=\Theta(|E(I)|)\); consequently \(T_E(I)=\Omega(|E(I)|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compilation cost counts primitive compiler operations and maximizes that count over valid source instances up to a given input size. Under a fixed finite output alphabet and a per-symbol writing cost, compilation time is at least proportional to output bit length.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is implemented by a terminating deterministic compiler.
Primitive compiler operations have unit cost in a fixed computation model.
The backend representation is written over a fixed finite alphabet, and emitting each output symbol requires at least one primitive operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_E(n)=\sup\{T_E(I):|I|\le n\}\) is the worst-case compilation cost of \(E\).

notation.meaning: Number of primitive operations used to compile instance I.
Worst-case compilation cost for inputs of length at most n.
Number of backend symbols emitted while compiling instance I.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Solving mathematical programming models p. 11

review_flags: compiler-cost formalization requires a directly supporting source

children.title: Size–Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships between compact output and compilation effort.

knowledge_statements.title: Size–Cost Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instancewise Pareto comparison of backend size and compiler cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed instance \(I\), encoding \(e_1\in\mathcal E\) dominates \(e_2\in\mathcal E\) in the size–cost order when \(S_{e_1}(I)\le S_{e_2}(I)\), \(C_{e_1}(I)\le C_{e_2}(I)\), and at least one inequality is strict. An encoding \(e\) is size–cost Pareto efficient on \(I\) precisely when no member of \(\mathcal E\) dominates it. Thus minimizing size alone or cost alone can discard efficient compromises, while every minimizer of a strictly positive weighted sum \(\alpha S_e(I)+\beta C_e(I)\), where \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta>0\), is Pareto efficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding is an efficient size–cost compromise when no portfolio alternative is no larger and no more expensive to compile, with one strict improvement. Any minimizer of a weighted sum using strictly positive weights for both criteria is Pareto efficient.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E\) is a finite set of semantics-preserving encodings.
Size and compilation cost are measured under common fixed conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An encoding is size–cost Pareto efficient exactly when no alternative encoding weakly improves both criteria and strictly improves at least one.

notation.meaning: Backend size and compilation cost of encoding e on instance I.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Pareto efficiency is applied to the two explicitly defined compilation criteria.

children.title: Compilation Bottleneck Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances where translation dominates total resource consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Compilation Bottleneck Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold and asymptotic regimes in which compilation dominates preprocessing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T_{\rm pre}(I)>0\), call instance \(I\) compilation-bottlenecked at threshold \(\theta\) when \[\frac{T_{\rm comp}(I)}{T_{\rm pre}(I)}\ge\theta.\] For an instance family \((I_n)_{n\ge1}\), compilation is asymptotically dominant when \(T_{\rm other}(I_n)=o(T_{\rm comp}(I_n))\); it is output-bound when \(T_{\rm comp}(I_n)=\Theta(|E(I_n)|)\); and it is transformation-bound when \(|E(I_n)|=o(T_{\rm comp}(I_n))\). These predicates distinguish dominance caused by writing a large encoding from dominance caused by computation internal to the compiler.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compilation is a bottleneck when it exceeds a chosen share of preprocessing. Along an instance family it is asymptotically dominant when other preprocessing is negligible, output-bound when compilation time is proportional to encoded size, and transformation-bound when encoded size is negligible relative to compilation time.
assumptions_latex: Total preprocessing time decomposes as \(T_{\rm pre}(I)=T_{\rm comp}(I)+T_{\rm other}(I)\).
The threshold satisfies \(0<\theta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Instance \(I\) is compilation-bottlenecked at threshold \(\theta\) exactly when \(T_{\rm comp}(I)/T_{\rm pre}(I)\ge\theta\).

notation.meaning: Required compilation share of preprocessing time.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The threshold and asymptotic predicates explicitly define the intended bottleneck regimes.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a constraint on finite-domain variables \(X\), and \(E(C)\) is satisfiability-equivalent after projection.
\(P_C\) and \(P_E\) are monotone, contracting, idempotent domain propagators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Propagation is preserved exactly when \(\pi(P_E(\iota(D)))=P_C(D)\) for every source-domain store \(D\).

notation.meaning: Canonical extension of a source store to encoding variables.
Projection from encoded stores onto source variables.

review_flags: exact propagation-equivalence terminology requires source certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of source pruning and projected backend pruning at propagator fixpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be any domain store on the source variables \(X\). Extend it canonically to the encoding variables by \(\iota(D)\), run the encoded propagator to its fixpoint, and project by \(\pi\). The encoding preserves the pruning strength of \(P_C\) when \[\pi\bigl(P_E(\iota(D))\bigr)=P_C(D)\qquad\text{for every }D.\] The one-sided inclusion \(\pi(P_E(\iota(D)))\subseteq P_C(D)\) means the encoding is at least as strong, whereas the reverse inclusion means it is no stronger than the source propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding preserves propagation when backend fixpoint pruning, projected to original variables, equals the source propagator’s pruning for every domain store.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Preservation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the propagation-preservation topic and is internally coherent under the stated domain-store order. The cited general constraint-programming section does not establish the exact extension–fixpoint–projection equality or its one-sided strength terminology; a propagation/encoding source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Induced Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary-variable symmetries introduced by an otherwise semantics-preserving encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the fiber-preserving symmetry group by \[H_E=\{g:g\text{ is a permutation of assignments to }X\cup Y,\ g(F_E)=F_E,\text{ and }\pi_X(g(z))=\pi_X(z)\text{ for every }z\in F_E\}.\] An encoding-induced symmetry is a nonidentity member \(g\in H_E\), equivalently a member satisfying \(g(z)\ne z\) for at least one \(z\in F_E\). Such a symmetry changes only auxiliary realizations of the same source solution. The set \(H_E\), which includes the identity, is a group under composition; nontrivial orbits within a fiber \(\pi_X^{-1}(x)\cap F_E\) represent redundant backend solutions created by the encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fiber-preserving symmetries form a group that includes the identity. An encoding-induced symmetry is a nonidentity member that permutes auxiliary realizations while preserving feasibility and every represented source solution.
assumptions_latex: \(E(I)\) has original variables \(X\), auxiliary variables \(Y\), and satisfying set \(F_E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonidentity permutation \(g\) is encoding-induced when it preserves \(F_E\), fixes the projection of every feasible assignment onto the original variables, and moves at least one feasible assignment.

notation.meaning: Satisfying assignments of the encoded model.
Group of feasible-set-preserving permutations that fix source projections.

review_flags: specialized symmetry definition requires a directly supporting source

children.title: Portfolio Generalization
children.top_down_role: Selection quality on models outside observed training or tuning distributions.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E\) is a finite encoding portfolio and \(L(e,I)\) is an integrable loss.
Training and deployment instances follow distributions \(Q\) and \(P\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selector \(h\) \(\varepsilon\)-generalizes from \(Q\) to \(P\) when \(R_P(h)\le\min_{e\in\mathcal E}R_P(e)+\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Expected deployment loss of selector h.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Expected-risk generalization is specialized here to finite encoding selection.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deployment-risk criterion for an encoding selector trained on another distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the deployment risk of selector \(h\) by \[R_P(h)=\mathbb E_{I\sim P}[L(h(I),I)].\] The selector \(\varepsilon\)-generalizes from training distribution \(Q\) to deployment distribution \(P\) relative to portfolio \(\mathcal E\) when \[R_P(h)\le \min_{e\in\mathcal E}\mathbb E_{I\sim P}[L(e,I)]+\varepsilon.\] This condition compares deployment performance with the best single portfolio encoding under \(P\); low empirical or expected loss under \(Q\) alone does not imply it when \(P\ne Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A portfolio selector generalizes when its expected deployment loss is within a chosen tolerance of the best fixed portfolio encoding on deployment data.
knowledge_statements.title: Portfolio Generalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically defined, but it labels a deployment comparison with the best fixed encoding under \(P\) as generalization from \(Q\), although \(Q\) does not enter the criterion except through the unspecified construction of \(h\). A portfolio-selection or learning-theory source is needed to certify this terminology and comparator.

children.title: Fallback Policies
children.top_down_role: Backup solver or encoding choices used after uncertain selection.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E\) is a finite portfolio, and \(A(e,I)\) decides whether encoding \(e\) is admissible for instance \(I\).
The fallback ordering \((f_1,\ldots,f_k)\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy returns the selector’s admissible choice, otherwise the first admissible fallback, and reports uncovered if none exists.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The record formally specifies a deterministic guarded fallback policy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic admissibility-guarded fallback for portfolio encoding selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given instance \(I\), compute \(e_0=h(I)\). If \(e_0\in\mathcal E\) and \(A(e_0,I)\) holds, return \(e_0\). Otherwise inspect \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\) in order and return \(f_j\) for the least index \(j\) satisfying \(A(f_j,I)\). If no such index exists, return the distinguished outcome \(\mathsf{uncovered}\). Compilation begins only after an encoding is returned; thus the policy never invokes an encoding that its admissibility predicate rejects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the selected encoding if admissible; otherwise use the first admissible encoding in a fixed fallback list, or report that the instance is uncovered.
knowledge_statements.title: Fallback Policies

children.title: Distribution-Shift Failures
children.top_down_role: Selection degradation under changed model families or instance distributions.

assumptions_latex: The portfolio contains encodings \(a\) and \(b\), and loss values are deterministic on instance types \(u\) and \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A selector optimal under \(Q(u)=1\) can have deployment regret \(M\) under \(P(v)=1\), for arbitrarily large \(M\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-instance construction showing unbounded regret after a support shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M>0\) and define losses by \(L(a,u)=0\), \(L(b,u)=M\), \(L(a,v)=M\), and \(L(b,v)=0\). Under the training distribution \(Q(u)=1\), the unique risk-minimizing constant selector chooses \(a\). Under the deployment distribution \(P(v)=1\), that selector has risk \(M\), while encoding \(b\) has risk \(0\). Its deployment regret is therefore \(M\). Since \(M\) is arbitrary, training optimality provides no finite distribution-free deployment-regret guarantee when the deployment support and loss ordering may shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two encodings can reverse their performance ordering across training and deployment instance types, producing arbitrarily large deployment regret.
knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Shift Failures

children.title: Fallback Coverage Gaps
children.top_down_role: Cases unsupported by available backup backends or encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Fallback Coverage Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instances outside every portfolio member’s admissibility domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the portfolio coverage set by \(D_{\mathcal E}=\bigcup_{e\in\mathcal E}D_e\) and the coverage gap by \[G=\mathcal X\setminus D_{\mathcal E}.\] For every \(I\in G\), no encoding in \(\mathcal E\) is admissible. Consequently, any fallback policy restricted to admissible portfolio members must return \(\mathsf{uncovered}\) on \(I\). Reordering fallbacks or changing the selector cannot remove this failure. Adding an encoding whose admissibility domain intersects \(G\) can reduce the gap; eliminating the gap requires the enlarged union of admissibility domains to cover all of \(\mathcal X\), or requires narrowing \(\mathcal X\) to the covered set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fallback coverage gap consists of intended instances accepted by no portfolio encoding, so selector or fallback reordering cannot cover them. Adding partially applicable encodings can reduce the gap, while eliminating it requires coverage of the entire intended instance class.
assumptions_latex: Each encoding \(e\in\mathcal E\) has an admissibility domain \(D_e\subseteq\mathcal X\).
A fallback policy may return only encodings admissible for its input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unavoidable coverage gap is \(G=\mathcal X\setminus\bigcup_{e\in\mathcal E}D_e\); every admissibility-respecting policy fails on each \(I\in G\).

notation.meaning: Instances covered by no portfolio encoding.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The gap follows directly from the union of encoding admissibility domains.

children.title: Partial-Expression Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures arising where expressions lack values for some inputs.

assumptions_latex: \(f:D\rightharpoonup R\) is partial, with proper definedness domain \(\operatorname{dom}(f)\subsetneq D\).
The modeling language permits \(f(x)\) without an explicit definedness guard.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unguarded occurrence of \(f(x)\) has no semantics determined solely by \(f\) when \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}(f)\).

notation.meaning: Partial function from D to R.
Inputs on which f has a value.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The failure follows from the definition of a partial function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic failure caused by using a partial operator outside its definedness domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an expression containing \(f(x)\), the guard \(x\in\operatorname{dom}(f)\) is necessary for ordinary two-valued evaluation. If the model admits some assignment \(x=d\notin\operatorname{dom}(f)\), then \(f(d)\) has no value in \(R\), so any enclosing equality, inequality, or objective term lacks a value unless an additional undefined-value convention is specified. For example, the unguarded constraint \(x/x=1\) over a domain containing \(0\) is undefined at \(x=0\), even though it is true at every nonzero domain value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial operator used without its domain guard makes enclosing constraints or objectives undefined on admitted inputs outside the operator’s domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Expression Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The underlying partial-function observation is correct and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the behavior of an unguarded partial expression depends on the modeling language's definedness, short-circuiting, and undefined-value conventions. A specific language-semantics source is required for the broader constraint and objective claims.

children.title: Undefined-Value Propagation
children.top_down_role: Effects of undefined subexpressions on enclosing model expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Undefined-Value Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict propagation of an undefined value through a typed expression tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each operator \(g:V_1\times\cdots\times V_k\to W\), let \(V_{i,\bot}=V_i\cup\{\bot\}\) and \(W_\bot=W\cup\{\bot\}\), and define its strict lifting by \[g_\bot(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=\begin{cases}g(v_1,\ldots,v_k),&v_i\ne\bot\text{ for every }i,\\ \bot,&v_i=\bot\text{ for some }i.\end{cases}\] Under recursive evaluation with these lifted operators, an undefined subexpression forces every strict ancestor to evaluate to \(\bot\). If a constraint root has ordinary codomain \(\{\mathsf{false},\mathsf{true}\}\), its lifted codomain also contains \(\bot\); an additional convention must therefore specify whether a root value of \(\bot\) means rejection, error, or a third truth value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict, typed lifted semantics, an undefined subexpression makes every strict enclosing expression undefined. A constraint whose root is undefined requires an additional convention to determine whether that outcome is rejection, an error, or a third truth value.
assumptions_latex: Each ordinary value domain \(V\) is lifted to \(V_\bot=V\cup\{\bot\}\).
Every primitive operator is strict: any undefined argument produces an undefined result.
Constraint roots have ordinary Boolean codomain \(\{\mathsf{false},\mathsf{true}\}\), lifted with \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If any evaluated leaf is \(\bot\), every strict ancestor on its path to the expression root also evaluates to \(\bot\).

notation.meaning: An ordinary value domain augmented with undefined.
Strict lifted version of a typed operator g.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Structural propagation follows from the explicitly stated strict lifted semantics.

children.title: Guard Coverage Gaps
children.top_down_role: Model regions where intended guards fail to protect partial expressions.

assumptions_latex: Each indexed expression has a declared domain of definition.
A guard is interpreted as a Boolean predicate over complete assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every evaluation path reaching a partial expression must imply that the expression is defined.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Guard coverage is characterized by implication from every active evaluation context to the partial expression's definedness predicate.
Exact finite-domain modeling source for guard coverage is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic failure criterion for guarded partial expressions under total assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite set of complete assignments and let \(e\) be an expression defined only on \(\operatorname{Def}(e)\subseteq X\). Suppose \(e\) is evaluated whenever a guard \(g_e:X\to\{0,1\}\) is true. Guard coverage is complete exactly when \[\{x\in X:g_e(x)=1\}\subseteq \operatorname{Def}(e).\] A guard coverage gap exists when there is an assignment \(x\in X\) such that \(g_e(x)=1\) but \(x\notin\operatorname{Def}(e)\). At such an assignment, the model requires evaluation of \(e(x)\) without assigning it a mathematical value, so the guarded expression does not define a total constraint relation on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A guard coverage gap occurs when some assignment activates a partial expression outside that expression's domain of definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Guard Coverage Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary formulation is mathematically coherent and fits the terminal container, but no inspectable source supports the definedness and guard-coverage criterion.

children.title: Index Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Invalid index sets, bounds, or indexing contexts.

assumptions_latex: Every indexed symbol has a declared finite index set.
Each constraint instance has an intended indexing set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An index mismatch occurs exactly when a referenced index tuple lies outside its declaration or when the generated instance set differs from the intended one.

notation.meaning: declared index set of an indexed object y

review_flags: The cited modeling section is provisional support; exact index-consistency terminology requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static and generated-index consistency in finite-domain model families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each indexed object \(y\), let \(I_y\) be its declared finite set of admissible index tuples. Let \(J\) be the set of constraint instances produced by a model generator and \(J^\star\) the set required by the specification. The model is index-consistent if every occurrence \(y_i\) satisfies \(i\in I_y\) and \(J=J^\star\). An index mismatch is witnessed either by an occurrence \(y_i\) with \(i\notin I_y\), or by an instance \(j\in J\mathbin{\triangle}J^\star\). The first case denotes an undefined reference; the second denotes an omitted or unintended constraint instance, even if every individual reference is declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Index mismatch means using an undeclared index tuple or generating a constraint-instance set different from the specified set.
knowledge_statements.title: Index Mismatch

children.title: Type Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Incompatible declared or inferred expression types.

assumptions_latex: Every variable and operator has a declared finite-domain sort.
Operator signatures specify accepted operand sorts and a result sort.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A model expression is well typed exactly when every variable occurrence and operator application respects its declared sort.
review_flags: The cited modeling section is provisional; a source explicitly treating typed constraint languages is desirable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sort consistency for variables, constants, operators, and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T\) be a finite collection of sorts and assign each variable \(x\) a sort \(\tau(x)\in\mathcal T\). For every operator with signature \(f:T_1\times\cdots\times T_k\to T\), the application \(f(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\) is well typed only if \(\tau(e_r)=T_r\) for every \(r\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), in which case its sort is \(T\). A type mismatch occurs when some variable value is outside its declared sort, some operand has a sort different from the corresponding signature sort, or a constraint expression fails to have Boolean sort. Such an expression does not denote the declared finite-domain relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A type mismatch occurs when a value or operand violates its declared sort, or when a purported constraint is not Boolean-valued.
knowledge_statements.title: Type Mismatch

children.title: Dimension Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Incompatible array ranks, shapes, or index dimensions.

assumptions_latex: Every array-valued expression has a declared finite shape.
Operators use scalar, elementwise, or contraction semantics fixed by their signatures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dimension mismatch is any operator application whose operand shapes fail its declared compatibility predicate.
review_flags: The modeling citation is provisional and does not yet certify the abstract shape-predicate formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shape compatibility of scalar, vector, matrix, and tensor expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign each array-valued expression \(e\) a shape \(\operatorname{sh}(e)=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\) with positive integer dimensions, and assign each operator \(f\) a compatibility predicate \(C_f\) on operand shapes. An application \(f(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\) is dimension-consistent exactly when \[C_f\bigl(\operatorname{sh}(e_1),\ldots,\operatorname{sh}(e_k)\bigr)=1.\] A dimension mismatch occurs when this predicate is false. Examples covered by the predicate include unequal shapes in nonbroadcast elementwise operations, unequal contracted dimensions in products, and equality constraints between arrays of different shapes. In that case the application does not denote an array or relation under the declared operator semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension mismatch occurs when operand shapes violate an operator's declared rules for elementwise use, contraction, broadcasting, or comparison.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Mismatch

children.title: Cross-Category Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Diagnostics for failures spanning multiple mismatch categories.

assumptions_latex: The model language supplies index, sort, and shape judgments for every expression.
Each diagnostic judgment is decidable on the finite model syntax.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagnostic must report every failed judgment because one expression can simultaneously exhibit index, type, and dimension mismatches.

notation.meaning: index, type, and dimension validity predicates

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Independent static judgments should be accumulated rather than short-circuited so overlapping model-shape errors remain visible.
A source for cross-category diagnostic completeness is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-short-circuiting static diagnosis of overlapping model-shape errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite expression set \(E\), initialize \(R:=\varnothing\). For each \(e\in E\), evaluate the independent predicates \(P_I(e)\), \(P_T(e)\), and \(P_D(e)\), representing index, type, and dimension validity. For every category \(K\in\{I,T,D\}\) with \(P_K(e)=0\), insert \((e,K,w_K)\) into \(R\), where \(w_K\) identifies the offending occurrence and expected declaration. Do not stop after the first failed predicate. Output \(R\); accept the model as shape-consistent exactly when \(R=\varnothing\). This procedure exposes cross-category faults because the same expression may contribute distinct witnesses for several predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check index, type, and dimension judgments independently and report all failures, since one expression may violate several categories at once.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Category Diagnostics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The non-short-circuiting diagnostic algorithm fits the diagnostics leaf and is well specified, but it has no cited source for its completeness and reporting requirements.

children.title: Vacuous Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraints that impose no effective restriction in their instantiated context.

knowledge_statements.title: Vacuous Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vacuity relative to the declared domains or current feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the finite assignment space induced by the declared variable domains, and let \(c:X\to\{0,1\}\) be a constraint predicate. The constraint is globally vacuous when \[\{x\in X:c(x)=1\}=X.\] More generally, relative to a feasible set \(F\subseteq X\) defined by the other constraints, \(c\) is vacuous when \(c(x)=1\) for every \(x\in F\), equivalently \(F\cap\{x:c(x)=1\}=F\). Vacuity can arise from an always-true predicate, an empty generating index set, or a guard that is false on every relevant assignment. Adding a vacuous constraint leaves the feasible set unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is vacuous when it is true for every relevant assignment and therefore removes no point from the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The model has a finite assignment space.
A constraint is interpreted as a Boolean predicate on that space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative to a relevant feasible set \(F\), a constraint is vacuous precisely when it excludes no assignment from \(F\).

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming
source_refs.locator: 8.1 Implicit equalities and redundant constraints p. 99
