children.title: Missing Constraints
children.top_down_role: Absent restrictions required by the intended model semantics.

assumptions_latex: A specification determines an intended feasible set over a finite assignment space.
The implemented model determines a feasible set over the same variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A missing-constraint failure is certified by an implemented-feasible assignment that violates the specification.
review_flags: The cited model-building section is provisional support for intended-versus-implemented formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional criterion for omitted feasibility requirements.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 The concept of a model p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite assignment space, let \(F^\star\subseteq X\) be the feasible set required by the specification, and let \(F\subseteq X\) be the feasible set defined by the implemented constraints. A missing-constraint failure exists when \[F\setminus F^\star\ne\varnothing.\] Any assignment \(x\in F\setminus F^\star\) is a witness: it satisfies every implemented constraint but violates at least one intended requirement. If the only modeling defect is omission of constraints, then \(F^\star\subsetneq F\); however, the witness criterion remains valid when omissions coexist with other errors. Equality \(F=F^\star\) rules out missing constraints at the extensional level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is missing when the implemented model admits an assignment that the intended specification forbids.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Constraints

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 The concept of a model p. 3

children.title: Misdirected Constraints
children.top_down_role: Restrictions applied to unintended variables, indices, or model regions.

assumptions_latex: An intended constraint family and an implemented constraint family are defined on one finite assignment space.
Constraint instances have specified target indices or variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A misdirected constraint is witnessed by a disagreement between intended and implemented predicates caused by applying the condition to the wrong target.

notation.meaning: intended constraint predicate for target i
implemented constraint predicate for target i

review_flags: The cited section is provisional; direct treatment of constraint-target errors is not yet confirmed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraints attached to incorrect indices, variables, guards, or scopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be the intended target set. For each \(i\in I\), let \(c_i^\star:X\to\{0,1\}\) be the specified predicate and let \(\widehat c_i:X\to\{0,1\}\) be the predicate actually imposed on target \(i\). A misdirected constraint exists when an intended condition is instantiated on an incorrect variable, index, guard branch, or scope, producing some \(i\in I\) and \(x\in X\) for which \[\widehat c_i(x)\ne c_i^\star(x).\] Unlike pure omission, the erroneous condition may overconstrain one target while leaving another underconstrained. A pair \((i,x)\) exhibiting the predicate disagreement is an extensional witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is misdirected when an intended condition is imposed on the wrong variable, index, branch, or scope, changing its predicate.
knowledge_statements.title: Misdirected Constraints

children.title: Constraint-Coverage Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Analysis of whether intended model regions receive effective restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The intended and implemented models share a finite assignment space.
Membership in both feasible sets is decidable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two directional set differences distinguish undercoverage from overcoverage; equality certifies extensional coverage.
review_flags: The cited model-building material is provisional; the exhaustive finite-enumeration diagnostic needs direct sourcing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional finite-space diagnosis; localization requires instance-level provenance.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Solving mathematical programming models p. 11

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite assignment space \(X\), an intended feasible set \(F^\star\subseteq X\), and an implemented feasible set \(F\subseteq X\), initialize \(U:=\varnothing\) and \(O:=\varnothing\). For every \(x\in X\), insert \(x\) into \(U\) when \(x\in F\setminus F^\star\), and insert \(x\) into \(O\) when \(x\in F^\star\setminus F\). Output \((U,O)\). The model has exact extensional constraint coverage exactly when \(U=O=\varnothing\). A nonempty \(U\) certifies undercoverage, while a nonempty \(O\) certifies overcoverage. To localize vacuous or misdirected constraints, retain the truth value and provenance of every generated constraint instance at each witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare intended and implemented feasible sets in both directions; witnesses identify undercoverage or overcoverage, while instance provenance helps localize the faulty constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Coverage Diagnostics

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Solving mathematical programming models p. 11

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Semantics Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-objective minimization, with maximization reduced by sign reversal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite feasible set, let \(f^{\star}:F\to\mathbb R\) encode the intended minimization objective, and let \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) be the implemented objective. Their semantics agree exactly when, for all \(x,y\in F\), \[f^{\star}(x)\le f^{\star}(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)\le f(y).\] An objective semantics failure exists when this equivalence fails, or when the implemented objective is undefined on some feasible assignment. Such failures include reversed optimization direction, omitted or incorrect terms, unintended weights, and inconsistent units. A pair \((x,y)\) whose intended and implemented comparisons disagree is a finite certificate of ordering failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective semantics failure changes the intended ranking or ties among feasible assignments, or leaves the objective undefined at a feasible assignment.
assumptions_latex: The intended problem has a finite feasible set.
The implemented objective is defined on every feasible assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective semantics are correct exactly when the implemented ordering of feasible assignments agrees with the intended ordering, including ties.
review_flags: The model-building citation is provisional; an exact source for order-equivalent objective semantics is needed.

assumptions_latex: A finite group acts on the finite assignment space.
The feasible set and objective are invariant under the action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without symmetry breaking, every feasible orbit is represented in full, so search may revisit equivalent assignments.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Model symmetry is invariance of feasibility and objective under a group action; unbroken orbits duplicate equivalent search states.
No supplied locator directly supports finite-domain symmetry breaking.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value or variable symmetries acting on complete finite-domain assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act on an assignment space \(X\). The action is a model symmetry when, for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\), feasibility satisfies \(x\in F\Longleftrightarrow gx\in F\), and the objective satisfies \(f(gx)=f(x)\). The symmetry is unbroken by an added constraint set \(B\subseteq X\) when some feasible orbit \(Gx\) contains more than one member of \(B\), that is, \[|Gx\cap B|>1.\] With no symmetry-breaking constraints, \(B=X\), so every nontrivial feasible orbit remains fully represented. This preserves correctness but can force a search procedure to explore multiple assignments that are equivalent in feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbroken symmetry leaves multiple feasible assignments from the same objective-preserving orbit available to search, creating equivalent search alternatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbroken Model Symmetry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The group-action and residual-orbit criterion is plausible and fits the failure container, but no source is supplied. Moreover, unbroken symmetry creates equivalent alternatives but does not, without assumptions on the search procedure, force their exploration.

knowledge_statements.title: Oversized Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oversizing relative to values participating in intended feasible assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have finite declared domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\), and let \(F^{\star}\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\) be the intended nonempty feasible set. The domain \(D_i\) is oversized relative to the specification when \[\pi_i(F^{\star})\subsetneq D_i,\] where \(\pi_i(F^{\star})=\{x_i:(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in F^{\star}\}\). Every value in \(D_i\setminus\pi_i(F^{\star})\) is semantically impossible but remains initially available unless propagation removes it. Replacing \(D_i\) by any domain containing \(\pi_i(F^{\star})\) preserves the intended feasible set; replacing it by the projection is the tightest unary-domain restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable domain is oversized when it contains values that occur in no intended feasible assignment.
assumptions_latex: Every variable has a finite declared domain.
The intended feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A declared domain \(D_i\) is oversized when \(\pi_i(F^{\star})\subsetneq D_i\).
review_flags: The simple-bounds citation provisionally supports domain restriction; full text must confirm the projection-based characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Global-Constraint Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise decomposition of an all-different constraint can lose domain-consistency deductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let three variables satisfy \(D(x_1)=D(x_2)=D(x_3)=\{1,2\}\). The global constraint \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) is inconsistent because three variables have only two available values. Replace it by the logically equivalent-on-total-assignments decomposition \(x_1
e x_2\), \(x_1
e x_3\), and \(x_2
e x_3\). Every value in every current domain has support in each individual binary disequality, so enforcing arc consistency on the decomposition removes no value and does not detect failure. Thus decomposition-level propagation is strictly weaker than domain consistency on the global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three variables with domains {1,2} violate all-different, but every pairwise disequality remains arc consistent, so the decomposition misses immediate failure.
assumptions_latex: Each binary disequality is propagated independently to arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{AC}(\bigwedge_{i<j}x_i\ne x_j)\) reaches a nonfailed fixpoint, whereas domain consistency for \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) detects inconsistency.

notation.meaning: current finite domain of variable x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Hall-set counterexample for pairwise all-different decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct, variables and propagation levels are explicit, and counterexample is the correct kind for this failure leaf. However, no inspectable source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(C\cup\{r\})=\operatorname{Sol}(C)\).

The baseline and augmented executions visit the same \(q\) search nodes and perform the same baseline work; the augmented execution differs only by invoking the propagator for \(r\) once at each node.
Each invocation of the propagator for \(r\) costs at least \(T\ge 0\) and leaves every domain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{work}(C\cup\{r\})-\operatorname{work}(C)\ge qT\).

notation.meaning: set of solutions of constraint set C
minimum cost of each additional invocation
total propagation and search work in the stipulated execution

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational cost comparison under a fixed execution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical redundancy need not imply computational harmlessness under a fixed propagation execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite-domain model and let \(r\) be logically redundant, so \(\operatorname{Sol}(C\cup\{r\})=\operatorname{Sol}(C)\). Compare a baseline execution for \(C\) with an augmented execution for \(C\cup\{r\}\) that visits the same \(q\) search nodes and performs the same baseline work, except that it additionally invokes the propagator for \(r\) once at each node. If each invocation costs at least \(T\ge 0\) and leaves every domain unchanged, then the augmented execution preserves the solution set and stipulated search tree while adding at least \(qT\) work. Under these conditions, the redundant constraint is computationally harmful whenever this added cost is not offset elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under otherwise identical executions, a redundant constraint that never prunes and is invoked at q nodes adds at least qT propagation work.
knowledge_statements.title: Harmful Constraint Redundancy

children.title: Table Size Explosion
children.top_down_role: Growth in extensional constraint representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Table Size Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive extensional tables can be exponential even for succinct Boolean relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), define the Boolean parity relation \(R_n=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\equiv 0\pmod 2\}\). A positive extensional table represents \(R_n\) by listing every satisfying tuple. Exactly half of the \(2^n\) Boolean tuples have even parity, so the table contains \(2^{n-1}\) rows and stores \(n2^{n-1}\) variable values. The same relation has an intensional parity description of size \(O(n)\); therefore conversion to a positive table incurs exponential space growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even Boolean parity has 2^(n−1) satisfying tuples, so its positive table is exponentially larger than its linear-size intensional description.
assumptions_latex: The extensional representation explicitly lists all satisfying tuples without compression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|R_n|=2^{n-1}\) and the explicit table stores \(n2^{n-1}\) entries.

notation.meaning: even-parity relation on n Boolean variables

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary parity counting establishes the exponential table size

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity count and resulting explicit-table space bound are correct, and complexity_bound fits the leaf. No inspectable citation is supplied for the extensional-representation convention or bound.

children.title: Tuple Enumeration Explosion
children.top_down_role: Growth in explicitly listed allowed or forbidden tuples.

knowledge_statements.title: Tuple Enumeration Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit candidate enumeration is exponential in arity for fixed nontrivial domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be Boolean variables and consider any conversion procedure that constructs an extensional relation by visiting every tuple in \(D(x_1)\times\cdots\times D(x_n)\) and testing a predicate \(P\). Since this Cartesian product has \(2^n\) members, the procedure performs exactly \(2^n\) predicate tests before completing, independently of how many tuples satisfy \(P\). If each test costs at least one unit, its running time is \(\Omega(2^n)\), even when \(P\) has a linear-size intensional description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A converter that tests every Boolean tuple performs 2^n tests, regardless of whether the final accepted table is small.
assumptions_latex: The procedure visits every Cartesian-product tuple and tests \(P\) once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{tests}}=2^n\) and the enumeration time is \(\Omega(2^n)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Cartesian-product cardinality gives the enumeration lower bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the explicitly exhaustive procedure, exactly 2^n predicate tests and an Omega(2^n) lower bound are correct. The record has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Sparse Representation Limits
children.top_down_role: Cases where sparse tuple storage remains prohibitively large.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Representation Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neither allowed-tuple nor forbidden-tuple tables are sparse for balanced relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), let \(R_n\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be the even-parity relation. A positive table for \(R_n\) contains \(|R_n|=2^{n-1}\) tuples, while a negative table listing the complement contains \(|\{0,1\}^n\setminus R_n|=2^{n-1}\) tuples. Consequently, selecting the smaller of allowed-tuple and forbidden-tuple representations cannot produce fewer than \(2^{n-1}\) rows. Sparse extensional storage therefore fails on balanced relations even though parity itself has a succinct intensional specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even parity and its complement each contain half of all Boolean tuples, so neither positive nor negative tables are sparse.
assumptions_latex: Tables list individual tuples without symbolic compression.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: balanced parity relation witnesses failure of both table polarities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The balanced-parity witness correctly shows that neither positive nor negative uncompressed tuple storage is sparse, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Extensional Conversion Blowups
children.top_down_role: Growth caused by converting intensional constraints into tables.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(n\ge 1\).
\(D(x_i)=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Conversion outputs every satisfying tuple explicitly and without compression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\operatorname{Sol}(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n))\rvert=n!\), and the output contains \(n!\) rows and \(n\,n!\) value entries.

notation.meaning: positive integer giving both the number of variables and the domain cardinality
number of permutations of n distinct values

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: permutation counting yields the factorial output bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converting a compact global relation to an explicit positive table can require factorial output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\ge 1\), and let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) each have domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Impose \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). Its satisfying tuples are precisely the permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), so an exact positive extensional conversion must output \(n!\) rows containing \(n\,n!\) value entries. Merely writing this uncompressed output takes \(\Omega(n\,n!)\) time and uses \(\Theta(n\,n!)\) entry storage. Thus such a conversion is not polynomial in \(n\), the size parameter of the compact global-constraint family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An all-different constraint on n variables with the common domain {1,...,n} has n! satisfying tuples, forcing factorial output in an uncompressed positive table.
knowledge_statements.title: Extensional Conversion Blowups

children.title: Automaton State Explosion
children.top_down_role: State growth in automaton representations of sequence constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Automaton State Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Remembering an arbitrary prefix can force exponentially many states in a layered deterministic automaton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge 1\), consider length-\(2m\) Boolean sequences satisfying \(x_{m+i}=x_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). In any deterministic layered automaton recognizing exactly these sequences, two distinct prefixes in \(\{0,1\}^m\) must reach distinct states after layer \(m\), because their required suffixes differ. Thus the middle layer contains at least \(2^m\) reachable states. The relation has only \(m\) equality constraints, yet its deterministic state representation is exponential in \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognizing a duplicated Boolean block requires remembering all 2^m possible first blocks, producing an exponential middle automaton layer.
assumptions_latex: The automaton is deterministic, layered, and recognizes the relation exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|Q_m|\ge 2^m\), where \(Q_m\) is the set of reachable states after reading the first block.

notation.meaning: reachable automaton states at layer m

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinguishable-prefix construction gives the state lower bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinguishable-prefix argument supports the 2^m middle-layer lower bound for exact deterministic layered automata, and complexity_bound fits the leaf. No formal automata citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Decision-Diagram Node Explosion
children.top_down_role: Node growth in diagram-based constraint representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Diagram Node Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A poor variable order makes an equality relation exponentially large as an ordered decision diagram.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f_m(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m)=1\) exactly when \(x_i=y_i\) for all \(i\). Consider a reduced ordered binary decision diagram with order \(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m\). After assigning the \(x\)-variables, each vector \(a\in\{0,1\}^m\) induces the distinct residual function that accepts only \(y=a\). Therefore the diagram has at least \(2^m\) distinct nodes or residual states across that cut. Under the interleaved order \(x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_m,y_m\), the same relation admits \(O(m)\) nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality has exponential ordered-BDD size when all x variables precede all y variables, despite a linear diagram under interleaving.
assumptions_latex: The decision diagram is reduced, ordered, binary, and uses the grouped variable order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{size}_{x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m}(f_m)\ge 2^m\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinct residual functions yield the ordered-BDD lower bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-function lower bound for the grouped ROBDD order and the linear interleaved-order comparison are standard and correctly scoped. An inspectable decision-diagram source locator is absent.

children.title: Representation Conversion Blowups
children.top_down_role: Growth during conversion between automata and decision diagrams.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Conversion Blowups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Determinizing a nondeterministic state representation can require every subset of source states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For infinitely many \(n\), there exists a regular language recognized by a nondeterministic finite automaton with \(n\) states whose minimal equivalent deterministic finite automaton has \(2^n\) states. Consequently, exact subset-construction conversion may create one reachable deterministic state for every subset of the nondeterministic state set. Thus a polynomial-size nondeterministic state-based constraint representation need not admit a polynomial-size deterministic counterpart, and the conversion can require \(\Theta(2^n)\) states and corresponding exponential construction time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Some n-state nondeterministic automata require 2^n states after exact determinization, so representation conversion can be exponentially expansive.
assumptions_latex: The source representation is an \(n\)-state nondeterministic finite automaton.
The target is an exact deterministic finite automaton for the same language.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{states}(A_{\mathrm{det}})=2^n\) is attainable in the worst case.

notation.meaning: deterministic automaton equivalent to the source automaton

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tight exponential determinization phenomenon is correctly stated as a worst-case attainable bound, and failure_boundary fits the conversion leaf. The classical theorem requires an authoritative source with a theorem, section, or page locator.

children.title: Reduction Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structures for which minimization or diagram reduction yields little compression.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State minimization cannot remove blowup when all generated states have distinct continuation behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a determinized automaton have reachable states indexed by subsets \(S\subseteq Q\). If for every distinct \(S,T\subseteq Q\) there exists a continuation word accepted from exactly one of the corresponding states, then those states are pairwise distinguishable. Any equivalent deterministic automaton must therefore retain at least \(2^{|Q|}\) states. State merging, bisimulation-style reduction, and deterministic minimization cannot reduce this family below exponential size because no two reachable subset states recognize the same residual language.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every reachable subset state has a different residual language, exact minimization cannot merge any pair or avoid exponential size.
assumptions_latex: Every subset \(S\subseteq Q\) is reachable.
Distinct subsets induce distinguishable residual languages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{states}(A_{\min})\ge 2^{|Q|}\).

notation.meaning: state set of the source nondeterministic representation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pairwise residual-language distinguishability blocks state merging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Given reachability and pairwise distinguishability of all subset states, the 2^|Q| lower bound for any equivalent deterministic automaton is correct. No minimization or residual-language source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Flattening Expansion
children.top_down_role: Growth in primitive expressions and constraints during flattening.

knowledge_statements.title: Flattening Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flattening without shared subexpressions can duplicate a recursively reused expression exponentially.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_0=z\) and define \(E_k=(E_{k-1}\land a_k)\lor(E_{k-1}\land b_k)\) for \(k\ge1\). A source representation with directed-acyclic-graph sharing stores one copy of each \(E_j\) and has size \(O(k)\). A flattening procedure that recursively inlines every occurrence of \(E_{k-1}\) before introducing primitive constraints produces \(2^k\) occurrences of \(z\) and a syntax tree of size \(\Theta(2^k)\). Hence loss of common-subexpression sharing marks an exponential flattening boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear shared expression becomes an exponential tree when flattening recursively duplicates every reused subexpression.
assumptions_latex: The source shares each \(E_j\), while flattening inlines occurrences without memoization or auxiliary sharing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{size}_{\mathrm{source}}(E_k)=O(k)\) but \(\operatorname{size}_{\mathrm{flat}}(E_k)=\Theta(2^k)\).

notation.meaning: recursively shared Boolean expression at level k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recurrence duplicates the prior expression twice per level

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly distinguishes a shared DAG from recursive inlining and derives the exponential syntax-tree size. The selected failure_boundary kind matches the flattening leaf, but no inspectable flattening or representation source is supplied.

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Proliferation
children.top_down_role: Growth in introduced variables used by flattened representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Proliferation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tuple-indicator flattening may introduce exponentially many auxiliary variables for a compact relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_n\) be the even-parity relation on \(n\) Boolean variables. Consider a flattening that introduces one Boolean indicator \(y_t\) for every satisfying tuple \(t\in R_n\), constrains \(y_t\) to imply the coordinate assignments of \(t\), and requires at least one indicator to hold. Since \(|R_n|=2^{n-1}\), the flattened model introduces \(2^{n-1}\) auxiliary variables and at least that many tuple-selection constraints. Thus tuple-wise reification causes exponential model growth although parity has an \(O(n)\)-size intensional encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One indicator per satisfying parity tuple creates 2^(n−1) auxiliaries, despite parity having a linear-size intensional encoding.
assumptions_latex: Flattening creates a distinct indicator \(y_t\) for every \(t\in R_n\).

notation.meaning: even-parity relation on n Boolean variables
auxiliary indicator associated with tuple t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: parity cardinality determines tuple-indicator count

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the explicitly stipulated one-indicator-per-satisfying-tuple flattening, the auxiliary-variable count is exactly 2^(n-1). The claim is correctly scoped as a failure boundary, but it lacks a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Expansion Feedback Effects
children.top_down_role: Mutual amplification between introduced variables and generated constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Expansion Feedback Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive flattening whose generated constructs trigger further rewrites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_k\) be the number of constraints and variables after rewrite stage \(k\). Suppose every newly generated construct triggers at least \(r\geq 1\) further constructs at the next stage, so that \(s_{k+1}\geq s_k+r^k\) for all \(k\geq 0\). Then \(s_k\geq s_0+k\) when \(r=1\), while \(s_k\geq s_0+(r^k-1)/(r-1)\) when \(r>1\). Thus a semantics-preserving local rewrite system can cause unbounded linear or exponential representation growth before reaching a backend model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When generated constraints trigger the same flattening rules again, model size grows at least linearly and may grow exponentially despite semantic preservation.
assumptions_latex: The rewrite stages preserve the projected solution set.
At least \(r^k\) new constructs are generated at stage \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The flattened representation has size at least \(s_0+k\) for \(r=1\), or \(s_0+(r^k-1)/(r-1)\) for \(r>1\).

notation.meaning: representation size after rewrite stage k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: follows directly from the stated rewrite-growth recurrence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence and resulting linear/geometric lower bounds are correct, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No cited source supports the modeling interpretation that recursive flattening exhibits this feedback pattern.

children.title: Source-Structure Loss
children.top_down_role: Diagnostic difficulty caused by large flattened expansions.

knowledge_statements.title: Source-Structure Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irrecoverability of source decomposition after many-to-one flattening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi\) map structured source models to flat backend models, preserving solutions after projection. If distinct source models \(M_1\neq M_2\) satisfy \(\Phi(M_1)=\Phi(M_2)\), then no reconstruction map \(R\) defined only on flat models can satisfy both \(R(\Phi(M_1))=M_1\) and \(R(\Phi(M_2))=M_2\). Consequently, source-level groupings, names, or global-constraint boundaries erased by \(\Phi\) cannot in general be recovered uniquely from the flattened artifact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A many-to-one flattening transformation can preserve solutions while making erased source-level structure impossible to reconstruct uniquely.
assumptions_latex: The flattening map \(\Phi\) is not injective on the source-model class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No left inverse \(R\) of \(\Phi\) exists on that class.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: noninjective maps have no left inverse
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The noninjectivity argument correctly establishes failure of unique reconstruction, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. A constraint-model translation source is required to support the application to erased source structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported or Decomposed Global Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation loss when a global constraint is replaced by supported primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\geq 3\), let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) all have domain \(\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\). The global constraint \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) is inconsistent by cardinality. If an unsupported backend replaces it with all pairwise disequalities \(x_i\neq x_j\), each individual disequality is arc consistent on these domains, so pairwise propagation alone detects no contradiction. The decomposition is logically equivalent over complete assignments but can be strictly weaker for propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposing an unsupported global constraint may preserve solutions while losing deductions that its dedicated propagator would make immediately.
assumptions_latex: The backend lacks a dedicated \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}\) propagator.
The decomposition uses only pairwise disequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global propagation detects inconsistency, whereas arc consistency on the decomposition does not.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical pigeonhole example for propagation loss under decomposition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pigeonhole example is valid if the global AllDifferent propagator enforces generalized arc consistency, while arc consistency is applied separately to the binary disequalities. That propagation-level qualification and an authoritative source are needed.

knowledge_statements.title: Annotation Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of operational directives during translation to a backend model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent an annotated source model as \((F,a)\), where \(F\) determines feasible assignments and \(a\) specifies an operational directive such as search order or propagation priority. If translation satisfies \(\Phi(F,a_1)=\Phi(F,a_2)\) for distinct annotations \(a_1\neq a_2\), then the backend artifact cannot determine which directive was intended. Although \(\operatorname{Sol}(F)\) may remain unchanged, preservation of the annotated operational behavior is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translation may preserve feasible solutions yet erase search or propagation annotations, leaving the backend unable to reproduce the intended behavior.
assumptions_latex: Annotations \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) do not alter \(\operatorname{Sol}(F)\).
The translation \(\Phi\) does not encode their distinction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The source annotation is not recoverable from \(\Phi(F,a_i)\), and its operational effect need not be preserved.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: information loss follows from annotations being identified by translation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The information-loss formulation is mathematically coherent and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but no backend or modeling-language source supports the claimed annotation-degradation phenomenon.

children.title: Representable Integer Ranges
children.top_down_role: Covers domain values that fit within the integer representation accepted by a target backend.

knowledge_statements.title: Representable Integer Ranges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical range of fixed-width signed and unsigned integer representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a positive width \(w\), the unsigned \(w\)-bit integer range is \(U_w=\{0,1,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). Under two's-complement representation, the signed \(w\)-bit integer range is \(S_w=\{-2^{w-1},-2^{w-1}+1,\ldots,2^{w-1}-1\}\). An integer-valued domain, coefficient, bound, or computed intermediate is representable in the selected format exactly when every value it may assume belongs to the corresponding range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unsigned w-bit integers range from zero to 2^w−1; two's-complement signed integers range from −2^(w−1) to 2^(w−1)−1.
assumptions_latex: The bit width satisfies \(w\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\).
Signed values use two's-complement representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Representability is membership in \(U_w\) or \(S_w\), according to the selected format.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard fixed-width integer representation definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unsigned and two's-complement ranges are correct, and definition is the appropriate kind. A specific authoritative computer-arithmetic reference is still required.

children.title: Backend Integer Capacity Limits
children.top_down_role: Covers solver-specific restrictions on integer magnitudes, domain endpoints, or internal numeric capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Backend Integer Capacity Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity boundary covering stored values and arithmetic intermediates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a backend's exact integer type represent precisely \([B_{\min},B_{\max}]\cap\mathbb{Z}\). Exact translation and evaluation require every variable bound, literal coefficient, objective value, and arithmetic intermediate to remain in this interval. This requirement can fail even when all input literals fit: if \(B_{\max}\geq 1\), the representable assignment \(x=B_{\max}\) makes the intermediate \(x+1=B_{\max}+1\) unrepresentable. Without checked rejection or wider arithmetic, the backend may overflow and cease to implement integer semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All bounds, coefficients, and intermediate results must fit the backend integer type; fitting input literals alone does not prevent overflow.
assumptions_latex: Backend arithmetic is bounded by \([B_{\min},B_{\max}]\cap\mathbb{Z}\).
The intended model uses mathematical integer arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any reachable value outside \([B_{\min},B_{\max}]\) crosses the backend's exact-integer capacity boundary.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bounded integer arithmetic requires operands and intermediates to remain representable
backend-specific source required for concrete capacities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The capacity-boundary example is correct for bounded exact arithmetic, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. Backend overflow, rejection, and intermediate-arithmetic behavior require a specific implementation or format source.

children.title: Range Translation Failures
children.top_down_role: Covers loss, rejection, truncation, or overflow risks when model-level integer domains cross backend limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Range Translation Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overflow introduced by an otherwise bijective domain re-encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the backend range be \([-M,M]\cap\mathbb{Z}\), where \(M>0\), and let a source variable satisfy \(x\in[-M,M]\cap\mathbb{Z}\). Translate it by the bijection \(y=x+M\), intending \(y\in[0,2M]\cap\mathbb{Z}\). Although every source value and the offset \(M\) are representable, the translated upper bound \(2M\) is not. Hence a semantics-preserving mathematical range translation can be unrepresentable in the backend format.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shifting a fully representable source domain can produce translated bounds outside the backend range, even when the shift constant itself fits.
assumptions_latex: The backend represents exactly \([-M,M]\cap\mathbb{Z}\).
The translation explicitly stores the domain of \(y=x+M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The translated bound \(2M>M\) is not backend-representable.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shifted-domain counterexample is arithmetically correct, and counterexample appropriately captures a concrete range-translation failure. No source is cited for the translation failure context.

knowledge_statements.title: Flattened-Model Capability Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate between a flat artifact and backend capabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a flattened model \(M\), let \(R(M)\) contain every required primitive constraint, numeric operation, domain representation, and annotation whose semantics must be preserved. Let \(S_B\) be the capabilities implemented by backend \(B\). A capability mismatch occurs exactly when \(R(M)\nsubseteq S_B\). Translation can proceed correctly only if each unsupported requirement is replaced by an encoding whose projected solution set and required operational semantics equal those of the original requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mismatch exists when the flat model requires a primitive, numeric feature, domain, or annotation the selected backend cannot implement or validly encode.
assumptions_latex: The required features \(R(M)\) and supported features \(S_B\) are specified at a common semantic level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Direct compatibility holds only if \(R(M)\subseteq S_B\); otherwise a validated encoding or rejection is required.

notation.meaning: capabilities required by flattened model M

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: set-inclusion formulation of an interface compatibility condition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-inclusion predicate is coherent, and condition fits this compatibility leaf. A source is needed for the asserted requirements on valid backend encodings and preservation of operational semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Failure Without Global Explanation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain wipeout without a retained derivation of global inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let propagation transform domains \(D^0,D^1,\ldots,D^t\) and end with \(D_i^t=\varnothing\) for some variable \(x_i\). The empty domain proves inconsistency only relative to the soundness of all preceding reductions. If the propagator reports merely \((i,D_i^t=\varnothing)\) and retains neither antecedent constraints nor checkable reduction steps, that report does not itself provide a verifier with a global derivation that the original constraint set \(C\) is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagator's empty-domain event signals failure, but without antecedents or a trace it is not an independently checkable explanation of global infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The propagation reductions are intended to preserve all solutions of \(C\).
No antecedent graph or checkable reduction trace is retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local fact \(D_i^t=\varnothing\) is not, by itself, an independently verifiable certificate that \(C\) is unsatisfiable.

notation.meaning: domain of variable i after propagation stage t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinguishes a solver event from a retained checkable derivation
formal proof-logging source required for promotion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly distinguishes a sound empty-domain event from an independently checkable retained derivation, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. A proof-logging or explanation source is required to substantiate the certificate distinction.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonminimal Unsatisfiable Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset-minimality criterion for explanations drawn from finite constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite constraint set. An unsatisfiable explanation is a subset \(E\subseteq C\) with \(\operatorname{Sol}(E)=\varnothing\). It is subset-minimal if \(\operatorname{Sol}(E\setminus\{c\})\neq\varnothing\) for every \(c\in E\). An unsatisfiable explanation is nonminimal exactly when there exists a proper subset \(E'\subsetneq E\) such that \(\operatorname{Sol}(E')=\varnothing\). Nonminimality concerns redundancy within the explanation and does not invalidate its unsatisfiability claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsatisfiable explanation is nonminimal when some proper subset is already unsatisfiable; it remains valid but contains unnecessary constraints.
assumptions_latex: The constraint set \(C\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonminimality is equivalent to the existence of an unsatisfiable proper subset \(E'\subsetneq E\).

notation.meaning: assignments satisfying every constraint in E

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subset-minimality and nonminimality definitions are correct and equivalent for finite constraint sets, and definition fits the leaf. A specific source for unsatisfiable cores or explanations is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Support Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absence or incompleteness of independently checkable infeasibility evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_B(I,\pi)\in\{0,1\}\) be an independently implemented verifier for backend \(B\), instance \(I\), and purported infeasibility certificate \(\pi\). Certificate support has a gap on a class \(\mathcal{I}\) if some unsatisfiable \(I\in\mathcal{I}\) has no accepted certificate, or if the backend can return UNSAT for \(I\) without producing any \(\pi\) satisfying \(V_B(I,\pi)=1\). In either case, the backend's status cannot always be converted into independently checkable evidence on \(\mathcal{I}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate support is incomplete when some unsatisfiable instances lack an accepted certificate or the backend can report UNSAT without emitting one.
assumptions_latex: Verifier acceptance is sound: \(V_B(I,\pi)=1\) implies that \(I\) is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some UNSAT results on \(\mathcal{I}\) lack independently checkable backend-supported certificates.

notation.meaning: independent certificate verifier for backend B

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes certificate completeness and certificate-production gaps
backend proof-system source required for promotion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record coherently distinguishes certificate-system incompleteness from failure to emit a certificate, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. A proof-system or backend source is required for this certificate-support formulation.
